cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is an open economy?
cards.back: An open economy is one which interacts with other countries through various channels.
cards.quote: An open economy is one which interacts with other countries through various channels.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Name the three ways in which an open economy is linked with other countries.
cards.back:
Output Market: An economy can trade in goods and services with other countries.
Financial Market: Most often an economy can buy financial assets from other countries.
Labour Market: Firms can choose where to locate production and workers to choose where to work.
cards.quote: Output Market: An economy can trade in goods and services with other countries. This widens choice in the sense that consumers and producers can choose between domestic and foreign goods. 2. Financial Market: Most often an economy can buy financial assets from other countries. This gives investors the opportunity to choose between domestic and foreign assets. 3. Labour Market: Firms can choose where to locate production and workers to choose where to work.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: In what does an open economy trade with other nations?
cards.back: An open economy is said to be one that trades with other nations in goods and services and most often, also in financial assets.
cards.quote: Thus, an open economy is said to be one that trades with other nations in goods and services and most often, also in financial assets.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: When Indians buy foreign goods, is the spending a leakage or an injection, and what happens to aggregate demand?
cards.back: When Indians buy foreign goods, this spending escapes as a leakage from the circular flow of income decreasing aggregate demand.
cards.quote: First, when Indians buy foreign goods, this spending escapes as a leakage from the circular flow of income decreasing aggregate demand.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: How do our exports to foreigners enter the circular flow, and what do they do to aggregate demand?
cards.back: Our exports to foreigners enter as an injection into the circular flow, increasing aggregate demand for goods produced within the domestic economy.
cards.quote: Second, our exports to foreigners enter as an injection into the circular flow, increasing aggregate demand for goods produced within the domestic economy.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: The price of one currency in terms of another currency is known as the ____ or simply the exchange rate.
cards.back: The price of one currency in terms of another currency is known as the **foreign exchange rate** or simply the exchange rate.
cards.quote: The price of one currency in terms of another currency is known as the foreign exchange rate or simply the exchange rate.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Define the balance of payments (BoP).
cards.back: The balance of payments (BoP) record the transactions in goods, services and assets between residents of a country with the rest of the world for a specified time period typically a year.
cards.quote: The balance of payments (BoP) record the transactions in goods, services and assets between residents of a country with the rest of the world for a specified time period typically a year.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Name the two main accounts in the BoP.
cards.back:
the current account
the capital account
cards.quote: There are two main accounts in the BoP – the current account and the capital account

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is the Current Account?
cards.back: Current Account is the record of trade in goods and services and transfer payments.
cards.quote: Current Account is the record of trade in goods and services and transfer payments.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Trade in goods includes ____ of goods.
cards.back: Trade in goods includes **exports and imports** of goods.
cards.quote: Trade in goods includes exports and imports of goods.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Trade in services includes ____ transactions.
cards.back: Trade in services includes **factor income and non-factor income** transactions.
cards.quote: Trade in services includes factor income and non-factor income transactions.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What are transfer payments?
cards.back: Transfer payments are the receipts which the residents of a country get for ‘free’, without having to provide any goods or services in return.
cards.quote: Transfer payments are the receipts which the residents of a country get for ‘free’, without having to provide any goods or services in return.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Transfer payments consist of which items?
cards.back:
gifts
remittances
grants
cards.quote: They consist of gifts, remittances and grants.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Current Account is in balance when ____ on current account are equal to the payments on the current account.
cards.back: Current Account is in balance when **receipts** on current account are equal to the payments on the current account.
cards.quote: Current Account is in balance when receipts on current account are equal to the payments on the current account.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Current account surplus vs deficit: the difference on the nation's position.
cards.back: A surplus current account means that the nation is a lender to other countries and a deficit current account means that the nation is a borrower from other countries.
cards.quote: A surplus current account means that the nation is a lender to other countries and a deficit current account means that the nation is a borrower from other countries.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Define Balance of Trade (BOT).
cards.back: Balance of Trade (BOT) is the difference between the value of exports and value of imports of goods of a country in a given period of time.
cards.quote: Balance of Trade (BOT) is the difference between the value of exports and value of imports of goods of a country in a given period of time.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Name the two components of the Balance on Current Account.
cards.back:
Balance of Trade or Trade Balance
Balance on Invisibles
cards.quote: Balance on Current Account has two components: Balance of Trade or Trade Balance Balance on Invisibles

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Export of goods is entered as a ____ item in BOT, whereas import of goods is entered as a ____ item in BOT.
cards.back: Export of goods is entered as a **credit** item in BOT, whereas import of goods is entered as a **debit** item in BOT.
cards.quote: Export of goods is entered as a credit item in BOT, whereas import of goods is entered as a debit item in BOT.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Trade surplus vs trade deficit: the difference on exports and imports of goods.
cards.back: Surplus BOT or Trade surplus will arise if country exports more goods than what it imports. Whereas, Deficit BOT or Trade deficit will arise if a country imports more goods than what it exports.
cards.quote: Surplus BOT or Trade surplus will arise if country exports more goods than what it imports. Whereas, Deficit BOT or Trade deficit will arise if a country imports more goods than what it exports.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Define Net Invisibles.
cards.back: Net Invisibles is the difference between the value of exports and value of imports of invisibles of a country in a given period of time.
cards.quote: Net Invisibles is the difference between the value of exports and value of imports of invisibles of a country in a given period of time.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What do invisibles include?
cards.back:
services
transfers
flows of income
cards.quote: Invisibles include services, transfers and flows of income that take place between different countries.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What does factor income include?
cards.back: Factor income includes net international earnings on factors of production (like labour, land and capital).
cards.quote: Factor income includes net international earnings on factors of production (like labour, land and capital).

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is non-factor income?
cards.back: Non-factor income is net sale of service products like shipping, banking, tourism, software services, etc.
cards.quote: Non-factor income is net sale of service products like shipping, banking, tourism, software services, etc.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What does the Capital Account record?
cards.back: Capital Account records all international transactions of assets.
cards.quote: Capital Account records all international transactions of assets.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is an asset?
cards.back: An asset is any one of the forms in which wealth can be held, for example: money, stocks, bonds, Government debt, etc.
cards.quote: An asset is any one of the forms in which wealth can be held, for example: money, stocks, bonds, Government debt, etc.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Purchase of assets is a ____ item on the capital account.
cards.back: Purchase of assets is a **debit** item on the capital account.
cards.quote: Purchase of assets is a debit item on the capital account.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Example: an Indian buys a UK car company. How does it enter the capital account?
cards.back: it enters capital account transactions as a debit item (as foreign exchange is flowing out of India)
cards.quote: If an Indian buys a UK Car Company, it enters capital account transactions as a debit item (as foreign exchange is flowing out of India).

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Sale of assets like sale of share of an Indian company to a Chinese customer is a ____ item on the capital account.
cards.back: Sale of assets like sale of share of an Indian company to a Chinese customer is a credit item on the capital account.
cards.quote: Sale of assets like sale of share of an Indian company to a Chinese customer is a credit item on the capital account.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Name the items which are a part of capital account transactions.
cards.back:
Foreign Direct Investments (FDIs)
Foreign Institutional Investments (FIIs)
external borrowings
assistance
cards.quote: These items are Foreign Direct Investments (FDIs), Foreign Institutional Investments (FIIs), external borrowings and assistance.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: When is the capital account in balance?
cards.back: Capital account is in balance when capital inflows (like receipt of loans from abroad, sale of assets or shares in foreign companies) are equal to capital outflows (like repayment of loans, purchase of assets or shares in foreign countries).
cards.quote: Capital account is in balance when capital inflows (like receipt of loans from abroad, sale of assets or shares in foreign companies) are equal to capital outflows (like repayment of loans, purchase of assets or shares in foreign countries).

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Capital account surplus vs deficit: the difference on capital inflows and outflows.
cards.back: Surplus in capital account arises when capital inflows are greater than capital outflows, whereas deficit in capital account arises when capital inflows are lesser than capital outflows.
cards.quote: Surplus in capital account arises when capital inflows are greater than capital outflows, whereas deficit in capital account arises when capital inflows are lesser than capital outflows.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Any current account deficit must be financed by a ____, that is, a net capital inflow.
cards.back: Any current account deficit must be financed by a capital account surplus, that is, a net capital inflow.
cards.quote: Any current account deficit must be financed by a capital account surplus, that is, a net capital inflow.

source.section: 6.1.3 Balance of Payments Surplus and Deficit

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Formula: balance of payments equilibrium (current account and capital account).
cards.back:
Current account + Capital account ≡ 0
In this case, in which a country is said to be in balance of payments equilibrium, the current account deficit is financed entirely by international lending without any reserve movements.
cards.quote: Current account + Capital account ≡ 0 In this case, in which a country is said to be in balance of payments equilibrium, the current account deficit is financed entirely by international lending without any reserve movements.

source.section: 6.1.3 Balance of Payments Surplus and Deficit

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is an official reserve sale?
cards.back: The reserve bank sells foreign exchange when there is a deficit. This is called official reserve sale.
cards.quote: The reserve bank sells foreign exchange when there is a deficit. This is called official reserve sale.

source.section: 6.1.3 Balance of Payments Surplus and Deficit

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: The decrease (increase) in official reserves is called the ____.
cards.back: The decrease (increase) in official reserves is called the **overall balance of payments deficit (surplus)**.
cards.quote: The decrease (increase) in official reserves is called the overall balance of payments deficit (surplus).

source.section: 6.1.3 Balance of Payments Surplus and Deficit

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: We note that official reserve transactions are more relevant under a regime of ____ than when exchange rates are floating.
cards.back: We note that official reserve transactions are more relevant under a regime of **fixed exchange rates** than when exchange rates are floating.
cards.quote: We note that official reserve transactions are more relevant under a regime of fixed exchange rates than when exchange rates are floating.

source.section: 6.1.3 Balance of Payments Surplus and Deficit

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: When are international economic transactions called autonomous?
cards.back: International economic transactions are called autonomous when transactions are made due to some reason other than to bridge the gap in the balance of payments, that is, when they are independent of the state of BoP.
cards.quote: International economic transactions are called autonomous when transactions are made due to some reason other than to bridge the gap in the balance of payments, that is, when they are independent of the state of BoP.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: In the BoP, are autonomous transactions the 'above the line' or the 'below the line' items?
cards.back: International economic transactions are called autonomous when transactions are made due to some reason other than to bridge the gap in the balance of payments, that is, when they are independent of the state of BoP. One reason could be to earn profit. These items are called ‘above the line’ items in the BoP.
cards.quote: International economic transactions are called autonomous when transactions are made due to some reason other than to bridge the gap in the balance of payments, that is, when they are independent of the state of BoP. One reason could be to earn profit. These items are called ‘above the line’ items in the BoP.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: The balance of payments is said to be in surplus (deficit) if ____ are greater (less) than ____.
cards.back: The balance of payments is said to be in surplus (deficit) if **autonomous receipts** are greater (less) than **autonomous payments**.
cards.quote: The balance of payments is said to be in surplus (deficit) if autonomous receipts are greater (less) than autonomous payments.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What are accommodating transactions?
cards.back: Accommodating transactions (termed ‘below the line’ items), on the other hand, are determined by the gap in the balance of payments, that is, whether there is a deficit or surplus in the balance of payments.
cards.quote: Accommodating transactions (termed ‘below the line’ items), on the other hand, are determined by the gap in the balance of payments, that is, whether there is a deficit or surplus in the balance of payments.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Which transactions are seen as the accommodating item in the BoP?
cards.back: Since the official reserve transactions are made to bridge the gap in the BoP, they are seen as the accommodating item in the BoP (all others being autonomous).
cards.quote: Since the official reserve transactions are made to bridge the gap in the BoP, they are seen as the accommodating item in the BoP (all others being autonomous).

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is the 'errors and omissions' element of the BoP?
cards.back: It is difficult to record all international transactions accurately. Thus, we have a third element of BoP (apart from the current and capital accounts) called errors and omissions which reflects this.
cards.quote: It is difficult to record all international transactions accurately. Thus, we have a third element of BoP (apart from the current and capital accounts) called errors and omissions which reflects this.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: BoP deficit, balanced BoP and BoP surplus: the overall balance and reserve change in each.
cards.back:
BoP Deficit Overall Balance < 0 Reserve Change > 0
Balanced BoP Overall Balance = 0 Reserve Change = 0
BoP Surplus Overall Balance > 0 Reserve Change < 0
cards.quote: BoP Deficit Overall Balance < 0 Reserve Change > 0 Balanced BoP Overall Balance = 0 Reserve Change = 0 BoP Surplus Overall Balance > 0 Reserve Change < 0

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is the foreign exchange market?
cards.back: The market in which national currencies are traded for one another is known as the foreign exchange market.
cards.quote: The market in which national currencies are traded for one another is known as the foreign exchange market.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Name the major participants in the foreign exchange market.
cards.back:
commercial banks
foreign exchange brokers
other authorised dealers and monetary authorities
cards.quote: The major participants in the foreign exchange market are commercial banks, foreign exchange brokers and other authorised dealers and monetary authorities.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Define the foreign exchange rate (forex rate).
cards.back: Foreign Exchange Rate (also called Forex Rate) is the price of one currency in terms of another. It links the currencies of different countries and enables comparison of international costs and prices.
cards.quote: Foreign Exchange Rate (also called Forex Rate) is the price of one currency in terms of another. It links the currencies of different countries and enables comparison of international costs and prices.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Name the reasons why people demand foreign exchange.
cards.back:
they want to purchase goods and services from other countries
they want to send gifts abroad
they want to purchase financial assets of a certain country
cards.quote: People demand foreign exchange because: they want to purchase goods and services from other countries; they want to send gifts abroad; and, they want to purchase financial assets of a certain country.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What happens to the demand for foreign exchange when its price rises?
cards.back: A rise in price of foreign exchange will increase the cost (in terms of rupees) of purchasing a foreign good. This reduces demand for imports and hence demand for foreign exchange also decreases, other things remaining constant.
cards.quote: A rise in price of foreign exchange will increase the cost (in terms of rupees) of purchasing a foreign good. This reduces demand for imports and hence demand for foreign exchange also decreases, other things remaining constant.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Name the reasons why foreign currency flows into the home country.
cards.back:
exports by a country lead to the purchase of its domestic goods and services by the foreigners
foreigners send gifts or make transfers
the assets of a home country are bought by the foreigners
cards.quote: Foreign currency flows into the home country due to the following reasons: exports by a country lead to the purchase of its domestic goods and services by the foreigners; foreigners send gifts or make transfers; and, the assets of a home country are bought by the foreigners.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: A rise in the price of foreign exchange: what happens to the foreigner’s cost of buying Indian products?
cards.back: A rise in price of foreign exchange will reduce the foreigner’s cost (in terms of USD) while purchasing products from India, other things remaining constant.
cards.quote: A rise in price of foreign exchange will reduce the foreigner’s cost (in terms of USD) while purchasing products from India, other things remaining constant.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Name the methods by which a currency's exchange rate can be determined.
cards.back:
Flexible Exchange Rate
Fixed Exchange Rate
Managed Floating Exchange Rate
cards.quote: Different countries have different methods of determining their currency’s exchange rate. It can be determined through Flexible Exchange Rate, Fixed Exchange Rate or Managed Floating Exchange Rate.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is a flexible exchange rate?
cards.back: This exchange rate is determined by the market forces of demand and supply. It is also known as Floating Exchange Rate.
cards.quote: This exchange rate is determined by the market forces of demand and supply. It is also known as Floating Exchange Rate.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: In a flexible exchange rate system, where is the exchange rate determined?
cards.back: The exchange rate is determined where the demand curve intersects with the supply curve
cards.quote: the exchange rate is determined where the demand curve intersects with the supply curve

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: In a completely flexible exchange rate system, what do the Central banks do in the foreign exchange market?
cards.back: In a completely flexible system, the Central banks do not intervene in the foreign exchange market.
cards.quote: In a completely flexible system, the Central banks do not intervene in the foreign exchange market.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is the rise in the price of foreign currency in terms of domestic currency called?
cards.back: This is called Depreciation of domestic currency (rupees) in terms of foreign currency (dollars).
cards.quote: This is called Depreciation of domestic currency (rupees) in terms of foreign currency (dollars).

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is it called when the price of domestic currency in terms of foreign currency increases (flexible regime)?
cards.back: Similarly, in a flexible exchange rate regime, when the price of domestic currency (rupees) in terms of foreign currency (dollars) increases, it is called Appreciation of the domestic currency (rupees) in terms of foreign currency (dollars).
cards.quote: Similarly, in a flexible exchange rate regime, when the price of domestic currency (rupees) in terms of foreign currency (dollars) increases, it is called Appreciation of the domestic currency (rupees) in terms of foreign currency (dollars).

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: How does speculation affect exchange rates?
cards.back: If Indians believe that British pound is going to increase in value relative to the rupee, they will want to hold pounds. Thus exchange rates also get affected when people hold foreign exchange on the expectation that they can make gains from the appreciation of the currency.
cards.quote: If Indians believe that British pound is going to increase in value relative to the rupee, they will want to hold pounds. Thus exchange rates also get affected when people hold foreign exchange on the expectation that they can make gains from the appreciation of the currency.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: If investors expect the pound to appreciate, how does this expectation affect the rupee-pound rate now?
cards.back: This expectation would increase the demand for pounds and cause the rupee-pound exchange rate to increase in the present, making the beliefs self-fulfilling.
cards.quote: This expectation would increase the demand for pounds and cause the rupee-pound exchange rate to increase in the present, making the beliefs self-fulfilling.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is the interest rate differential?
cards.back: the interest rate differential i.e. the difference between interest rates between countries.
cards.quote: In the short run, another factor that is important in determining exchange rate movements is the interest rate differential i.e. the difference between interest rates between countries.

source.section: Interest Rates and the Exchange Rate

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is the effect of a rise in the interest rates at home on the domestic currency?
cards.back: A rise in the interest rates at home often leads to an appreciation of the domestic currency.
cards.quote: Thus, a rise in the interest rates at home often leads to an appreciation of the domestic currency.

source.section: Interest Rates and the Exchange Rate

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: When imports increase, the demand curve for foreign exchange shifts to the ____. There is a ____ of the domestic currency.
cards.back: When imports increase, the demand curve for foreign exchange shifts to the **right**. There is a **depreciation** of the domestic currency.
cards.quote: When imports increase, the demand curve for foreign exchange shifts to the right. There is a depreciation of the domestic currency.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What happens to the currency of a country whose aggregate demand grows faster than the rest of the world’s?
cards.back: In general, other things remaining equal, a country whose aggregate demand grows faster than the rest of the world’s normally finds its currency depreciating because its imports grow faster than its exports.
cards.quote: In general, other things remaining equal, a country whose aggregate demand grows faster than the rest of the world’s normally finds its currency depreciating because its imports grow faster than its exports.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is the purchasing power parity (PPP) theory used for?
cards.back: The purchasing Power (PPP) theory is used to make long-run predictions about exchange rates in a flexible exchange rate system.
cards.quote: The purchasing Power (PPP) theory is used to make long-run predictions about exchange rates in a flexible exchange rate system.

source.section: Exchange Rates in the Long Run

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What does the PPP theory say exchange rates should eventually do?
cards.back: exchange rates should eventually adjust so that the same product costs the same whether measured in rupees in India, or dollars in the US, yen in Japan and so on, except for differences in transportation.
cards.quote: exchange rates should eventually adjust so that the same product costs the same whether measured in rupees in India, or dollars in the US, yen in Japan and so on, except for differences in transportation.

source.section: Exchange Rates in the Long Run

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Over the long run, therefore, exchange rates between any two national currencies adjust to reflect differences in the ____ in the two countries.
cards.back: Over the long run, therefore, exchange rates between any two national currencies adjust to reflect differences in the **price levels** in the two countries.
cards.quote: Over the long run, therefore, exchange rates between any two national currencies adjust to reflect differences in the price levels in the two countries.

source.section: Exchange Rates in the Long Run

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: PPP example: a shirt costs $8 in the US and Rs 400 in India. What should the rupee-dollar exchange rate be?
cards.back: the rupee-dollar exchange rate should be Rs 50
cards.quote: If a shirt costs $8 in the US and Rs 400 in India, the rupee-dollar exchange rate should be Rs 50.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is a fixed exchange rate system?
cards.back: In this exchange rate system, the Government fixes the exchange rate at a particular level.
cards.quote: In this exchange rate system, the Government fixes the exchange rate at a particular level.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Under a fixed rate with excess demand for dollars, what happens if the government fails to withdraw dollars from its holdings?
cards.back: To meet this excess demand for dollars, the government would have to withdraw dollars from its past holdings of dollars. If it fails to do so, a black market for dollars may come up.
cards.quote: To meet this excess demand for dollars, the government would have to withdraw dollars from its past holdings of dollars. If it fails to do so, a black market for dollars may come up.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is devaluation?
cards.back: In a fixed exchange rate system, when some government action increases the exchange rate (thereby, making domestic currency cheaper) is called Devaluation.
cards.quote: In a fixed exchange rate system, when some government action increases the exchange rate (thereby, making domestic currency cheaper) is called Devaluation.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: When does revaluation occur?
cards.back: On the other hand, a Revaluation is said to occur, when the Government decreases the exchange rate (thereby, making domestic currency costlier) in a fixed exchange rate system.
cards.quote: On the other hand, a Revaluation is said to occur, when the Government decreases the exchange rate (thereby, making domestic currency costlier) in a fixed exchange rate system.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is the main feature of the fixed exchange rate system?
cards.back: The main feature of the fixed exchange rate system is that there must be credibility that the government will be able to maintain the exchange rate at the level specified.
cards.quote: The main feature of the fixed exchange rate system is that there must be credibility that the government will be able to maintain the exchange rate at the level specified.

source.section: 6.2.3 Merits and Demerits of Flexible and Fixed Exchange Rate Systems

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is a speculative attack on a currency?
cards.back: When this belief translates into aggressive buying of one currency thereby forcing the government to devalue, it is said to constitute a speculative attack on a currency.
cards.quote: When this belief translates into aggressive buying of one currency thereby forcing the government to devalue, it is said to constitute a speculative attack on a currency.

source.section: 6.2.3 Merits and Demerits of Flexible and Fixed Exchange Rate Systems

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Name the merits of the flexible exchange rate system.
cards.back:
gives the government more flexibility and they do not need to maintain large stocks of foreign exchange reserves
movements in the exchange rate automatically take care of the surpluses and deficits in the BoP
countries gain independence in conducting their monetary policies
cards.quote: The flexible exchange rate system gives the government more flexibility and they do not need to maintain large stocks of foreign exchange reserves. The major advantage of flexible exchange rates is that movements in the exchange rate automatically take care of the surpluses and deficits in the BoP. Also, countries gain independence in conducting their monetary policies, since they do not have to intervene to maintain exchange rate which are automatically taken care of by the market.

source.section: 6.2.3 Merits and Demerits of Flexible and Fixed Exchange Rate Systems

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is a managed floating exchange rate system?
cards.back: Without any formal international agreement, the world has moved on to what can be best described as a managed floating exchange rate system. It is a mixture of a flexible exchange rate system (the float part) and a fixed rate system (the managed part).
cards.quote: Without any formal international agreement, the world has moved on to what can be best described as a managed floating exchange rate system. It is a mixture of a flexible exchange rate system (the float part) and a fixed rate system (the managed part).

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: How do central banks act under managed floating (also called dirty floating)?
cards.back: Under this system, also called dirty floating, central banks intervene to buy and sell foreign currencies in an attempt to moderate exchange rate movements whenever they feel that such actions are appropriate.
cards.quote: Under this system, also called dirty floating, central banks intervene to buy and sell foreign currencies in an attempt to moderate exchange rate movements whenever they feel that such actions are appropriate.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Under managed floating, what is true of official reserve transactions?
cards.back: Under this system, also called dirty floating, central banks intervene to buy and sell foreign currencies in an attempt to moderate exchange rate movements whenever they feel that such actions are appropriate. Official reserve transactions are, therefore, not equal to zero.
cards.quote: Under this system, also called dirty floating, central banks intervene to buy and sell foreign currencies in an attempt to moderate exchange rate movements whenever they feel that such actions are appropriate. Official reserve transactions are, therefore, not equal to zero.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Development Experiences of India: A Comparison with Neighbours
cards.front: When did India and Pakistan become independent, and when was the People's Republic of China established?
cards.back: While India and Pakistan became independent nations in 1947, People's Republic of China was established in 1949.
cards.quote: While India and Pakistan became independent nations in 1947, People's Republic of China was established in 1949.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Development Experiences of India: A Comparison with Neighbours
cards.front: When did India, Pakistan and China announce their first Five Year Plans?
cards.back: While India announced its first Five Year Plan for 1951–56, Pakistan announced its first five year plan, now called the Medium Term Development Plan, in 1956. China announced its First Five Year Plan in 1953.
cards.quote: While India announced its first Five Year Plan for 1951–56, Pakistan announced its first five year plan, now called the Medium Term Development Plan, in 1956. China announced its First Five Year Plan in 1953.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Development Experiences of India: A Comparison with Neighbours
cards.front: Until ____, India has been following Five Year Plan-based development model.
cards.back: Until March 2017, India has been following Five Year Plan-based development model.
cards.quote: Until March 2017, India has been following Five Year Plan-based development model.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Development Experiences of India: A Comparison with Neighbours
cards.front: What similar strategies did India and Pakistan adopt for development, according to NCERT?
cards.back:
A large public sector; more public spending on social development
India and Pakistan adopted similar strategies, such as creating a large public sector and raising public expenditure on social development.

cards.subject: economics

They were allowed to keep all income from the land after paying stipulated taxes. In the later phase, reforms were initiated in the industrial sector.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Development Experiences of India: A Comparison with Neighbours
cards.front: India, Pakistan and China have similar physical endowments but totally different ____.
cards.back: India, Pakistan and China have similar physical endowments but totally different political systems.
cards.quote: India, Pakistan and China have similar physical endowments but totally different political systems.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Development Experiences of India: A Comparison with Neighbours
cards.front: All the three countries follow the similar ____ pattern of development.
cards.back: All the three countries follow the similar planned pattern of development.
cards.quote: All the three countries follow the similar planned pattern of development.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Development Experiences of India: A Comparison with Neighbours
cards.front: China introduced structural reforms on its ____ while they were forced upon India and Pakistan by international agencies.
cards.back: China introduced structural reforms on its own initiative while they were forced upon India and Pakistan by international agencies.
cards.quote: China introduced structural reforms on its own initiative while they were forced upon India and Pakistan by international agencies.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Development Experiences of India: A Comparison with Neighbours
cards.front: Even after seventy years of planned development, majority of the workforce in all the countries depends on ____. The dependency is greater in ____.
cards.back: Even after seventy years of planned development, majority of the workforce in all the countries depends on agriculture. The dependency is greater in India.
cards.quote: Even after seventy years of planned development, majority of the workforce in all the countries depends on agriculture. The dependency is greater in India.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Development Experiences of India: A Comparison with Neighbours
cards.front: How does the sectoral shift in China differ from that in India and Pakistan?
cards.back:
China: via manufacturing; India and Pakistan: directly to services
China has followed the classical development pattern of gradual shift from agriculture to manufacturing and then to services, India and Pakistan’s shift has been directly from agriculture to service sector.
cards.quote: China has followed the classical development pattern of gradual shift from agriculture to manufacturing and then to services, India and Pakistan’s shift has been directly from agriculture to service sector.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Development Experiences of India: A Comparison with Neighbours
cards.front: Which sector of China has maintained a high growth rate, unlike in India and Pakistan?
cards.back:
China's industrial sector
China’s industrial sector has maintained a high growth rate while it is not so in both India and Pakistan.
cards.quote: China’s industrial sector has maintained a high growth rate while it is not so in both India and Pakistan.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Development Experiences of India: A Comparison with Neighbours
cards.front: To what are China's improvements in human development indicators attributed?
cards.back:
The strategies China adopted in the pre-reform period
China is ahead of India and Pakistan on many human development indicators. However these improvements were attributed not to the reform process but the strategies that China adopted in the pre-reform period.
cards.quote: China is ahead of India and Pakistan on many human development indicators. However these improvements were attributed not to the reform process but the strategies that China adopted in the pre-reform period.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Development Experiences of India: A Comparison with Neighbours
cards.front: While assessing the developmental indicators, one also has to consider the ____.
cards.back: While assessing the developmental indicators, one also has to consider the liberty indicators.
cards.quote: While assessing the developmental indicators, one also has to consider the liberty indicators.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What had India achieved after forty years of planned development, and what led to the 1991 reforms?
cards.back: After forty years of planned development, India has been able to achieve a strong industrial base and became self-sufficient in the production of food grains. Nevertheless, a major segment of the population continues to depend on agriculture for its livelihood. In 1991, a crisis in the balance of payments led to the introduction of economic reforms in the country.
cards.quote: After forty years of planned development, India has been able to achieve a strong industrial base and became self-sufficient in the production of food grains. Nevertheless, a major segment of the population continues to depend on agriculture for its livelihood. In 1991, a crisis in the balance of payments led to the introduction of economic reforms in the country.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: In 1991, foreign exchange reserves were not sufficient for imports for how long?
cards.back: foreign exchange reserves, which we generally maintain to import petroleum and other important items, dropped to levels that were not sufficient for even a fortnight.
cards.quote: foreign exchange reserves, which we generally maintain to import petroleum and other important items, dropped to levels that were not sufficient for even a fortnight.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: The origin of the financial crisis can be traced to what?
cards.back: The origin of the financial crisis can be traced from the inefficient management of the Indian economy in the 1980s.
cards.quote: The origin of the financial crisis can be traced from the inefficient management of the Indian economy in the 1980s.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What happened to government expenditure and revenue in the late 1980s?
cards.back: In the late 1980s, government expenditure began to exceed its revenue by such large margins that meeting the expenditure through borrowings became unsustainable.
cards.quote: In the late 1980s, government expenditure began to exceed its revenue by such large margins that meeting the expenditure through borrowings became unsustainable.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: From which two institutions did India get a loan in 1991, and how much?
cards.back: India approached the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD), popularly known as World Bank and the International Monetary Fund (IMF), and received $7 billion as loan to manage the crisis.
cards.quote: India approached the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD), popularly known as World Bank and the International Monetary Fund (IMF), and received $7 billion as loan to manage the crisis.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What did the World Bank and IMF expect from India for availing the loan?
cards.back: For availing the loan, these international agencies expected India to liberalise and open up the economy by removing restrictions on the private sector, reduce the role of the government in many areas and remove trade restrictions between India and other countries.
cards.quote: For availing the loan, these international agencies expected India to liberalise and open up the economy by removing restrictions on the private sector, reduce the role of the government in many areas and remove trade restrictions between India and other countries.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: India agreed to the conditionalities of World Bank and IMF and announced the ____ (NEP).
cards.back: India agreed to the conditionalities of World Bank and IMF and announced the New Economic Policy (NEP).
cards.quote: India agreed to the conditionalities of World Bank and IMF and announced the New Economic Policy (NEP).

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Types: the two groups into which NEP policies are broadly classified.
cards.back: the stabilisation measures and the structural reform measures
cards.quote: This set of policies can broadly be classified into two groups: the stabilisation measures and the structural reform measures.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What are stabilisation measures?
cards.back: Stabilisation measures are short-term measures, intended to correct some of the weaknesses that have developed in the balance of payments and to bring inflation under control.
cards.quote: Stabilisation measures are short-term measures, intended to correct some of the weaknesses that have developed in the balance of payments and to bring inflation under control.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What are structural reform policies?
cards.back: structural reform policies are long-term measures, aimed at improving the efficiency of the economy and increasing its international competitiveness by removing the rigidities in various segments of the Indian economy.
cards.quote: structural reform policies are long-term measures, aimed at improving the efficiency of the economy and increasing its international competitiveness by removing the rigidities in various segments of the Indian economy.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Types: the three heads under which the NEP policies fall.
cards.back: liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation
cards.quote: viz., liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What was liberalisation introduced to do?
cards.back: Liberalisation was introduced to put an end to these restrictions and open various sectors of the economy.
cards.quote: Liberalisation was introduced to put an end to these restrictions and open various sectors of the economy.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Name the five areas that received greater attention in and after 1991.
cards.back:
industrial sector
financial sector
tax reforms
foreign exchange markets
trade and investment sectors
cards.quote: the industrial sector, financial sector, tax reforms, foreign exchange markets and trade and investment sectors

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Name the four ways regulatory mechanisms were enforced on the industrial sector.
cards.back:
industrial licensing under which every entrepreneur had to get permission from government officials to start a firm, close a firm or decide the amount of goods that could be produced
private sector was not allowed in many industries
some goods could be produced only in small-scale industries
controls on price fixation and distribution of selected industrial products
cards.quote: industrial licensing under which every entrepreneur had to get permission from government officials to start a firm, close a firm or decide the amount of goods that could be produced (ii) private sector was not allowed in many industries (iii) some goods could be produced only in small-scale industries, and (iv) controls on price fixation and distribution of selected industrial products.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: For which product categories was industrial licensing retained after 1991?
cards.back:
alcohol
cigarettes
hazardous chemicals
industrial explosives
electronics
aerospace
drugs and pharmaceuticals
cards.quote: alcohol, cigarettes, hazardous chemicals, industrial explosives, electronics, aerospace and drugs and pharmaceuticals

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Which industries are now reserved for the public sector?
cards.back: The only industries which are now reserved for the public sector are a part of atomic energy generation and some core activities in railway transport.
cards.quote: The only industries which are now reserved for the public sector are a part of atomic energy generation and some core activities in railway transport.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What does the financial sector include?
cards.back: Financial sector includes financial institutions, such as commercial banks, investment banks, stock exchange operations and foreign exchange market.
cards.quote: Financial sector includes financial institutions, such as commercial banks, investment banks, stock exchange operations and foreign exchange market.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: One of the major aims of financial sector reforms is to reduce the role of RBI from ____ to ____ of financial sector.
cards.back: One of the major aims of financial sector reforms is to reduce the role of RBI from regulator to facilitator of financial sector.
cards.quote: One of the major aims of financial sector reforms is to reduce the role of RBI from regulator to facilitator of financial sector.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What did the reform policies lead to in banking?
cards.back: The reform policies led to the establishment of private sector banks, Indian as well as foreign.
cards.quote: The reform policies led to the establishment of private sector banks, Indian as well as foreign.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Foreign investment limit in banks was raised to around ____.
cards.back: Foreign investment limit in banks was raised to around 74 per cent.
cards.quote: Foreign investment limit in banks was raised to around 74 per cent.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What are tax reforms?
cards.back: Tax reforms are concerned with the reforms in the government's taxation and public expenditure policies, which are collectively known as its fiscal policy.
cards.quote: Tax reforms are concerned with the reforms in the government's taxation and public expenditure policies, which are collectively known as its fiscal policy.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Types of taxes.
cards.back: direct and indirect
cards.quote: There are two types of taxes: direct and indirect.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What are direct taxes?
cards.back: Direct taxes consist of taxes on incomes of individuals, as well as, profits of business enterprises.
cards.quote: Direct taxes consist of taxes on incomes of individuals, as well as, profits of business enterprises.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What are indirect taxes?
cards.back: indirect taxes, taxes levied on goods and services
cards.quote: indirect taxes, taxes levied on goods and services

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What rates of income tax, per NCERT, encourage savings and voluntary disclosure of income?
cards.back: It is now widely accepted that moderate rates of income tax encourage savings and voluntary disclosure of income.
cards.quote: It is now widely accepted that moderate rates of income tax encourage savings and voluntary disclosure of income.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What happened in 2016 that led to the introduction of GST in India?
cards.back: In the year 2016, Indian constitution was amended to empower state governments and union Government to come out with laws to impose Goods and Services Tax. This has led to introduction of GST in India.
cards.quote: In the year 2016, Indian constitution was amended to empower state governments and union Government to come out with laws to impose Goods and Services Tax. This has led to introduction of GST in India.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Name the expected benefits of GST.
cards.back:
generate additional revenue for the government
reduce tax evasion
create 'one nation, one tax and one market'
cards.quote: This is expected to generate additional revenue for the government, reduce tax evasion and create 'one nation, one tax and one market'.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What immediate step was taken in 1991 to resolve the balance of payments crisis?
cards.back: In 1991, as an immediate measure to resolve the balance of payments crisis, the rupee was devalued against foreign currencies. This led to an increase in the inflow of foreign exchange.
cards.quote: In 1991, as an immediate measure to resolve the balance of payments crisis, the rupee was devalued against foreign currencies. This led to an increase in the inflow of foreign exchange.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Now, more often than not, markets determine exchange rates based on the ____ of foreign exchange.
cards.back: Now, more often than not, markets determine exchange rates based on the demand and supply of foreign exchange.
cards.quote: Now, more often than not, markets determine exchange rates based on the demand and supply of foreign exchange.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Why was liberalisation of the trade and investment regime initiated?
cards.back: Liberalisation of trade and investment regime was initiated to increase international competitiveness of industrial production and also foreign investments and technology into the economy.
cards.quote: Liberalisation of trade and investment regime was initiated to increase international competitiveness of industrial production and also foreign investments and technology into the economy.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What regime was India following to protect domestic industries?
cards.back: In order to protect domestic industries, India was following a regime of quantitative restrictions on imports.
cards.quote: In order to protect domestic industries, India was following a regime of quantitative restrictions on imports.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Name the three aims of the trade policy reforms.
cards.back:
dismantling of quantitative restrictions on imports and exports
reduction of tariff rates
removal of licensing procedures for imports
cards.quote: dismantling of quantitative restrictions on imports and exports (ii) reduction of tariff rates and (iii) removal of licensing procedures for imports

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Import licensing was abolished except for which industries?
cards.back: Import licensing was abolished except in case of hazardous and environmentally sensitive industries.
cards.quote: Import licensing was abolished except in case of hazardous and environmentally sensitive industries.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Quantitative restrictions on imports of manufactured consumer goods and agricultural products were also fully removed from ____.
cards.back: Quantitative restrictions on imports of manufactured consumer goods and agricultural products were also fully removed from April 2001.
cards.quote: Quantitative restrictions on imports of manufactured consumer goods and agricultural products were also fully removed from April 2001.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What effect did India's pre-reform tight import controls and very high tariffs have on manufacturing?
cards.back: In order to protect domestic industries, India was following a regime of quantitative restrictions on imports. This was encouraged through tight control over imports and by keeping the tariffs very high. These policies reduced efficiency and competitiveness which led to slow growth of the manufacturing sector.
cards.quote: In order to protect domestic industries, India was following a regime of quantitative restrictions on imports. This was encouraged through tight control over imports and by keeping the tariffs very high. These policies reduced efficiency and competitiveness which led to slow growth of the manufacturing sector.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is privatisation?
cards.back: It implies shedding of the ownership or management of a government owned enterprise.
cards.quote: It implies shedding of the ownership or management of a government owned enterprise.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Types: the two ways government companies are converted into private companies.
cards.back:
by withdrawal of the government from ownership and management of public sector companies
by outright sale of public sector companies
cards.quote: Government companies are converted into private companies in two ways (i) by withdrawal of the government from ownership and management of public sector companies and or (ii) by outright sale of public sector companies.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Define disinvestment.
cards.back: Privatisation of the public sector enterprises by selling off part of the equity of PSEs to the public is known as disinvestment.
cards.quote: Privatisation of the public sector enterprises by selling off part of the equity of PSEs to the public is known as disinvestment.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: The purpose of the sale, according to the government, was mainly to improve ____ and facilitate ____.
cards.back: The purpose of the sale, according to the government, was mainly to improve financial discipline and facilitate modernisation.
cards.quote: The purpose of the sale, according to the government, was mainly to improve financial discipline and facilitate modernisation.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Types: the status categories given to Central Public Sector Enterprises.
cards.back: maharatnas, navratnas and miniratnas
cards.quote: the government identifies PSEs and declare them as maharatnas, navratnas and miniratnas.

source.section: Box 3.1 Navratnas and Public Enterprise Policies

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What did maharatna, navratna and miniratna status give to PSEs?
cards.back: They were given greater financial, managerial and operational autonomy, in taking various decisions to run the company efficiently and thus increase their profits.
cards.quote: They were given greater financial, managerial and operational autonomy, in taking various decisions to run the company efficiently and thus increase their profits.

source.section: Box 3.1 Navratnas and Public Enterprise Policies

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Indian Oil Corporation Limited and Steel Authority of India Limited are examples of which status?
cards.back: Maharatnas (a) Indian Oil Corporation Limited, and (b) Steel Authority of India Limited
cards.quote: Maharatnas (a) Indian Oil Corporation Limited, and (b) Steel Authority of India Limited

source.section: Box 3.1 Navratnas and Public Enterprise Policies

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Hindustan Aeronautics, MTNL and IRCTC are examples of which status?
cards.back: Navratnas (a) Hindustan Aeronautics Limited, (b) Mahanagar Telephone Nigam Limited; and (c) Indian Railway Catering and Tourism Corporation Limited.
cards.quote: Navratnas (a) Hindustan Aeronautics Limited, (b) Mahanagar Telephone Nigam Limited; and (c) Indian Railway Catering and Tourism Corporation Limited.

source.section: Box 3.1 Navratnas and Public Enterprise Policies

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Bharat Sanchar Nigam Limited and Airport Authority of India are examples of which status?
cards.back: Miniratnas (a) Bharat Sanchar Nigam Limited; (b) Airport Authority of India.
cards.quote: Miniratnas (a) Bharat Sanchar Nigam Limited; (b) Airport Authority of India.

source.section: Box 3.1 Navratnas and Public Enterprise Policies

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: The government envisaged that privatisation could provide strong impetus to the inflow of ____.
cards.back: The government envisaged that privatisation could provide strong impetus to the inflow of FDI.
cards.quote: The government envisaged that privatisation could provide strong impetus to the inflow of FDI.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Define globalisation.
cards.back: Although globalisation is generally understood to mean integration of the economy of the country with the world economy, it is a complex phenomenon.
cards.quote: Although globalisation is generally understood to mean integration of the economy of the country with the world economy, it is a complex phenomenon.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is outsourcing?
cards.back: In outsourcing, a company hires regular service from external sources, mostly from other countries, which was previously provided internally or from within the country
cards.quote: In outsourcing, a company hires regular service from external sources, mostly from other countries, which was previously provided internally or from within the country

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Why has outsourcing intensified in recent times?
cards.back: As a form of economic activity, outsourcing has intensified, in recent times, because of the growth of fast modes of communication, particularly the growth of Information Technology (IT).
cards.quote: As a form of economic activity, outsourcing has intensified, in recent times, because of the growth of fast modes of communication, particularly the growth of Information Technology (IT).

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: WTO is expected to establish a ____ in which nations cannot place arbitrary restrictions on trade.
cards.back: WTO is expected to establish a rule-based trading regime in which nations cannot place arbitrary restrictions on trade.
cards.quote: WTO is expected to establish a rule-based trading regime in which nations cannot place arbitrary restrictions on trade.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: According to NCERT, the WTO aims to ensure optimum utilisation of what, and to protect what?
cards.back: to ensure optimum utilisation of world resources and to protect the environment.
cards.quote: to ensure optimum utilisation of world resources and to protect the environment.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What do the WTO agreements cover, and how do they facilitate trade?
cards.back: The WTO agreements cover trade in goods as well as services to facilitate international trade (bilateral and multilateral) through removal of tariff as well as non-tariff barriers and providing greater market access to all member countries.
cards.quote: The WTO agreements cover trade in goods as well as services to facilitate international trade (bilateral and multilateral) through removal of tariff as well as non-tariff barriers and providing greater market access to all member countries.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What role has India played as an important member of the WTO?
cards.back: As an important member of WTO, India has been in the forefront of framing fair global rules, regulations and safeguards and advocating the interests of the developing world.
cards.quote: As an important member of WTO, India has been in the forefront of framing fair global rules, regulations and safeguards and advocating the interests of the developing world.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: In economics, the growth of an economy is measured by the ____.
cards.back: In economics, the growth of an economy is measured by the Gross Domestic Product.
cards.quote: In economics, the growth of an economy is measured by the Gross Domestic Product.

source.section: 3.6 Indian Economy During Reforms: An Assessment

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: The growth of GDP increased from ____ per cent during 1980–91 to ____ per cent during 2021–22.
cards.back: The growth of GDP increased from 5.6 per cent during 1980–91 to 9.4 per cent during 2021–22.
cards.quote: The growth of GDP increased from 5.6 per cent during 1980–91 to 9.4 per cent during 2021–22.

source.section: 3.6 Indian Economy During Reforms: An Assessment

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: During the reform period, what happened to growth of agriculture, industry and services?
cards.back: During the reform period, the growth of agriculture has declined. While the industrial sector reported fluctuation, the growth of the service sector has gone up. This indicates that GDP growth is mainly driven by growth in the service sector.
cards.quote: During the reform period, the growth of agriculture has declined. While the industrial sector reported fluctuation, the growth of the service sector has gone up. This indicates that GDP growth is mainly driven by growth in the service sector.

source.section: 3.6 Indian Economy During Reforms: An Assessment

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What has the opening of the economy led to?
cards.back: The opening of the economy has led to a rapid increase in foreign direct investment and foreign exchange reserves.
cards.quote: The opening of the economy has led to a rapid increase in foreign direct investment and foreign exchange reserves.

source.section: 3.6 Indian Economy During Reforms: An Assessment

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: How much did foreign investment (FDI and FII) rise from 1990-91 to 2022-23?
cards.back: The foreign investment, which includes foreign direct investment (FDI) and foreign institutional investment (FII), has increased from about US $100 million in 1990–91 to US $ 23 billion in 2022–23.
cards.quote: The foreign investment, which includes foreign direct investment (FDI) and foreign institutional investment (FII), has increased from about US $100 million in 1990–91 to US $ 23 billion in 2022–23.

source.section: 3.6 Indian Economy During Reforms: An Assessment

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: How much did foreign exchange reserves rise from 1990-91 to 2023-24?
cards.back: There has been an increase in the foreign exchange reserves from about US $ 6 billion in 1990-91 to about US $ 646 billion in 2023–24.
cards.quote: There has been an increase in the foreign exchange reserves from about US $ 6 billion in 1990-91 to about US $ 646 billion in 2023–24.

source.section: 3.6 Indian Economy During Reforms: An Assessment

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Name the goods of which India is seen as a successful exporter since 1991.
cards.back:
auto parts
pharmaceutical goods
engineering goods
IT software
textiles
cards.quote: Since 1991, India is seen as a successful exporter of auto parts, pharmaceutical goods, engineering goods, IT software and textiles.

source.section: 3.6 Indian Economy During Reforms: An Assessment

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Name the areas in which the reform process has been criticised for not addressing basic problems.
cards.back:
employment
agriculture
industry
infrastructure development
fiscal management
cards.quote: The reform process has been widely criticised for not being able to address some of the basic problems facing our economy especially in areas of employment, agriculture, industry, infrastructure development and fiscal management.

source.section: 3.6 Indian Economy During Reforms: An Assessment

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What do scholars point out about reform-led growth and employment?
cards.back: Though the GDP growth rate has increased in the reform period, scholars point out that the reform-led growth has not generated sufficient employment opportunities in the country.
cards.quote: Though the GDP growth rate has increased in the reform period, scholars point out that the reform-led growth has not generated sufficient employment opportunities in the country.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What happened to public investment in agricultural infrastructure after 1991?
cards.back: Since 1991, public investment in agriculture sector especially in infrastructure, which includes irrigation, power, roads, market linkages and research and extension (which played a crucial role in the Green Revolution), has fallen.
cards.quote: Since 1991, public investment in agriculture sector especially in infrastructure, which includes irrigation, power, roads, market linkages and research and extension (which played a crucial role in the Green Revolution), has fallen.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What did the partial removal of fertiliser subsidy lead to?
cards.back: Further, the partial removal of fertiliser subsidy has led to increase in the cost of production, which has severely affected the small and marginal farmers.
cards.quote: Further, the partial removal of fertiliser subsidy has led to increase in the cost of production, which has severely affected the small and marginal farmers.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Name the policy changes agriculture has experienced since the reforms.
cards.back:
reduction in import duties on agricultural products
low minimum support price
lifting of quantitative restrictions on the imports of agricultural products
cards.quote: a number of policy changes such as reduction in import duties on agricultural products, low minimum support price and lifting of quantitative restrictions on the imports of agricultural products.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What shift has export-oriented agricultural strategy caused?
cards.back: Moreover, because of export-oriented policy strategies in agriculture, there has been a shift from production for the domestic market towards production for the export market focusing on cash crops in lieu of production of food grains. This puts pressure on prices of food grains.
cards.quote: Moreover, because of export-oriented policy strategies in agriculture, there has been a shift from production for the domestic market towards production for the export market focusing on cash crops in lieu of production of food grains. This puts pressure on prices of food grains.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Why has industrial growth slowed down?
cards.back: Industrial growth has also recorded a slowdown. This is because of decreasing demand of industrial products due to various reasons such as cheaper imports, inadequate investment in infrastructure etc.
cards.quote: Industrial growth has also recorded a slowdown. This is because of decreasing demand of industrial products due to various reasons such as cheaper imports, inadequate investment in infrastructure etc.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: How is globalisation often seen as affecting local industries and employment?
cards.back: Globalisation is, thus, often seen as creating conditions for the free movement of goods and services from foreign countries that adversely affect the local industries and employment opportunities in developing countries.
cards.quote: Globalisation is, thus, often seen as creating conditions for the free movement of goods and services from foreign countries that adversely affect the local industries and employment opportunities in developing countries.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Why does India still lack access to developed countries' markets?
cards.back: Moreover, a developing country like India still does not have the access to developed countries' markets because of high non-tariff barriers.
cards.quote: Moreover, a developing country like India still does not have the access to developed countries' markets because of high non-tariff barriers.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Which example shows India lacks market access because of non-tariff barriers?
cards.back: For example, although all quota restrictions on exports of textiles and clothing have been removed in India, USA has not removed their quota restriction on import of textiles from India and China.
cards.quote: For example, although all quota restrictions on exports of textiles and clothing have been removed in India, USA has not removed their quota restriction on import of textiles from India and China.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: How much was targeted to be mobilised through disinvestment in 1991-92?
cards.back: in 1991-92, it was targeted to mobilise Rs 2500 crore through disinvestment.
cards.quote: in 1991-92, it was targeted to mobilise Rs 2500 crore through disinvestment.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What do critics say about the assets of PSEs sold through disinvestment?
cards.back: the assets of PSEs have been undervalued and sold to the private sector.
cards.quote: the assets of PSEs have been undervalued and sold to the private sector.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Critics say disinvestment proceeds are used for what, rather than for what?
cards.back: Moreover, the proceeds from disinvestment are used to offset the shortage of government revenues rather than using it for the development of PSEs and building social infrastructure in the country.
cards.quote: Moreover, the proceeds from disinvestment are used to offset the shortage of government revenues rather than using it for the development of PSEs and building social infrastructure in the country.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Economic reforms have placed limits on the growth of public expenditure, especially in ____.
cards.back: Economic reforms have placed limits on the growth of public expenditure, especially in social sectors.
cards.quote: Economic reforms have placed limits on the growth of public expenditure, especially in social sectors.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Did tax reductions in the reform period increase tax revenue?
cards.back: The tax reductions in the reform period, aimed at yielding larger revenue and curb tax evasion, have not resulted in increase in tax revenue for the government.
cards.quote: The tax reductions in the reform period, aimed at yielding larger revenue and curb tax evasion, have not resulted in increase in tax revenue for the government.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: How have tariff reductions affected revenue from custom duties?
cards.back: the reform policies, involving tariff reduction, have curtailed the scope for raising revenue through custom duties.
cards.quote: the reform policies, involving tariff reduction, have curtailed the scope for raising revenue through custom duties.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Why has the scope for raising tax revenues reduced further?
cards.back: In order to attract foreign investment, tax incentives are provided to foreign investors which further reduced the scope for raising tax revenues.
cards.quote: In order to attract foreign investment, tax incentives are provided to foreign investors which further reduced the scope for raising tax revenues.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What results has globalisation through liberalisation and privatisation produced?
cards.back: The process of globalisation through liberalisation and privatisation policies has produced positive, as well as, negative results both for India and other countries.
cards.quote: The process of globalisation through liberalisation and privatisation policies has produced positive, as well as, negative results both for India and other countries.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Why do some scholars see globalisation as an opportunity?
cards.back: Some scholars argue that globalisation should be seen as an opportunity in terms of greater access to global markets, high technology and increased possibility of large industries of developing countries to become important players in the international arena.
cards.quote: Some scholars argue that globalisation should be seen as an opportunity in terms of greater access to global markets, high technology and increased possibility of large industries of developing countries to become important players in the international arena.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What do critics argue about globalisation?
cards.back: On the contrary, the critics argue that globalisation is a strategy of the developed countries to expand their markets in other countries.
cards.quote: On the contrary, the critics argue that globalisation is a strategy of the developed countries to expand their markets in other countries.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What has market-driven globalisation done to economic disparities?
cards.back: It has further been pointed out that market-driven globalisation has widened the economic disparities among nations and people.
cards.quote: It has further been pointed out that market-driven globalisation has widened the economic disparities among nations and people.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Name the select services-sector areas where growth has been concentrated.
cards.back:
telecommunication
information technology
finance
entertainment
travel and hospitality services
real estate and trade
cards.quote: telecommunication, information technology, finance, entertainment, travel and hospitality services, real estate and trade

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Name the problems the economy was facing before the 1991 reforms.
cards.back:
declining foreign exchange
growing imports without matching rise in exports
high inflation
cards.quote: The economy was facing problems of declining foreign exchange, growing imports without matching rise in exports and high inflation.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Why did India change its economic policies in 1991?
cards.back: India changed its economic policies in 1991 due to a financial crisis and pressure from international organisations like the World Bank and IMF.
cards.quote: India changed its economic policies in 1991 due to a financial crisis and pressure from international organisations like the World Bank and IMF.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: In which sectors were major domestic reforms undertaken?
cards.back: In the domestic economy, major reforms were undertaken in the industrial and financial sectors.
cards.quote: In the domestic economy, major reforms were undertaken in the industrial and financial sectors.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: How was the role of the public sector reduced, and how was it opened to the private sector?
cards.back: With a view to improving the performance of the public sector, there was a consensus on reducing its role and opening it up to the private sector. This was done through disinvestment and liberalisation measures.
cards.quote: With a view to improving the performance of the public sector, there was a consensus on reducing its role and opening it up to the private sector. This was done through disinvestment and liberalisation measures.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Globalisation is the outcome of the policies of ____ and ____.
cards.back: Globalisation is the outcome of the policies of liberalisation and privatisation.
cards.quote: Globalisation is the outcome of the policies of liberalisation and privatisation.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: The objective of the WTO is to establish a ____ to ensure optimum utilisation of world resources.
cards.back: The objective of the WTO is to establish a rule based trade regime to ensure optimum utilisation of world resources.
cards.quote: The objective of the WTO is to establish a rule based trade regime to ensure optimum utilisation of world resources.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: During the reforms, growth of agriculture and industry has gone down but the ____ has registered growth.
cards.back: During the reforms, growth of agriculture and industry has gone down but the service sector has registered growth.
cards.quote: During the reforms, growth of agriculture and industry has gone down but the service sector has registered growth.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What has happened to the agriculture sector and public investment in it under the reforms?
cards.back: Reforms have not benefited the agriculture sector. There has also been a decline in public investment in this sector.
cards.quote: Reforms have not benefited the agriculture sector. There has also been a decline in public investment in this sector.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: What are economic activities?
cards.back: Those activities which contribute to the gross national product are called economic activities.
cards.quote: Those activities which contribute to the gross national product are called economic activities.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: Who is a worker?
cards.back: All those who are engaged in economic activities, in whatever capacity — high or low, are workers.
cards.quote: All those who are engaged in economic activities, in whatever capacity — high or low, are workers.

cards.subject: economics
