cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: What is gross domestic product (GDP)?
cards.back: The total money value of all such final goods and services produced in a country in a year is called its gross domestic product for that year.
cards.quote: The total money value of all such final goods and services produced in a country in a year is called its gross domestic product for that year.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: What was the size of India's workforce in 2022-23?
cards.back: During 2022-23, India had a workforce of about 545 million.
cards.quote: During 2022-23, India had a workforce of about 545 million.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: What share of India's workers are men and what share women?
cards.back: About 77 per cent of the workers are men and the rest are women (men and women include child labourers in respective sexes).
cards.quote: About 77 per cent of the workers are men and the rest are women (men and women include child labourers in respective sexes).

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: What share of the rural and the urban workforce are women?
cards.back: Women workers account for one-fourth of the rural workforce whereas in urban areas, they are just one-fifth of the workforce.
cards.quote: Women workers account for one-fourth of the rural workforce whereas in urban areas, they are just one-fifth of the workforce.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: Why are women who cook, fetch water and fuelwood and do unpaid farm labour not categorised as workers?
cards.back: Women carry out works like cooking, fetching water and fuelwood and participate in farm labour. They are not paid wages in cash or in the form of grains; at times they are not paid at all. For this reason, these women are not categorised as workers.
cards.quote: Women carry out works like cooking, fetching water and fuelwood and participate in farm labour. They are not paid wages in cash or in the form of grains; at times they are not paid at all. For this reason, these women are not categorised as workers.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: What is the worker-population ratio?
cards.back: Worker-population ratio is an indicator which is used for analysing the employment situation in the country.
cards.quote: Worker-population ratio is an indicator which is used for analysing the employment situation in the country.
cards.note: It shows what proportion of the population is actively contributing to production.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: What does a higher worker-population ratio mean, and what does a medium or low ratio mean?
cards.back: If the ratio is higher, it means that the engagement of people is greater; if the ratio for a country is medium, or low, it means that a very high proportion of its population is not involved directly in economic activities.
cards.quote: If the ratio is higher, it means that the engagement of people is greater; if the ratio for a country is medium, or low, it means that a very high proportion of its population is not involved directly in economic activities.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: What is population?
cards.back: Population is defined as the total number of people who reside in a particular locality at a particular point of time.
cards.quote: Population is defined as the total number of people who reside in a particular locality at a particular point of time.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: Formula: worker-population ratio for India
cards.back: divide the total number of workers in India by the population in India and multiply it by 100, you will get the worker-population ratio for India.
cards.quote: If you want to know the worker-population ratio for India, divide the total number of workers in India by the population in India and multiply it by 100, you will get the worker-population ratio for India.
cards.note: Worker-population ratio = (total workers / population) x 100.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: About how many of every 100 persons in India are workers?
cards.back: For every 100 persons, about 41 (by rounding off 41.1) are workers in India. In urban areas, the proportion is about 38, whereas in rural India, the ratio is about 42.
cards.quote: For every 100 persons, about 41 (by rounding off 41.1) are workers in India. In urban areas, the proportion is about 38, whereas in rural India, the ratio is about 42.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: Give NCERT's reasons why the worker-population ratio is higher in rural areas than in urban areas.
cards.back: People in rural areas have limited resources to earn a higher income and participate more in the employment market. Many do not go to schools, colleges and other training institutions. Even if some go, they discontinue in the middle to join the workforce
cards.quote: People in rural areas have limited resources to earn a higher income and participate more in the employment market. Many do not go to schools, colleges and other training institutions. Even if some go, they discontinue in the middle to join the workforce

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: What does the narrow definition of work lead to, as regards the work of women?
cards.back: This narrow definition of work leads to non-recognition of women's work and, therefore, to the underestimation of the number of women workers in the country.
cards.quote: This narrow definition of work leads to non-recognition of women's work and, therefore, to the underestimation of the number of women workers in the country.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: Types of workers by status in employment (Chart 6.1).
cards.back:
Self-employed
Regular Salaried Employees
Casual Wage Labourers
cards.quote: Self-employed Regular Salaried Employees Casual Wage Labourers

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: What share of men and of women work as regular salaried employees?
cards.back: Men form 21 per cent whereas women form 16 per cent.
cards.quote: Men form 21 per cent whereas women form 16 per cent.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: In rural areas, since majority of those depending on farming own plots of land and cultivate independently, the share of ____ is greater.
cards.back: In rural areas, since majority of those depending on farming own plots of land and cultivate independently, the share of self-employed is greater.
cards.quote: In rural areas, since majority of those depending on farming own plots of land and cultivate independently, the share of self-employed is greater.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: In the course of economic development of a country, labour flows from ____ and other related activities to industry and services.
cards.back: In the course of economic development of a country, labour flows from agriculture and other related activities to industry and services.
cards.quote: In the course of economic development of a country, labour flows from agriculture and other related activities to industry and services.

source.section: 6.5 Employment in Firms, Factories and Offices

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: Sectors in which the workforce is distributed (Table 6.2).
cards.back:
Primary Sector
Secondary Sector
Tertiary / Service Sector
cards.quote: Primary Sector Secondary Sector Tertiary / Service Sector

source.section: 6.5 Employment in Firms, Factories and Offices

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: What share of India's workforce is in the secondary and the service sector?
cards.back: Secondary sector provides employment to only about 24 per cent of workforce. About 30 per cent of workers are in the service sector.
cards.quote: Secondary sector provides employment to only about 24 per cent of workforce. About 30 per cent of workers are in the service sector.

source.section: 6.5 Employment in Firms, Factories and Offices

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: What share of rural India's workforce depends on agriculture, forestry and fishing?
cards.back: Table 6.2 also shows that about 60 per cent of the workforce in rural India depends on agriculture, forestry and fishing.
cards.quote: Table 6.2 also shows that about 60 per cent of the workforce in rural India depends on agriculture, forestry and fishing.

source.section: 6.5 Employment in Firms, Factories and Offices

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: What share of urban workers are in the service sector?
cards.back: Agriculture is not a major source of employment in urban areas where people are mainly engaged in the service sector. About 61 per cent of urban workers are in the service sector.
cards.quote: Agriculture is not a major source of employment in urban areas where people are mainly engaged in the service sector. About 61 per cent of urban workers are in the service sector.

source.section: 6.5 Employment in Firms, Factories and Offices

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: What share of the female and of the male workforce is employed in the primary sector?
cards.back: About 64 per cent of the female workforce is employed in the primary sector whereas 36 per cent of males work in that sector.
cards.quote: About 64 per cent of the female workforce is employed in the primary sector whereas 36 per cent of males work in that sector.

source.section: 6.5 Employment in Firms, Factories and Offices

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: How did GDP growth compare with employment growth during 1951-2023?
cards.back: During the period 1951-2023, Gross Domestic Product (GDP) of India grew positively and was higher than the employment growth.
cards.quote: During the period 1951-2023, Gross Domestic Product (GDP) of India grew positively and was higher than the employment growth.

source.section: 6.6 Growth and Changing Structure of Employment

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: During this period, employment grew at the rate of not more than ____ most of the times.
cards.back: During this period, employment grew at the rate of not more than 2 per cent most of the times.
cards.quote: During this period, employment grew at the rate of not more than 2 per cent most of the times.

source.section: 6.6 Growth and Changing Structure of Employment

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: When did employment growth go beyond 2 per cent?
cards.back: Only during two points of time (2022-2023 and 1999-2005), over the period of seven decades employment growth went beyond 2 per cent.
cards.quote: Only during two points of time (2022-2023 and 1999-2005), over the period of seven decades employment growth went beyond 2 per cent.

source.section: 6.6 Growth and Changing Structure of Employment

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: What happened to India's employment growth in the late 1990s?
cards.back: employment growth started declining and reached the level of growth that India had in the early stages of planning.
cards.quote: Chart 6.3 also points at another disheartening development in the late 1990s: employment growth started declining and reached the level of growth that India had in the early stages of planning.

source.section: 6.6 Growth and Changing Structure of Employment

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: What is jobless growth?
cards.back: This means that in the Indian economy, without generating employment, we have been able to produce more goods and services. Scholars refer to this phenomenon as jobless growth.
cards.quote: This means that in the Indian economy, without generating employment, we have been able to produce more goods and services. Scholars refer to this phenomenon as jobless growth.

source.section: 6.6 Growth and Changing Structure of Employment

cards.note: Output rises without a matching rise in jobs.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: What happened to the primary sector's share of the workforce between 1972-73 and 2023-24?
cards.back: In 1972-73, about 74 per cent of workforce was engaged in primary sector and in 2023-24, this proportion has declined to about 46 per cent.
cards.quote: In 1972-73, about 74 per cent of workforce was engaged in primary sector and in 2023-24, this proportion has declined to about 46 per cent.

source.section: 6.6 Growth and Changing Structure of Employment

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: How did the shares of the secondary and service sectors change between 1972-73 and 2023-24?
cards.back: Secondary and service sectors are showing promising future for the Indian workforce. You may notice that the shares of these sectors have increased from 11 to 24 per cent and 15 to 30 per cent, respectively.
cards.quote: Secondary and service sectors are showing promising future for the Indian workforce. You may notice that the shares of these sectors have increased from 11 to 24 per cent and 15 to 30 per cent, respectively.

source.section: 6.6 Growth and Changing Structure of Employment

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: How has the workforce moved between types of employment status since 1972?
cards.back: last five decades (1972-2024), people have moved from self-employment and regular salaried employment to casual wage work. Yet self-employment continues to be the major employment provider.
cards.quote: last five decades (1972-2024), people have moved from self-employment and regular salaried employment to casual wage work. Yet self-employment continues to be the major employment provider.

source.section: 6.6 Growth and Changing Structure of Employment

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: What is casualisation of workforce?
cards.back: Scholars call the process of moving from self-employment and regular salaried employment to casual wage work as casualisation of workforce. This makes the workers highly vulnerable.
cards.quote: Scholars call the process of moving from self-employment and regular salaried employment to casual wage work as casualisation of workforce. This makes the workers highly vulnerable.

source.section: 6.6 Growth and Changing Structure of Employment

cards.note: Casualisation: the shift from self-employment and regular salaried jobs to casual wage work.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: The government, through its ____, enable them to protect their rights in various ways.
cards.back: The government, through its labour laws, enable them to protect their rights in various ways.
cards.quote: The government, through its labour laws, enable them to protect their rights in various ways.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: To know this we classify workforce into two categories: workers in formal and informal sectors, which are also referred to as ____ and ____ sectors.
cards.back: To know this we classify workforce into two categories: workers in formal and informal sectors, which are also referred to as organised and unorganised sectors.
cards.quote: To know this we classify workforce into two categories: workers in formal and informal sectors, which are also referred to as organised and unorganised sectors.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: What are formal sector establishments and who are formal sector workers?
cards.back: All the public sector establishments and those private sector establishments which employ 10 hired workers or more are called formal sector establishments and those who work in such establishments are formal sector workers.
cards.quote: All the public sector establishments and those private sector establishments which employ 10 hired workers or more are called formal sector establishments and those who work in such establishments are formal sector workers.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: What constitutes the informal sector?
cards.back: All other enterprises and workers working in those enterprises form the informal sector.
cards.quote: All other enterprises and workers working in those enterprises form the informal sector.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: What does the informal sector include (NCERT)?
cards.back: Thus, informal sector includes millions of farmers, agricultural labourers, owners of small enterprises and people working in those enterprises as also the self-employed who do not have any hired workers. It also includes all non-farm casual wage labourers who work for more than one employer such as construction workers and headload workers.
cards.quote: Thus, informal sector includes millions of farmers, agricultural labourers, owners of small enterprises and people working in those enterprises as also the self-employed who do not have any hired workers. It also includes all non-farm casual wage labourers who work for more than one employer such as construction workers and headload workers.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: In 2012, how many of the about 30 million formal sector workers were employed by the public sector?
cards.back: In 2012, out of about 30 million formal sector workers, about 18 million workers were employed by the public sector.
cards.quote: In 2012, out of about 30 million formal sector workers, about 18 million workers were employed by the public sector.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: What share of the formal sector workforce are women?
cards.back: Here also men form the majority, as women constitute only about one-sixth of the formal sector workforce.
cards.quote: Here also men form the majority, as women constitute only about one-sixth of the formal sector workforce.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: What did the reform process initiated in the early 1990s do to the number of formal sector workers?
cards.back: Economists point out that the reform process initiated in the early 1990s resulted in a decline in the number of workers employed in the formal sector.
cards.quote: Economists point out that the reform process initiated in the early 1990s resulted in a decline in the number of workers employed in the formal sector.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: Name the features of the informal sector (NCERT).
cards.back:
Workers and enterprises in the informal sector do not get regular income; they do not have any protection or regulation from the government.
Workers are dismissed without any compensation.
Technology used in the informal sector enterprises is outdated; they also do not maintain any accounts.
Workers of this sector live in slums and are squatters.
cards.quote: Workers and enterprises in the informal sector do not get regular income; they do not have any protection or regulation from the government. Workers are dismissed without any compensation. Technology used in the informal sector enterprises is outdated; they also do not maintain any accounts. Workers of this sector live in slums and are squatters.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: What is disguised unemployment, in NCERT's example of a farmer with four acres of land?
cards.back: Suppose a farmer has four acres of land and he actually needs only two workers and himself to carry out various operations on his farm in a year, but if he employs five workers and his family members such as his wife and children, this situation is known as disguised unemployment.
cards.quote: Suppose a farmer has four acres of land and he actually needs only two workers and himself to carry out various operations on his farm in a year, but if he employs five workers and his family members such as his wife and children, this situation is known as disguised unemployment.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: Define unemployment (National Statistical Office).
cards.back: The National Statistical Office (Previously it was known as National Sample Survey Organisation) defines unemployment as a situation in which all those who, owing to lack of work, are not working but either seek work through employment exchanges, intermediaries, friends or relatives or by making applications to prospective employers or express their willingness or availability for work under the prevailing condition of work and remunerations.
cards.quote: The National Statistical Office (Previously it was known as National Sample Survey Organisation) defines unemployment as a situation in which all those who, owing to lack of work, are not working but either seek work through employment exchanges, intermediaries, friends or relatives or by making applications to prospective employers or express their willingness or availability for work under the prevailing condition of work and remunerations.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: What does the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act 2005 promise?
cards.back: It promises 100 days of guaranteed wage employment to all rural households who volunteer to do unskilled manual work.
cards.quote: You may recall about the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act 2005. It promises 100 days of guaranteed wage employment to all rural households who volunteer to do unskilled manual work.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: Two ways in which the government generates employment (NCERT).
cards.back:
direct
indirect
cards.quote: Their efforts can be broadly categorised into two — direct and indirect.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: How does the government generate employment directly?
cards.back: the government employs people in various departments for administrative purposes. It also runs industries, hotels and transport companies, and hence, provides employment directly to workers.
cards.quote: the government employs people in various departments for administrative purposes. It also runs industries, hotels and transport companies, and hence, provides employment directly to workers.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: A government owned steel company raises its output; private companies buying its steel also raise employment. Which kind of generation is this?
cards.back: when a government owned steel company increases its output, it will result in direct increase in employment in that government company. Simultaneously, private companies, which purchase steel from it, will also increase their output and thus employment. This is the indirect generation of employment opportunities by the government initiatives in the economy.
cards.quote: when a government owned steel company increases its output, it will result in direct increase in employment in that government company. Simultaneously, private companies, which purchase steel from it, will also increase their output and thus employment. This is the indirect generation of employment opportunities by the government initiatives in the economy.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: What is the unemployment called when farm work is seasonal and villagers find no work in some months of the year?
cards.back: This kind of unemployment is known as seasonal unemployment. This is also a common form of unemployment prevailing in India.
cards.quote: This kind of unemployment is known as seasonal unemployment. This is also a common form of unemployment prevailing in India.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: What are employment generation programmes?
cards.back: Many programmes that the governments implement, aimed at alleviating poverty, are through employment generation. They are also known as employment generation programmes.
cards.quote: Many programmes that the governments implement, aimed at alleviating poverty, are through employment generation. They are also known as employment generation programmes.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: Newly emerging jobs are found mostly in the ____.
cards.back: Newly emerging jobs are found mostly in the service sector.
cards.quote: Newly emerging jobs are found mostly in the service sector.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: The nature of employment has become more ____ with only limited availability of social security measures to the workers.
cards.back: The nature of employment has become more informal with only limited availability of social security measures to the workers.
cards.quote: The nature of employment has become more informal with only limited availability of social security measures to the workers.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: In the last few decades, there has been rapid growth in the gross domestic product, but without simultaneous increase in ____.
cards.back: In the last few decades, there has been rapid growth in the gross domestic product, but without simultaneous increase in employment opportunities.
cards.quote: In the last few decades, there has been rapid growth in the gross domestic product, but without simultaneous increase in employment opportunities.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: About ____ of the total population in the country is engaged in various economic activities.
cards.back: About two-fifth of the total population in the country is engaged in various economic activities.
cards.quote: About two-fifth of the total population in the country is engaged in various economic activities.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: Men particularly ____, form the major section of workforce in India.
cards.back: Men particularly rural men, form the major section of workforce in India.
cards.quote: Men particularly rural men, form the major section of workforce in India.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: Which status in employment covers the majority of India's workers (NCERT Recap)?
cards.back: Majority of workers in India are self-employed.
cards.quote: Majority of workers in India are self-employed.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: Casual wage labourers and regular salaried employees together account for ____ the proportion of India's workforce.
cards.back: Casual wage labourers and regular salaried employees together account for less than half the proportion of India's workforce.
cards.quote: Casual wage labourers and regular salaried employees together account for less than half the proportion of India's workforce.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: What has happened to the growth of employment in recent years (NCERT Recap)?
cards.back: In recent years, the growth of employment has decelerated.
cards.quote: In recent years, the growth of employment has decelerated.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: ____ is the major formal sector employer in the country.
cards.back: Government is the major formal sector employer in the country.
cards.quote: Government is the major formal sector employer in the country.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: What is meant by environment?
cards.back: Environment is defined as the total planetary inheritance and the totality of all resources. It includes all the biotic and abiotic factors that influence each other.
cards.quote: Environment is defined as the total planetary inheritance and the totality of all resources. It includes all the biotic and abiotic factors that influence each other.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: Name the two kinds of elements in the environment, with NCERT’s examples.
cards.back:
all living elements — the birds, animals and plants, forests, fisheries etc.— are biotic elements
abiotic elements include air, water, land etc.
cards.quote: While all living elements — the birds, animals and plants, forests, fisheries etc.— are biotic elements, abiotic elements include air, water, land etc.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: Name the four vital functions of the environment.
cards.back:
it supplies resources
it assimilates waste
it sustains life by providing genetic and bio diversity
it also provides aesthetic services like scenery etc.
cards.quote: The environment performs four vital functions (i) it supplies resources: resources here include both renewable and non-renewable resources. Renewable resources are those which can be used without the possibility of the resource becoming depleted or exhausted. That is, a continuous supply of the resource remains available. Examples of renewable resources are the trees in the forests and the fishes in the ocean. Non-renewable resources, on the other hand, are those which get exhausted with extraction and use, for example, fossil fuel (ii) it assimilates waste (iii) it sustains life by providing genetic and bio diversity and (iv) it also provides aesthetic services like scenery etc.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: What are renewable resources?
cards.back: Renewable resources are those which can be used without the possibility of the resource becoming depleted or exhausted. That is, a continuous supply of the resource remains available.
cards.quote: Renewable resources are those which can be used without the possibility of the resource becoming depleted or exhausted. That is, a continuous supply of the resource remains available.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: What are non-renewable resources? Give NCERT’s example.
cards.back: Non-renewable resources, on the other hand, are those which get exhausted with extraction and use, for example, fossil fuel
cards.quote: Non-renewable resources, on the other hand, are those which get exhausted with extraction and use, for example, fossil fuel

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: If the demand on its functions is within the environment's carrying capacity, what does that imply for extraction and wastes?
cards.back: This implies that the resource extraction is not above the rate of regeneration of the resource and the wastes generated are within the assimilating capacity of the environment.
cards.quote: This implies that the resource extraction is not above the rate of regeneration of the resource and the wastes generated are within the assimilating capacity of the environment.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: What is absorptive capacity of the environment?
cards.back: Absorptive capacity means the ability of the environment to absorb degradation.
cards.quote: Absorptive capacity means the ability of the environment to absorb degradation.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: What has placed a huge stress on the environment in terms of its first two functions?
cards.back: The rising population of the developing countries and the affluent consumption and production standards of the developed world have placed a huge stress on the environment in terms of its first two functions.
cards.quote: The rising population of the developing countries and the affluent consumption and production standards of the developed world have placed a huge stress on the environment in terms of its first two functions.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: Name the reasons NCERT gives for why the opportunity costs of negative environmental impacts are high.
cards.back:
we are compelled to spend huge amounts on technology and research to explore new resources
the health costs of degraded environmental quality
global environmental issues such as global warming and ozone depletion also contribute to increased financial commitments for the government
cards.quote: we are compelled to spend huge amounts on technology and research to explore new resources. Added to these are the health costs of degraded environmental quality -- decline in air and water quality (seventy per cent of water in India is polluted) have resulted in increased incidence of respiratory and water-borne diseases. Hence the expenditure on health is also rising. To make matters worse, global environmental issues such as global warming and ozone depletion also contribute to increased financial commitments for the government. Thus, it is clear that the opportunity costs of negative environmental impacts are high.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: In the early days of civilisation, how did demand for environmental resources compare with their supply?
cards.back: In the early days when civilisation just began, or before this phenomenal increase in population, and before countries took to industrialisation, the demand for environmental resources and services was much less than their supply.
cards.quote: In the early days when civilisation just began, or before this phenomenal increase in population, and before countries took to industrialisation, the demand for environmental resources and services was much less than their supply.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: What is global warming?
cards.back: Global warming is a gradual increase in the average temperature of the earth’s lower atmosphere as a result of the increase in greenhouse gases since the Industrial Revolution.
cards.quote: Global warming is a gradual increase in the average temperature of the earth’s lower atmosphere as a result of the increase in greenhouse gases since the Industrial Revolution.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: What is global warming caused by, according to NCERT Box 7.1?
cards.back: Much of the recent observed and projected global warming is human-induced. It is caused by man-made increases in carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases through the burning of fossil fuels and deforestation.
cards.quote: Much of the recent observed and projected global warming is human-induced. It is caused by man-made increases in carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases through the burning of fossil fuels and deforestation.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: Name the longer-term results of global warming.
cards.back:
melting of polar ice with a resulting rise in sea level and coastal flooding
disruption of drinking water supplies dependent on snow melts
extinction of species as ecological niches disappear
more frequent tropical storms
an increased incidence of tropical diseases
cards.quote: Some of the longer-term results of global warming are melting of polar ice with a resulting rise in sea level and coastal flooding; disruption of drinking water supplies dependent on snow melts; extinction of species as ecological niches disappear; more frequent tropical storms; and an increased incidence of tropical diseases.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: Name the factors that may be contributing to global warming.
cards.back:
the burning of coal and petroleum products (sources of carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide, ozone)
deforestation, which increases the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere
methane gas released in animal waste
increased cattle production, which contributes to deforestation, methane production, and use of fossil fuels
cards.quote: Among factors that may be contributing to global warming are the burning of coal and petroleum products (sources of carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide, ozone); deforestation, which increases the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere; methane gas released in animal waste; and increased cattle production, which contributes to deforestation, methane production, and use of fossil fuels.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: What is ozone depletion?
cards.back: Ozone depletion refers to the phenomenon of reductions in the amount of ozone in the stratosphere.
cards.quote: Ozone depletion refers to the phenomenon of reductions in the amount of ozone in the stratosphere.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: What causes the problem of ozone depletion?
cards.back: The problem of ozone depletion is caused by high levels of chlorine and bromine compounds in the stratosphere.
cards.quote: The problem of ozone depletion is caused by high levels of chlorine and bromine compounds in the stratosphere.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: What are the origins of the chlorine and bromine compounds that deplete the ozone layer?
cards.back: The origins of these compounds are chlorofluorocarbons (CFC), used as cooling substances in airconditioners and refrigerators, or as aerosol propellants, and bromofluorocarbons (halons), used in fire extinguishers.
cards.quote: The origins of these compounds are chlorofluorocarbons (CFC), used as cooling substances in airconditioners and refrigerators, or as aerosol propellants, and bromofluorocarbons (halons), used in fire extinguishers.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: Which protocol banned the use of chlorofluorocarbon (CFC) compounds and other ozone depleting chemicals?
cards.back: This led to the adoption of the Montreal Protocol banning the use of chlorofluorocarbon (CFC) compounds, as well as other ozone depleting chemicals such as carbon tetrachloride, trichloroethane (also known as methyl chloroform), and bromine compounds known as halons.
cards.quote: This led to the adoption of the Montreal Protocol banning the use of chlorofluorocarbon (CFC) compounds, as well as other ozone depleting chemicals such as carbon tetrachloride, trichloroethane (also known as methyl chloroform), and bromine compounds known as halons.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: What dichotomy does the threat to India’s environment pose?
cards.back: The threat to India’s environment poses a dichotomy —threat of poverty-induced environmental degradation and, at the same time, threat of pollution from affluence and a rapidly growing industrial sector.
cards.quote: The threat to India’s environment poses a dichotomy —threat of poverty-induced environmental degradation and, at the same time, threat of pollution from affluence and a rapidly growing industrial sector.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: Name the five 'most pressing environmental concerns of India' (not the priority issues).
cards.back:
Air pollution
water contamination
soil erosion
deforestation
wildlife extinction
cards.quote: Air pollution, water contamination, soil erosion, deforestation and wildlife extinction are some of the most pressing environmental concerns of India.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: Name the priority environmental issues identified in India.
cards.back:
land degradation
biodiversity loss
air pollution with special reference to vehicular pollution in urban cities
management of fresh water
solid waste management
cards.quote: The priority issues identified are (i) land degradation (ii) biodiversity loss (iii) air pollution with special reference to vehicular pollution in urban cities (iv) management of fresh water and (v) solid waste management.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: Name the first nine factors, (i) to (ix), that NCERT lists as responsible for land degradation.
cards.back:
loss of vegetation occuring due to deforestation
unsustainable fuel wood and fodder extraction
shifting cultivation
encroachment into forest lands
forest fires and over grazing
non-adoption of adequate soil conservation measures
improper crop rotation
indiscriminate use of agro-chemicals such as fertilisers and pesticides
improper planning and management of irrigation systems
cards.quote: Some of the factors responsible for land degradation are (i) loss of vegetation occuring due to deforestation (ii) unsustainable fuel wood and fodder extraction (iii) shifting cultivation (iv) encroachment into forest lands (v) forest fires and over grazing (vi) non-adoption of adequate soil conservation measures (vii) improper crop rotation (viii) indiscriminate use of agro-chemicals such as fertilisers and pesticides (ix) improper planning and management of irrigation systems

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: What share of the world’s human and livestock population does India support, on how much of the world’s area?
cards.back: India supports approximately 17 per cent of the world’s human and 20 per cent of livestock population on a mere 2.5 per cent of the world’s geographical area.
cards.quote: India supports approximately 17 per cent of the world’s human and 20 per cent of livestock population on a mere 2.5 per cent of the world’s geographical area.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: The per capita forest land in the country is only ____ against the requirement of ____ to meet basic needs
cards.back: The per capita forest land in the country is only 0.06 hectare against the requirement of 0.47 hectare to meet basic needs
cards.quote: The per capita forest land in the country is only 0.06 hectare against the requirement of 0.47 hectare to meet basic needs

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: NCERT's land degradation factors end with ground-water over-extraction; name the last two, (xi) and (xii).
cards.back:
open access resource
poverty of the agriculture-dependent people
cards.quote: (xi) open access resource and (xii) poverty of the agriculture-dependent people

source.section: 7.3 State of India's Environment: Land Degradation

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: When and why did the government set up the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB)?
cards.back: In order to address two major environmental concerns in India, viz. water and air pollution, the government set up the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) in 1974.
cards.quote: In order to address two major environmental concerns in India, viz. water and air pollution, the government set up the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) in 1974.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: What do the pollution control boards investigate and lay standards for?
cards.back: They investigate, collect and disseminate information relating to water, air and land pollution, lay down standards for sewage/trade effluent and emissions.
cards.quote: They investigate, collect and disseminate information relating to water, air and land pollution, lay down standards for sewage/trade effluent and emissions.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: Vehicular emissions are of particular concern since these are ____ and, thus, have the maximum impact on the general population.
cards.back: Vehicular emissions are of particular concern since these are ground level sources and, thus, have the maximum impact on the general population.
cards.quote: Vehicular emissions are of particular concern since these are ground level sources and, thus, have the maximum impact on the general population.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: The number of motor vehicles has increased from about ____ in 1951 to ____ in 2022.
cards.back: The number of motor vehicles has increased from about 3 lakh in 1951 to 35 crores in 2022.
cards.quote: The number of motor vehicles has increased from about 3 lakh in 1951 to 35 crores in 2022.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: How many categories of industries (large and medium scale) has the CPCB identified as significantly polluting?
cards.back: has identified seventeen categories of industries (large and medium scale) as significantly polluting
cards.quote: has identified seventeen categories of industries (large and medium scale) as significantly polluting

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: How are environment and economy related, according to NCERT?
cards.back: Environment and economy are interdependent and need each other.
cards.quote: Environment and economy are interdependent and need each other.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: What is sustainable development? (UNCED definition)
cards.back: ‘Development that meets the need of the present generation without compromising the ability of the future generation to meet their own needs’.
cards.quote: ‘Development that meets the need of the present generation without compromising the ability of the future generation to meet their own needs’.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: Define sustainable development in terms of the quality of life of future generations.
cards.back: development that will allow all future generations to have a potential average quality of life that is at least as high as that which is being enjoyed by the current generation.
cards.quote: development that will allow all future generations to have a potential average quality of life that is at least as high as that which is being enjoyed by the current generation.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: How did the report ‘Our Common Future’ explain sustainable development?
cards.back: The seminal report — Our Common Future — that gave the above definition explained sustainable development as ‘meeting the basic needs of all and extending to all the opportunity to satisfy their aspirations for a better life’.
cards.quote: The seminal report — Our Common Future — that gave the above definition explained sustainable development as ‘meeting the basic needs of all and extending to all the opportunity to satisfy their aspirations for a better life’.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: Define sustainable development (Edward Barbier).
cards.back: Edward Barbier defined sustainable development as one which is directly concerned with increasing the material standard of living of the poor at the grass root level
cards.quote: Edward Barbier defined sustainable development as one which is directly concerned with increasing the material standard of living of the poor at the grass root level

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: What basic needs of the poor majority must sustainable development meet?
cards.back: Sustainable development is, in this sense, a development that meets the basic needs of all, particularly the poor majority, for employment, food, energy, water, housing, and ensures growth of agriculture, manufacturing, power and services to meet these needs.
cards.quote: Sustainable development is, in this sense, a development that meets the basic needs of all, particularly the poor majority, for employment, food, energy, water, housing, and ensures growth of agriculture, manufacturing, power and services to meet these needs.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: Which commission emphasises protecting the future generation, in line with the environmentalists' moral argument?
cards.back: The Brundtland Commission emphasises on protecting the future generation.
cards.quote: The Brundtland Commission emphasises on protecting the future generation.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: Development that enhances the natural and built environment must be compatible with which three things?
cards.back:
conservation of natural assets
preservation of the regenerative capacity of the world’s natural ecological system
avoiding the imposition of added costs or risks on future generations
cards.quote: The present generation can promote development that enhances the natural and built environment in ways that are compatible with (i) conservation of natural assets (ii) preservation of the regenerative capacity of the world’s natural ecological system (iii) avoiding the imposition of added costs or risks on future generations.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: What needs to be done to achieve sustainable development, according to Herman Daly?
cards.back:
limiting the human population to a level within the carrying capacity of the environment
technological progress should be input efficient and not input consuming
renewable resources should be extracted on a sustainable basis, that is, rate of extraction should not exceed rate of regeneration
for non-renewable resources rate of depletion should not exceed the rate of creation of renewable substitutes
inefficiencies arising from pollution should be corrected
cards.quote: According to Herman Daly, a leading environmental economist, to achieve sustainable development, the following needs to be done (i) limiting the human population to a level within the carrying capacity of the environment. The carrying capacity of the environment is like a ‘plimsoll line’ of the ship which is its load limit mark. In the absence of the plimsoll line for the economy, human scale grows beyond the carrying capacity of the earth and deviates from sustainable development (ii) technological progress should be input efficient and not input consuming (iii) renewable resources should be extracted on a sustainable basis, that is, rate of extraction should not exceed rate of regeneration (iv) for non-renewable resources rate of depletion should not exceed the rate of creation of renewable substitutes and (v) inefficiencies arising from pollution should be corrected.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: The carrying capacity of the environment is like a ‘____’ of the ship which is its load limit mark.
cards.back: The carrying capacity of the environment is like a ‘plimsoll line’ of the ship which is its load limit mark.
cards.quote: The carrying capacity of the environment is like a ‘plimsoll line’ of the ship which is its load limit mark.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: How many Sustainable Development Goals did the UN formulate in 2015, and by when are they to be achieved?
cards.back: In 2015, the UN formulated 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) intended to be achieved by the year 2030.
cards.quote: In 2015, the UN formulated 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) intended to be achieved by the year 2030.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: What are the adverse environmental impacts of thermal power plants?
cards.back: Thermal power plants emit large quantities of carbon dioxide which is a green house gas. It also produces fly ash which, if not used properly, can cause pollution of water bodies, land and other components of the environment.
cards.quote: Thermal power plants emit large quantities of carbon dioxide which is a green house gas. It also produces fly ash which, if not used properly, can cause pollution of water bodies, land and other components of the environment.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: What are the adverse environmental impacts of hydroelectric projects?
cards.back: Hydroelectric projects inundate forests and interfere with the natural flow of water in catchment areas and the river basins.
cards.quote: Hydroelectric projects inundate forests and interfere with the natural flow of water in catchment areas and the river basins.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: What are the adverse implications of rural households using wood, dung cake or other biomass as fuel?
cards.back: This practice has several adverse implications like deforestation, reduction in green cover, wastage of cattle dung and air pollution.
cards.quote: This practice has several adverse implications like deforestation, reduction in green cover, wastage of cattle dung and air pollution.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: As far as liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) is concerned, it is a ____ — it reduces household pollution to a large extent.
cards.back: As far as liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) is concerned, it is a clean fuel — it reduces household pollution to a large extent.
cards.quote: As far as liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) is concerned, it is a clean fuel — it reduces household pollution to a large extent.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: How does a gobar gas plant work, and what is the leftover slurry used for?
cards.back: For the gobar gas plant to function, cattle dung is fed to the plant and gas is produced which is used as fuel while the slurry which is left over is a very good organic fertiliser and soil conditioner.
cards.quote: For the gobar gas plant to function, cattle dung is fed to the plant and gas is produced which is used as fuel while the slurry which is left over is a very good organic fertiliser and soil conditioner.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: What effect has the use of CNG as fuel in Delhi’s public transport had?
cards.back: In Delhi, the use of Compressed Natural Gas (CNG) as fuel in public transport system has significantly lowered air pollution and the air has become cleaner.
cards.quote: In Delhi, the use of Compressed Natural Gas (CNG) as fuel in public transport system has significantly lowered air pollution and the air has become cleaner.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: Where can wind power provide electricity without any adverse impact on the environment?
cards.back: In areas where speed of wind is usually high, wind mills can provide electricity without any adverse impact on the environment.
cards.quote: In areas where speed of wind is usually high, wind mills can provide electricity without any adverse impact on the environment.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: Now, with the help of ____, solar energy can be converted into electricity.
cards.back: Now, with the help of photovoltaic cells, solar energy can be converted into electricity.
cards.quote: Now, with the help of photovoltaic cells, solar energy can be converted into electricity.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: India is also leading an International body called ____ (ISA).
cards.back: India is also leading an International body called International Solar Alliance (ISA).
cards.quote: India is also leading an International body called International Solar Alliance (ISA).

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: How do mini-hydel plants work?
cards.back: Mini-hydel plants use the energy of such streams to move small turbines. The turbines generate electricity which can be used locally.
cards.quote: Mini-hydel plants use the energy of such streams to move small turbines. The turbines generate electricity which can be used locally.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: Why are mini-hydel plants considered environment-friendly?
cards.back: Such power plants are more or less environment-friendly as they do not change the land use pattern in areas where they are located; they generate enough power to meet local demands. This means that they can also do away with the need for large scale transmission towers and cables and avoid transmission loss.
cards.quote: Such power plants are more or less environment-friendly as they do not change the land use pattern in areas where they are located; they generate enough power to meet local demands. This means that they can also do away with the need for large scale transmission towers and cables and avoid transmission loss.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: How many plant species with medicinal properties does India have, and how many are in regular use?
cards.back: India is very much privileged to have about 15,000 species of plants which have medicinal properties. About 8,000 of these are in regular use in various systems of treatment including the folk tradition.
cards.quote: India is very much privileged to have about 15,000 species of plants which have medicinal properties. About 8,000 of these are in regular use in various systems of treatment including the folk tradition.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: What did farmers neglect in the quest to increase agricultural production over the last five decades?
cards.back: In our quest to increase agricultural production during the last five decades or so, we almost totally neglected the use of compost and completely switched over to chemical fertilisers.
cards.quote: In our quest to increase agricultural production during the last five decades or so, we almost totally neglected the use of compost and completely switched over to chemical fertilisers.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: In NCERT's strategies for sustainable development (biocomposting), what converts organic matter into compost faster than the normal process?
cards.back: Earthworms can convert organic matter into compost faster than the normal composting process.
cards.quote: Earthworms can convert organic matter into compost faster than the normal composting process.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: Several types of pest controlling chemicals have been isolated from ____ and these are being used.
cards.back: Several types of pest controlling chemicals have been isolated from neem and these are being used.
cards.quote: Several types of pest controlling chemicals have been isolated from neem and these are being used.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: Which animals and birds help in controlling pests, according to NCERT?
cards.back: For example, snakes are one of the prime group of animals which prey upon rats, mice and various other pests. Similarly, large varieties of birds, for example, owls and peacocks, prey upon vermin and pests. If these are allowed to dwell around the agricultural areas, they can clear large varieties of pests including insects. Lizards are also important in this regard.
cards.quote: For example, snakes are one of the prime group of animals which prey upon rats, mice and various other pests. Similarly, large varieties of birds, for example, owls and peacocks, prey upon vermin and pests. If these are allowed to dwell around the agricultural areas, they can clear large varieties of pests including insects. Lizards are also important in this regard.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: Now the world is faced with ____ for environmental resources but their supply is limited due to ____.
cards.back: Now the world is faced with increased demand for environmental resources but their supply is limited due to overuse and misuse.
cards.quote: Now the world is faced with increased demand for environmental resources but their supply is limited due to overuse and misuse.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: According to the Recap, what would lead to sustainable development?
cards.back: Promotion of natural resources, conservation, preserving regenerative capacity of ecological system and avoiding the imposition of environmental risks on future generations would lead to sustainable development.
cards.quote: Promotion of natural resources, conservation, preserving regenerative capacity of ecological system and avoiding the imposition of environmental risks on future generations would lead to sustainable development.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Which Article requires the government to present its estimated receipts and expenditures to Parliament every year?
cards.back: There is a constitutional requirement in India (Article 112) to present before the Parliament a statement of estimated receipts and expenditures of the government in respect of every financial year which runs from 1 April to 31 March.
cards.quote: There is a constitutional requirement in India (Article 112) to present before the Parliament a statement of estimated receipts and expenditures of the government in respect of every financial year which runs from 1 April to 31 March.

source.section: Government Budget: Meaning and its Components

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is the main budget document of the government called?
cards.back:
The Annual Financial Statement (Article 112).
This ‘Annual Financial Statement’ constitutes the main budget document of the government.
cards.quote: This ‘Annual Financial Statement’ constitutes the main budget document of the government.

source.section: Government Budget: Meaning and its Components

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Two accounts of the government budget: what does each cover?
cards.back: those that relate to the current financial year only are included in the revenue account (also called revenue budget) and those that concern the assets and liabilities of the government into the capital account (also called capital budget).
cards.quote: those that relate to the current financial year only are included in the revenue account (also called revenue budget) and those that concern the assets and liabilities of the government into the capital account (also called capital budget).

source.section: Government Budget: Meaning and its Components

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: How is the government budget divided, and why?
cards.back: The budget, which gives a statement of the receipts and expenditure of the government, is divided into the revenue budget and capital budget to distinguish between current financial needs and investment in the country's capital stock.
cards.quote: The budget, which gives a statement of the receipts and expenditure of the government, is divided into the revenue budget and capital budget to distinguish between current financial needs and investment in the country's capital stock.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Name the three functions of the government budget.
cards.back: The three functions of allocation, redistribution and stabilisation operate through the expenditure and receipts of the government.
cards.quote: The three functions of allocation, redistribution and stabilisation operate through the expenditure and receipts of the government.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is the allocation function of the government budget?
cards.back: Government provides certain goods and services which cannot be provided by the market mechanism i.e. by exchange between individual consumers and producers.
cards.quote: Government provides certain goods and services which cannot be provided by the market mechanism i.e. by exchange between individual consumers and producers.

source.section: Objectives of Government Budget: Allocation Function

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Examples of such goods are national defence, roads, government administration etc. which are referred to as ____.
cards.back: Examples of such goods are national defence, roads, government administration etc. which are referred to as public goods.
cards.quote: Examples of such goods are national defence, roads, government administration etc. which are referred to as public goods.

source.section: Objectives of Government Budget: Allocation Function

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Public goods vs private goods: the difference on who can enjoy the benefits.
cards.back: One, the benefits of public goods are available to all and are not only restricted to one particular consumer. For example, if a person eats a chocolate or wears a shirt, these will not be available to others.
cards.quote: One, the benefits of public goods are available to all and are not only restricted to one particular consumer. For example, if a person eats a chocolate or wears a shirt, these will not be available to others.

source.section: Objectives of Government Budget: Allocation Function

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Public goods vs private goods: the difference on excluding non-payers.
cards.back: Two, in case of private goods anyone who does not pay for the goods can be excluded from enjoying its benefits. If you do not buy a ticket, you will not be allowed to watch a movie at a local cinema hall. However, in case of public goods, there is no feasible way of excluding anyone from enjoying the benefits of the good.
cards.quote: Two, in case of private goods anyone who does not pay for the goods can be excluded from enjoying its benefits. If you do not buy a ticket, you will not be allowed to watch a movie at a local cinema hall. However, in case of public goods, there is no feasible way of excluding anyone from enjoying the benefits of the good.

source.section: Objectives of Government Budget: Allocation Function

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Why are public goods called non-excludable?
cards.back:
There is no feasible way of excluding anyone from the benefits.
However, in case of public goods, there is no feasible way of excluding anyone from enjoying the benefits of the good. That is why public goods are called non-excludable.
cards.quote: However, in case of public goods, there is no feasible way of excluding anyone from enjoying the benefits of the good. That is why public goods are called non-excludable.

source.section: Objectives of Government Budget: Allocation Function

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What are ‘free-riders’ in the case of public goods?
cards.back: Even if some users do not pay, it is difficult and sometimes impossible to collect fees for the public good. These non-paying users are known as ‘free-riders’.
cards.quote: Even if some users do not pay, it is difficult and sometimes impossible to collect fees for the public good. These non-paying users are known as ‘free-riders’.

source.section: Objectives of Government Budget: Allocation Function

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Public provision vs public production: what is the difference?
cards.back: Public provision means that they are financed through the budget and can be used without any direct payment. Public goods may be produced by the government or the private sector. When goods are produced directly by the government it is called public production.
cards.quote: Public provision means that they are financed through the budget and can be used without any direct payment. Public goods may be produced by the government or the private sector. When goods are produced directly by the government it is called public production.

source.section: Objectives of Government Budget: Allocation Function

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: When goods are produced directly by the government it is called ____.
cards.back: When goods are produced directly by the government it is called public production.
cards.quote: When goods are produced directly by the government it is called public production.

source.section: Objectives of Government Budget: Allocation Function

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Name the two important features of public goods.
cards.back: they are non-rivalrous in that one person can increase her satisfaction from the good without reducing that obtained by others and they are non-excludable, and there is no feasible way of excluding anyone from enjoying the benefits of the good.
cards.quote: they are non-rivalrous in that one person can increase her satisfaction from the good without reducing that obtained by others and they are non-excludable, and there is no feasible way of excluding anyone from enjoying the benefits of the good.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is the redistribution function of the government budget?
cards.back: The government sector affects the personal disposable income of households by making transfers and collecting taxes. It is through this that the government can change the distribution of income and bring about a distribution that is considered ‘fair’ by society. This is the redistribution function.
cards.quote: The government sector affects the personal disposable income of households by making transfers and collecting taxes. It is through this that the government can change the distribution of income and bring about a distribution that is considered ‘fair’ by society. This is the redistribution function.

source.section: Objectives of Government Budget: Redistribution Function

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Out of private income, what finally reaches the households is known as ____ and the amount that can be spent is the ____.
cards.back: Out of private income, what finally reaches the households is known as personal income and the amount that can be spent is the personal disposable income.
cards.quote: Out of private income, what finally reaches the households is known as personal income and the amount that can be spent is the personal disposable income.

source.section: Objectives of Government Budget: Redistribution Function

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is the stabilisation function of the government budget?
cards.back: The intervention of the government whether to expand demand or reduce it constitutes the stabilisation function.
cards.quote: The intervention of the government whether to expand demand or reduce it constitutes the stabilisation function.

source.section: Objectives of Government Budget: Stabilisation Function

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Under high employment, what may demand exceeding available output give rise to?
cards.back:
Inflation; restrictive conditions may be needed to reduce demand.
On the other hand, there may be times when demand exceeds available output under conditions of high employment and thus may give rise to inflation. In such situations, restrictive conditions may be needed to reduce demand.
cards.quote: On the other hand, there may be times when demand exceeds available output under conditions of high employment and thus may give rise to inflation. In such situations, restrictive conditions may be needed to reduce demand.

source.section: Objectives of Government Budget: Stabilisation Function

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What are revenue receipts?
cards.back: Revenue receipts are those receipts that do not lead to a claim on the government. They are therefore termed non-redeemable.
cards.quote: Revenue receipts are those receipts that do not lead to a claim on the government. They are therefore termed non-redeemable.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Revenue receipts are divided into which two heads?
cards.back: They are divided into tax and non-tax revenues.
cards.quote: They are divided into tax and non-tax revenues.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Types of tax revenue: direct and indirect taxes, with NCERT's examples.
cards.back:
direct taxes (personal income tax) and firms (corporation tax)
indirect taxes like excise taxes (duties levied on goods produced within the country), customs duties (taxes imposed on goods imported into and exported out of India) and service tax
cards.quote: Tax revenues, an important component of revenue receipts, have for long been divided into direct taxes (personal income tax) and firms (corporation tax), and indirect taxes like excise taxes (duties levied on goods produced within the country), customs duties (taxes imposed on goods imported into and exported out of India) and service tax

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What are excise taxes?
cards.back: duties levied on goods produced within the country
cards.quote: excise taxes (duties levied on goods produced within the country)

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What are customs duties?
cards.back: taxes imposed on goods imported into and exported out of India
cards.quote: customs duties (taxes imposed on goods imported into and exported out of India)

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What are wealth tax, gift tax and estate duty referred to as, as they never brought in large revenue?
cards.back:
They are referred to as ‘paper taxes’.
Other direct taxes like wealth tax, gift tax and estate duty (now abolished) have never brought in large amount of revenue and thus have been referred to as ‘paper taxes’.
cards.quote: Other direct taxes like wealth tax, gift tax and estate duty (now abolished) have never brought in large amount of revenue and thus have been referred to as ‘paper taxes’.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: The redistribution objective is sought to be achieved through ____, in which higher the income, higher is the tax rate.
cards.back: The redistribution objective is sought to be achieved through progressive income taxation, in which higher the income, higher is the tax rate.
cards.quote: The redistribution objective is sought to be achieved through progressive income taxation, in which higher the income, higher is the tax rate.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: How are excise taxes graded across necessities, comforts and luxuries?
cards.back:
Necessities exempt or low; comforts moderate; luxuries heavy.
With respect to excise taxes, necessities of life are exempted or taxed at low rates, comforts and semi-luxuries are moderately taxed, and luxuries, tobacco and petroleum products are taxed heavily.
cards.quote: With respect to excise taxes, necessities of life are exempted or taxed at low rates, comforts and semi-luxuries are moderately taxed, and luxuries, tobacco and petroleum products are taxed heavily.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Name the main components of non-tax revenue of the central government.
cards.back: Non-tax revenue of the central government mainly consists of interest receipts on account of loans by the central government, dividends and profits on investments made by the government, fees and other receipts for services rendered by the government. Cash grants-in-aid from foreign countries and international organisations are also included.
cards.quote: Non-tax revenue of the central government mainly consists of interest receipts on account of loans by the central government, dividends and profits on investments made by the government, fees and other receipts for services rendered by the government. Cash grants-in-aid from foreign countries and international organisations are also included.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is a Finance Bill?
cards.back: A Finance Bill, presented along with the Annual Financial Statement, provides details on the imposition, abolition, remission, alteration or regulation of taxes proposed in the Budget.
cards.quote: A Finance Bill, presented along with the Annual Financial Statement, provides details on the imposition, abolition, remission, alteration or regulation of taxes proposed in the Budget.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Loans will have to be returned to the agencies from which they have been borrowed. Thus they create ____.
cards.back: Loans will have to be returned to the agencies from which they have been borrowed. Thus they create liability.
cards.quote: Loans will have to be returned to the agencies from which they have been borrowed. Thus they create liability.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What are capital receipts?
cards.back: All those receipts of the government which create liability or reduce financial assets are termed as capital receipts.
cards.quote: All those receipts of the government which create liability or reduce financial assets are termed as capital receipts.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Capital receipts can be of which two types?
cards.back: Thus, these receipts can be debt creating or non-debt creating.
cards.quote: Thus, these receipts can be debt creating or non-debt creating.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is revenue expenditure?
cards.back: Revenue Expenditure is expenditure incurred for purposes other than the creation of physical or financial assets of the central government.
