cards.quote: Revenue Expenditure is expenditure incurred for purposes other than the creation of physical or financial assets of the central government.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What does revenue expenditure relate to?
cards.back: It relates to those expenses incurred for the normal functioning of the government departments and various services, interest payments on debt incurred by the government, and grants given to state governments and other parties (even though some of the grants may be meant for creation of assets).
cards.quote: It relates to those expenses incurred for the normal functioning of the government departments and various services, interest payments on debt incurred by the government, and grants given to state governments and other parties (even though some of the grants may be meant for creation of assets).

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is plan revenue expenditure?
cards.back: According to this classification, plan revenue expenditure relates to central Plans (the Five-Year Plans) and central assistance for State and Union Territory plans.
cards.quote: According to this classification, plan revenue expenditure relates to central Plans (the Five-Year Plans) and central assistance for State and Union Territory plans.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Name the main items of non-plan expenditure.
cards.back: The main items of non-plan expenditure are interest payments, defence services, subsidies, salaries and pensions.
cards.quote: The main items of non-plan expenditure are interest payments, defence services, subsidies, salaries and pensions.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: ____ on market loans, external loans and from various reserve funds constitute the single largest component of non-plan revenue expenditure.
cards.back: Interest payments on market loans, external loans and from various reserve funds constitute the single largest component of non-plan revenue expenditure.
cards.quote: Interest payments on market loans, external loans and from various reserve funds constitute the single largest component of non-plan revenue expenditure.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Defence expenditure, is ____ in the sense that given the national security concerns, there exists little scope for drastic reduction.
cards.back: Defence expenditure, is committed expenditure in the sense that given the national security concerns, there exists little scope for drastic reduction.
cards.quote: Defence expenditure, is committed expenditure in the sense that given the national security concerns, there exists little scope for drastic reduction.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: On which items does the government extend subsidies explicitly?
cards.back: the government also extends subsidies explicitly on items such as exports, interest on loans, food and fertilisers.
cards.quote: the government also extends subsidies explicitly on items such as exports, interest on loans, food and fertilisers.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is capital expenditure?
cards.back: There are expenditures of the government which result in creation of physical or financial assets or reduction in financial liabilities.
cards.quote: There are expenditures of the government which result in creation of physical or financial assets or reduction in financial liabilities.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What does capital expenditure include?
cards.back: This includes expenditure on the acquisition of land, building, machinery, equipment, investment in shares, and loans and advances by the central government to state and union territory governments, PSUs and other parties.
cards.quote: This includes expenditure on the acquisition of land, building, machinery, equipment, investment in shares, and loans and advances by the central government to state and union territory governments, PSUs and other parties.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Plan capital expenditure vs non-plan capital expenditure.
cards.back: Plan capital expenditure, like its revenue counterpart, relates to central plan and central assistance for state and union territory plans. Non-plan capital expenditure covers various general, social and economic services provided by the government.
cards.quote: Plan capital expenditure, like its revenue counterpart, relates to central plan and central assistance for state and union territory plans. Non-plan capital expenditure covers various general, social and economic services provided by the government.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is a balanced budget?
cards.back: The government may spend an amount equal to the revenue it collects. This is known as a balanced budget.
cards.quote: The government may spend an amount equal to the revenue it collects. This is known as a balanced budget.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: When is the budget said to be in surplus?
cards.back: When tax collection exceeds the required expenditure, the budget is said to be in surplus.
cards.quote: When tax collection exceeds the required expenditure, the budget is said to be in surplus.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: When does the government run a budget deficit?
cards.back: However, the most common feature is the situation when expenditure exceeds revenue. This is when the government runs a budget deficit.
cards.quote: However, the most common feature is the situation when expenditure exceeds revenue. This is when the government runs a budget deficit.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Formally, what is a budget deficit?
cards.back: More formally, it refers to the excess of total expenditure (both revenue and capital) over total receipts (both revenue and capital).
cards.quote: More formally, it refers to the excess of total expenditure (both revenue and capital) over total receipts (both revenue and capital).

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: From which budget was the practice of showing budget deficit discontinued in India?
cards.back: From the 1997-98 budget, the practice of showing budget deficit has been discontinued in India.
cards.quote: From the 1997-98 budget, the practice of showing budget deficit has been discontinued in India.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is the revenue deficit?
cards.back: The revenue deficit refers to the excess of government's revenue expenditure over revenue receipts
cards.quote: The revenue deficit refers to the excess of government's revenue expenditure over revenue receipts

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Formula: revenue deficit.
cards.back: Revenue deficit = Revenue expenditure – Revenue receipts
cards.quote: Revenue deficit = Revenue expenditure – Revenue receipts

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What does it imply when the government incurs a revenue deficit?
cards.back:
The government is dissaving, using up other sectors’ savings.
When the government incurs a revenue deficit, it implies that the government is dissaving and is using up the savings of the other sectors of the economy to finance a part of its consumption expenditure.
cards.quote: When the government incurs a revenue deficit, it implies that the government is dissaving and is using up the savings of the other sectors of the economy to finance a part of its consumption expenditure.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: When the government must cut expenditure, what kind of expenditure forms a major part of revenue expenditure and cannot be reduced?
cards.back: Since a major part of revenue expenditure is committed expenditure, it cannot be reduced.
cards.quote: Since a major part of revenue expenditure is committed expenditure, it cannot be reduced.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is the fiscal deficit?
cards.back: Fiscal deficit is the difference between the government's total expenditure and its total receipts excluding borrowing
cards.quote: Fiscal deficit is the difference between the government's total expenditure and its total receipts excluding borrowing

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Formula: gross fiscal deficit (from the expenditure and receipts side).
cards.back: Gross fiscal deficit = Total expenditure – (Revenue receipts + Non-debt creating capital receipts)
cards.quote: Gross fiscal deficit = Total expenditure – (Revenue receipts + Non-debt creating capital receipts)

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What are non-debt creating capital receipts?
cards.back: Non-debt creating capital receipts are those receipts which are not borrowings and, therefore, do not give rise to debt. Examples are recovery of loans and the proceeds from the sale of PSUs.
cards.quote: Non-debt creating capital receipts are those receipts which are not borrowings and, therefore, do not give rise to debt. Examples are recovery of loans and the proceeds from the sale of PSUs.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: The fiscal deficit will have to be financed through borrowing. Thus, it indicates the ____ of the government from all sources.
cards.back: The fiscal deficit will have to be financed through borrowing. Thus, it indicates the total borrowing requirements of the government from all sources.
cards.quote: The fiscal deficit will have to be financed through borrowing. Thus, it indicates the total borrowing requirements of the government from all sources.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Formula: gross fiscal deficit (from the financing side).
cards.back: Gross fiscal deficit = Net borrowing at home + Borrowing from RBI + Borrowing from abroad
cards.quote: Gross fiscal deficit = Net borrowing at home + Borrowing from RBI + Borrowing from abroad

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What does net borrowing at home include?
cards.back: Net borrowing at home includes that directly borrowed from the public through debt instruments (for example, the various small savings schemes) and indirectly from commercial banks through Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR).
cards.quote: Net borrowing at home includes that directly borrowed from the public through debt instruments (for example, the various small savings schemes) and indirectly from commercial banks through Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR).

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: How is the revenue deficit related to the gross fiscal deficit?
cards.back:
Revenue deficit is a part of fiscal deficit.
From the way gross fiscal deficit is measured as given above, it can be seen that revenue deficit is a part of fiscal deficit
cards.quote: From the way gross fiscal deficit is measured as given above, it can be seen that revenue deficit is a part of fiscal deficit

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Formula: fiscal deficit in terms of revenue deficit (NCERT's bracketed line).
cards.back: Fiscal Deficit = Revenue Deficit + Capital Expenditure - non-debt creating capital receipts
cards.quote: Fiscal Deficit = Revenue Deficit + Capital Expenditure - non-debt creating capital receipts
cards.note: The full line ends '... non-debt creating capital receipts'. Fiscal deficit = revenue deficit + capital expenditure - non-debt creating capital receipts.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: The growth of ____ as a percentage of fiscal deficit points to a deterioration in the quality of government expenditure
cards.back: The growth of revenue deficit as a percentage of fiscal deficit points to a deterioration in the quality of government expenditure
cards.quote: The growth of revenue deficit as a percentage of fiscal deficit points to a deterioration in the quality of government expenditure

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is the primary deficit?
cards.back: To obtain an estimate of borrowing on account of current expenditures exceeding revenues, we need to calculate what has been called the primary deficit. It is simply the fiscal deficit minus the interest payments
cards.quote: To obtain an estimate of borrowing on account of current expenditures exceeding revenues, we need to calculate what has been called the primary deficit. It is simply the fiscal deficit minus the interest payments

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Formula: gross primary deficit.
cards.back: Gross primary deficit = Gross fiscal deficit – Net interest liabilities
cards.quote: Gross primary deficit = Gross fiscal deficit – Net interest liabilities

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What do net interest liabilities consist of?
cards.back: Net interest liabilities consist of interest payments minus interest receipts by the government on net domestic lending.
cards.quote: Net interest liabilities consist of interest payments minus interest receipts by the government on net domestic lending.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is one of the main criticisms of government deficits, and why?
cards.back: One of the main criticisms of deficits is that they are inflationary. This is because when government increases spending or cuts taxes, aggregate demand increases.
cards.quote: One of the main criticisms of deficits is that they are inflationary. This is because when government increases spending or cuts taxes, aggregate demand increases.

source.section: Other Perspectives on Deficits and Debt

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: How can a government deficit be reduced?
cards.back: Government deficit can be reduced by an increase in taxes or reduction in expenditure.
cards.quote: Government deficit can be reduced by an increase in taxes or reduction in expenditure.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: Why does an educated person generate more income than an uneducated one (NCERT 4.1)?
cards.back: We know that the labour skill of an educated person is more than that of an uneducated person and hence the former is able to generate more income than the latter
cards.quote: We know that the labour skill of an educated person is more than that of an uneducated person and hence the former is able to generate more income than the latter

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: Name the other highly valued benefits of education, besides higher earning capacity (NCERT 4.1).
cards.back:
it gives one a better social standing and pride
it enables one to make better choices in life
it provides knowledge to understand the changes taking place in society
it also stimulates innovations
cards.quote: Education is sought not only as it confers higher earning capacity on people but also for its other highly valued benefits: it gives one a better social standing and pride; it enables one to make better choices in life; it provides knowledge to understand the changes taking place in society; it also stimulates innovations.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: What is human capital? (NCERT recap)
cards.back: Investments in education convert human beings into human capital; human capital represents enhanced labour productivity, which is an acquired ability and an outcome of deliberate investment decisions with an expectation that it will increase future income sources.
cards.quote: Investments in education convert human beings into human capital; human capital represents enhanced labour productivity, which is an acquired ability and an outcome of deliberate investment decisions with an expectation that it will increase future income sources.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: Name the sources of human capital formation (NCERT recap).
cards.back:
Education
On-the-job training
Health
Migration
Information
cards.quote: Investments in education, on-the-job training, health, migration and information are the sources of human capital formation.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: Why is expenditure on health a source of human capital formation (NCERT 4.3)?
cards.back: A sick labourer without access to medical facilities is compelled to abstain from work and there is loss of productivity. Hence, expenditure on health is an important source of human capital formation.
cards.quote: A sick labourer without access to medical facilities is compelled to abstain from work and there is loss of productivity. Hence, expenditure on health is an important source of human capital formation.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: Name the various forms of health expenditure (NCERT 4.3).
cards.back:
preventive medicine (vaccination)
curative medicine (medical intervention during illness)
social medicine (spread of health literacy)
provision of clean drinking water and good sanitation
cards.quote: The amount of money spent on preventive medicine (vaccination), curative medicine (medical intervention during illness), social medicine (spread of health literacy) and provision of clean drinking water and good sanitation are the various forms of health expenditures.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: Health expenditure directly increases the supply of ____ and is, thus, a source of human capital formation.
cards.back: Health expenditure directly increases the supply of healthy labour force and is, thus, a source of human capital formation.
cards.quote: Health expenditure directly increases the supply of healthy labour force and is, thus, a source of human capital formation.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: What are the two forms of on-the-job training given by firms (NCERT 4.3)?
cards.back:
the workers may be trained in the firm itself under the supervision of a skilled worker
the workers may be sent for off-campus training
cards.quote: This may take different forms: one, the workers may be trained in the firm itself under the supervision of a skilled worker; two, the workers may be sent for off-campus training.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: Expenditure regarding ____ is a source of human capital formation as the return of such expenditure in the form of ____ is more than the cost of it.
cards.back: Expenditure regarding on-the-job training is a source of human capital formation as the return of such expenditure in the form of enhanced labour productivity is more than the cost of it.
cards.quote: Expenditure regarding on-the-job training is a source of human capital formation as the return of such expenditure in the form of enhanced labour productivity is more than the cost of it.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: NCERT 4.3: what drives rural-urban migration in India, unlike emigration of engineers and doctors for higher salaries?
cards.back: Unemployment is the reason for the rural-urban migration in India.
cards.quote: Unemployment is the reason for the rural-urban migration in India.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: Name the costs involved in migration (NCERT 4.3).
cards.back:
cost of transport
higher cost of living in the migrated places
psychic costs of living in a strange sociocultural setup
cards.quote: Migration in both these cases involves cost of transport, higher cost of living in the migrated places and psychic costs of living in a strange sociocultural setup.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: Why is expenditure on migration a source of human capital formation (NCERT 4.3)?
cards.back: The enhanced earnings in the new place outweigh the costs of migration; hence, expenditure on migration is also a source of human capital formation.
cards.quote: The enhanced earnings in the new place outweigh the costs of migration; hence, expenditure on migration is also a source of human capital formation.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: Expenditure incurred for ____ relating to the labour market and other markets is also a source of human capital formation.
cards.back: Expenditure incurred for acquiring information relating to the labour market and other markets is also a source of human capital formation.
cards.quote: Expenditure incurred for acquiring information relating to the labour market and other markets is also a source of human capital formation.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: Both the forms of capital formation are outcomes of ____.
cards.back: Both the forms of capital formation are outcomes of conscious investment decisions.
cards.quote: Both the forms of capital formation are outcomes of conscious investment decisions.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: Human capital formation is partly a ____ and partly a ____ of the possessor of the human capital.
cards.back: Human capital formation is partly a social process and partly a conscious decision of the possessor of the human capital.
cards.quote: Human capital formation is partly a social process and partly a conscious decision of the possessor of the human capital.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: Physical capital vs human capital: the difference on tangibility and sale in the market.
cards.back: Physical capital is tangible and can be easily sold in the market like any other commodity. Human capital is intangible; it is endogenously built in the body and mind of its owner.
cards.quote: Physical capital is tangible and can be easily sold in the market like any other commodity. Human capital is intangible; it is endogenously built in the body and mind of its owner.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: Physical capital vs human capital: the difference on separability from the owner.
cards.back: The physical capital is separable from its owner, whereas, human capital is inseparable from its owner.
cards.quote: The physical capital is separable from its owner, whereas, human capital is inseparable from its owner.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: Physical capital vs human capital: the difference on mobility across countries.
cards.back: The two forms of capital differ in terms of mobility across space. Physical capital is completely mobile between countries except for some artificial trade restrictions. Human capital is not perfectly mobile between countries as movement is restricted by nationality and culture.
cards.quote: The two forms of capital differ in terms of mobility across space. Physical capital is completely mobile between countries except for some artificial trade restrictions. Human capital is not perfectly mobile between countries as movement is restricted by nationality and culture.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: Physical capital vs human capital: the difference on how capital formation is built.
cards.back: Therefore, physical capital formation can be built even through imports, whereas human capital formation is to be done through conscious policy formulations in consonance with the nature of the society and economy and expenditure by the state and the individuals.
cards.quote: Therefore, physical capital formation can be built even through imports, whereas human capital formation is to be done through conscious policy formulations in consonance with the nature of the society and economy and expenditure by the state and the individuals.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: Physical capital vs human capital: the difference on depreciation.
cards.back: Both forms of capital depreciate with time but the nature of depreciation differs between the two. Continuous use of machine leads to depreciation and change of technology makes a machine obsolete. In the case of human capital, depreciation takes place with ageing but can be reduced, to a large extent, through continuous investment in education, health, etc.
cards.quote: Both forms of capital depreciate with time but the nature of depreciation differs between the two. Continuous use of machine leads to depreciation and change of technology makes a machine obsolete. In the case of human capital, depreciation takes place with ageing but can be reduced, to a large extent, through continuous investment in education, health, etc.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: Physical capital vs human capital: the difference on private and social benefits.
cards.back: Human capital creates both private and social benefits, whereas physical capital creates only private benefit.
cards.quote: Human capital creates both private and social benefits, whereas physical capital creates only private benefit.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: What is the external benefit of human capital? (NCERT Box 4.1)
cards.back: Human capital benefits not only the owner but also the society in general. This is called external benefit.
cards.quote: Human capital benefits not only the owner but also the society in general. This is called external benefit.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: How does an educated person and a healthy person benefit the society (examples of external benefit in NCERT Box 4.1)?
cards.back: An educated person can effectively take part in a democratic process and contribute to the socio-economic progress of a nation. A healthy person, by maintaining personal hygiene and sanitation, stops the spread of contagious diseases and epidemics.
cards.quote: An educated person can effectively take part in a democratic process and contribute to the socio-economic progress of a nation. A healthy person, by maintaining personal hygiene and sanitation, stops the spread of contagious diseases and epidemics.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: What is economic growth? (NCERT 4.3)
cards.back: Economic growth means the increase in real national income of a country
cards.quote: Economic growth means the increase in real national income of a country

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: Education provides ____ to understand changes in society and scientific advancements, thus, facilitate ____.
cards.back: Education provides knowledge to understand changes in society and scientific advancements, thus, facilitate inventions and innovations.
cards.quote: Education provides knowledge to understand changes in society and scientific advancements, thus, facilitate inventions and innovations.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: The human capital growth in developing countries has been faster but the growth of ____ has not been that fast.
cards.back: The human capital growth in developing countries has been faster but the growth of per capita real income has not been that fast.
cards.quote: The human capital growth in developing countries has been faster but the growth of per capita real income has not been that fast.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: That is, ____ causes building of high level of human capital and vice versa, that is, high level of human capital causes ____.
cards.back: That is, higher income causes building of high level of human capital and vice versa, that is, high level of human capital causes growth of income.
cards.quote: That is, higher income causes building of high level of human capital and vice versa, that is, high level of human capital causes growth of income.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: Which Five Year Plan said that human resources development must be given a key role in any development strategy? Give its words.
cards.back: The Seventh Five Year Plan says, "Human resources development (read human capital) has necessarily to be assigned a key role in any development strategy, particularly in a country with a large population. Trained and educated on sound lines, a large population can itself become an asset in accelerating economic growth and in ensuring social change in desired directions."
cards.quote: The Seventh Five Year Plan says, "Human resources development (read human capital) has necessarily to be assigned a key role in any development strategy, particularly in a country with a large population. Trained and educated on sound lines, a large population can itself become an asset in accelerating economic growth and in ensuring social change in desired directions."

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: Human capital vs human development: the difference on how education and health are viewed.
cards.back: Human capital considers education and health as a means to increase labour productivity. Human development is based on the idea that education and health are integral to human well-being because only when people have the ability to read and write and the ability to lead a long and healthy life, they will be able to make other choices which they value.
cards.quote: Human capital considers education and health as a means to increase labour productivity. Human development is based on the idea that education and health are integral to human well-being because only when people have the ability to read and write and the ability to lead a long and healthy life, they will be able to make other choices which they value.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: Human capital vs human development: the difference on how human beings are treated.
cards.back: Human capital treats human beings as a means to an end; the end being the increase in productivity. In this view, any investment in education and health is unproductive if it does not enhance output of goods and services. In the human development perspective, human beings are ends in themselves.
cards.quote: Human capital treats human beings as a means to an end; the end being the increase in productivity. In this view, any investment in education and health is unproductive if it does not enhance output of goods and services. In the human development perspective, human beings are ends in themselves.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: ____ should be increased through investments in education and health even if such investments do not result in ____.
cards.back: Human welfare should be increased through investments in education and health even if such investments do not result in higher labour productivity.
cards.quote: Human welfare should be increased through investments in education and health even if such investments do not result in higher labour productivity.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: In the human development view, what right does every individual have (NCERT 4.4)?
cards.back: every individual has a right to be literate and lead a healthy life
cards.quote: every individual has a right to be literate and lead a healthy life

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: Name the three tiers of government in India that carry out expenditure on education and health (NCERT 4.5).
cards.back:
union government
state governments
local governments (Municipal Corporations, Municipalities and Village Panchayats)
cards.quote: We know that India is a federal country with a union government, state governments and local governments (Municipal Corporations, Municipalities and Village Panchayats).

source.section: 4.5 State of Human Capital Formation in India

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: What two kinds of benefits do education and health care services create (NCERT 4.5)?
cards.back: education and health care services create both private and social benefits and this is the reason for the existence of both private and public institutions in the education and health service markets
cards.quote: education and health care services create both private and social benefits and this is the reason for the existence of both private and public institutions in the education and health service markets

source.section: 4.5 State of Human Capital Formation in India

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: Expenditures on education and health make substantial long-term impact and they ____; hence, ____ is essential.
cards.back: Expenditures on education and health make substantial long-term impact and they cannot be easily reversed; hence, government intervention is essential.
cards.quote: Expenditures on education and health make substantial long-term impact and they cannot be easily reversed; hence, government intervention is essential.

source.section: 4.5 State of Human Capital Formation in India

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: What is the government's role towards private providers of education and health services (NCERT 4.5)?
cards.back: The role of government in this situation is to ensure that the private providers of these services adhere to the standards stipulated by the government and charge the correct price.
cards.quote: The role of government in this situation is to ensure that the private providers of these services adhere to the standards stipulated by the government and charge the correct price.

source.section: 4.5 State of Human Capital Formation in India

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: NCERT 4.5 gives three example organisations that facilitate institutions in India's education sector. Name them.
cards.back:
National Council of Educational Research and Training (NCERT)
University Grants Commission (UGC)
All India Council of Technical Education (AICTE)
cards.quote: In India, the ministries of education at the union and state level, departments of education and various organisations like National Council of Educational Research and Training (NCERT), University Grants Commission (UGC) and All India Council of Technical Education (AICTE) facilitate institutions which come under the education sector.

source.section: 4.5 State of Human Capital Formation in India

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: In what two ways is government expenditure on education expressed (NCERT 4.6)?
cards.back:
as a percentage of 'total government expenditure'
as a percentage of Gross Domestic Product (GDP)
cards.quote: This expenditure by the government is expressed in two ways (i) as a percentage of 'total government expenditure' (ii) as a percentage of Gross Domestic Product (GDP).

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: The percentage of 'education expenditure of total government expenditure' indicates the ____ in the scheme of things before the government.
cards.back: The percentage of 'education expenditure of total government expenditure' indicates the importance of education in the scheme of things before the government.
cards.quote: The percentage of 'education expenditure of total government expenditure' indicates the importance of education in the scheme of things before the government.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: What does the percentage of 'education expenditure of GDP' express (NCERT 4.6)?
cards.back: The percentage of 'education expenditure of GDP' expresses how much of people's income is being committed to the development of education in the country.
cards.quote: The percentage of 'education expenditure of GDP' expresses how much of people's income is being committed to the development of education in the country.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: Which level of education takes the major share of total education expenditure, and which the least (NCERT 4.6)?
cards.back: Elementary education takes a major share of total education expenditure and the share of the higher/tertiary education (institutions of higher learning like colleges, polytechnics and universities) is the least.
cards.quote: Elementary education takes a major share of total education expenditure and the share of the higher/tertiary education (institutions of higher learning like colleges, polytechnics and universities) is the least.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: Though, on an average, the government spends less on tertiary education, '____' in tertiary education is ____ than that of elementary.
cards.back: Though, on an average, the government spends less on tertiary education, 'expenditure per student' in tertiary education is higher than that of elementary.
cards.quote: Though, on an average, the government spends less on tertiary education, 'expenditure per student' in tertiary education is higher than that of elementary.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: In 2020-21, which state had the highest and which the lowest per capita public expenditure on elementary education (NCERT 4.6)?
cards.back: In 2020-21, the per capita public expenditure on elementary education differs considerably across states from as high as Rs 96,968 in Sikkim to as low as Rs 10,710 in Bihar.
cards.quote: In 2020-21, the per capita public expenditure on elementary education differs considerably across states from as high as Rs 96,968 in Sikkim to as low as Rs 10,710 in Bihar.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: Compared to this desired level of education expenditure of around ____ of GDP, the current level of a little over ____ has been quite inadequate.
cards.back: Compared to this desired level of education expenditure of around 6 per cent of GDP, the current level of a little over 4 per cent has been quite inadequate.
cards.quote: Compared to this desired level of education expenditure of around 6 per cent of GDP, the current level of a little over 4 per cent has been quite inadequate.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: What are the indicators of educational achievement in a country (NCERT 4.6)?
cards.back:
adult literacy level
primary education completion rate
youth literacy rate
cards.quote: Generally, educational achievements in a country are indicated in terms of adult literacy level, primary education completion rate and youth literacy rate.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: Within how many years of the commencement of the Constitution were the Directive Principles to provide free and compulsory education up to age 14?
cards.back: the government should provide free and compulsory education for all children up to the age of 14 years within 10 years from the commencement of the Constitution.
cards.quote: the government should provide free and compulsory education for all children up to the age of 14 years within 10 years from the commencement of the Constitution.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: What is happening to male-female differences in literacy rates in India (NCERT 4.7)?
cards.back: The differences in literacy rates between males and females are narrowing signifying a positive development in gender equity
cards.quote: The differences in literacy rates between males and females are narrowing signifying a positive development in gender equity

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: Name the reasons NCERT gives for promoting women's education in India.
cards.back:
improving economic independence and social status of women
women education makes a favourable impact on fertility rate and health care of women and children
cards.quote: still the need to promote education for women in India is imminent for various reasons such as improving economic independence and social status of women and also because women education makes a favourable impact on fertility rate and health care of women and children.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: What does NCERT say about the shape of the Indian education pyramid (4.7)?
cards.back: The Indian education pyramid is steep, indicating lesser and lesser number of people reaching the higher education level.
cards.quote: The Indian education pyramid is steep, indicating lesser and lesser number of people reaching the higher education level.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: In India's education pyramid (Higher Education: few takers), which group has the highest level of unemployment?
cards.back: The level of unemployment among educated youth is the highest.
cards.quote: the level of unemployment among educated youth is the highest.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: The spread of education and health services across different sectors of society should be ensured so as to simultaneously attain ____.
cards.back: The spread of education and health services across different sectors of society should be ensured so as to simultaneously attain economic growth and equity.
cards.quote: The spread of education and health services across different sectors of society should be ensured so as to simultaneously attain economic growth and equity.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: The basic objective of macroeconomics is to develop theoretical tools, called ____
cards.back: The basic objective of macroeconomics is to develop theoretical tools, called models
cards.quote: The basic objective of macroeconomics is to develop theoretical tools, called models

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is the assumption of ceteris paribus?
cards.back: This is a stylisation typical of almost any theoretical exercise and is called the assumption of ceteris paribus, which literally means 'other things remaining equal'.
cards.quote: This is a stylisation typical of almost any theoretical exercise and is called the assumption of ceteris paribus, which literally means 'other things remaining equal'.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: In this chapter we deal with the determination of National Income under the assumption of ____ of final goods and ____ in the economy.
cards.back: In this chapter we deal with the determination of National Income under the assumption of fixed price of final goods and constant rate of interest in the economy.
cards.quote: In this chapter we deal with the determination of National Income under the assumption of fixed price of final goods and constant rate of interest in the economy.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: On whose theory is the model of this chapter based?
cards.back: The theoretical model used in this chapter is based on the theory given by John Maynard Keynes.
cards.quote: The theoretical model used in this chapter is based on the theory given by John Maynard Keynes.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What are ex post measures of consumption, investment or output?
cards.back: We call these actual or accounting values ex post measures of these items.
cards.quote: We call these actual or accounting values ex post measures of these items.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What are ex ante measures of consumption, investment or output?
cards.back: We call the planned values of the variables – consumption, investment or output of final goods – their ex ante measures.
cards.quote: We call the planned values of the variables – consumption, investment or output of final goods – their ex ante measures.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: In simple words, ex-ante depicts what has been ____, and ex-post depicts what has actually ____.
cards.back: In simple words, ex-ante depicts what has been planned, and ex-post depicts what has actually happened.
cards.quote: In simple words, ex-ante depicts what has been planned, and ex-post depicts what has actually happened.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Planned stock addition Rs 100, but Rs 30 sold from stock. Name her ex ante and ex post investment.
cards.back: Her planned investment is Rs 100 whereas her actual, or ex post, investment is Rs 70 only.
cards.quote: Her planned investment is Rs 100 whereas her actual, or ex post, investment is Rs 70 only.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is a consumption function?
cards.back: A consumption function describes the relation between consumption and income.
cards.quote: A consumption function describes the relation between consumption and income.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: The most important determinant of consumption demand is ____.
cards.back: The most important determinant of consumption demand is household income.
cards.quote: The most important determinant of consumption demand is household income.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is autonomous consumption?
cards.back: Autonomous consumption is denoted by C̅ and shows the consumption which is independent of income.
cards.quote: Autonomous consumption is denoted by C̅ and shows the consumption which is independent of income.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Formula: the consumption function (4.1).
cards.back:
C = C̅ + cY
Here C is the consumption expenditure by households.
Autonomous consumption is denoted by C̅ and shows the consumption which is independent of income.
The induced component of consumption, cY shows the dependence of consumption on income.
When income rises by Re 1. induced consumption rises by MPC i.e. c or the marginal propensity to consume.
cards.quote: We can describe this function as: C = C̅ + cY (4.1) The above equation is called the consumption function. Here C is the consumption expenditure by households. This consists of two components: autonomous consumption and induced consumption ( cY ). Autonomous consumption is denoted by C̅ and shows the consumption which is independent of income. If consumption takes place even when income is zero, it is because of autonomous consumption. The induced component of consumption, cY shows the dependence of consumption on income. When income rises by Re 1. induced consumption rises by MPC i.e. c or the marginal propensity to consume.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: If consumption takes place even when ____, it is because of ____.
cards.back: If consumption takes place even when income is zero, it is because of autonomous consumption.
cards.quote: If consumption takes place even when income is zero, it is because of autonomous consumption.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Formula: marginal propensity to consume (MPC).
cards.back:
Marginal propensity to consume (MPC): it is the change in consumption per unit change in income.
It is denoted by c and is equal to ∆C/∆Y.
cards.quote: Marginal propensity to consume (MPC): it is the change in consumption per unit change in income. It is denoted by c and is equal to ∆C/∆Y.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Generally, MPC lies between ____ and ____ (inclusive of both values).
cards.back: Generally, MPC lies between 0 and 1 (inclusive of both values).
cards.quote: Generally, MPC lies between 0 and 1 (inclusive of both values).
cards.note: MPC cannot exceed 1 because consumption cannot rise by more than income.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: The maximum value which c can take is ____.
cards.back: The maximum value which c can take is 1.
cards.quote: The maximum value which c can take is 1.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Imagenia: C = 100 + 0.8Y. Give autonomous consumption, MPC, and the rise in C if Y rises by Rs 100.
cards.back: Imagenia's autonomous consumption is 100. Its marginal propensity to consume is 0.8. This means that if income goes up by Rs. 100 in Imagenia, consumption will go up by Rs. 80.
cards.quote: Imagenia's autonomous consumption is 100. Its marginal propensity to consume is 0.8. This means that if income goes up by Rs. 100 in Imagenia, consumption will go up by Rs. 80.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is savings?
cards.back: Savings is that part of income that is not consumed.
cards.quote: Savings is that part of income that is not consumed.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Formula: savings (S) in terms of income and consumption.
cards.back:
S = Y – C
Savings is that part of income that is not consumed.
cards.quote: Savings is that part of income that is not consumed. In other words, S = Y – C

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Define marginal propensity to consume (MPC).
cards.back: Marginal propensity to consume (MPC): it is the change in consumption per unit change in income.
cards.quote: Marginal propensity to consume (MPC): it is the change in consumption per unit change in income.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Define marginal propensity to save (MPS).
cards.back: Marginal propensity to save (MPS): it is the change in savings per unit change in income. It is denoted by s and is equal to 1 – c.
cards.quote: Marginal propensity to save (MPS): it is the change in savings per unit change in income. It is denoted by s and is equal to 1 – c.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Formula: MPS in terms of MPC (c).
cards.back:
Marginal propensity to save (MPS): it is the change in savings per unit change in income.
It is denoted by s and is equal to 1 – c.
It implies that s + c = 1.
cards.quote: Marginal propensity to save (MPS): it is the change in savings per unit change in income. It is denoted by s and is equal to 1 – c. It implies that s + c = 1.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Define average propensity to consume (APC).
cards.back: Average propensity to consume (APC): it is the consumption per unit of income
cards.quote: Average propensity to consume (APC): it is the consumption per unit of income

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Define average propensity to save (APS).
cards.back: Average propensity to save (APS): it is the savings per unit of income
cards.quote: Average propensity to save (APS): it is the savings per unit of income

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Define investment.
cards.back: Investment is defined as addition to the stock of physical capital (such as machines, buildings, roads etc., i.e. anything that adds to the future productive capacity of the economy) and changes in the inventory (or the stock of finished goods) of a producer.
cards.quote: Investment is defined as addition to the stock of physical capital (such as machines, buildings, roads etc., i.e. anything that adds to the future productive capacity of the economy) and changes in the inventory (or the stock of finished goods) of a producer.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Note that 'investment goods' (such as machines) are also part of the ____ – they are not ____ like raw materials.
cards.back: Note that 'investment goods' (such as machines) are also part of the final goods – they are not intermediate goods like raw materials.
cards.quote: Note that 'investment goods' (such as machines) are also part of the final goods – they are not intermediate goods like raw materials.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Investment decisions by producers, such as whether to buy a new machine, depend, to a large extent, on the ____.
cards.back: Investment decisions by producers, such as whether to buy a new machine, depend, to a large extent, on the market rate of interest.
cards.quote: Investment decisions by producers, such as whether to buy a new machine, depend, to a large extent, on the market rate of interest.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Formula: ex ante investment demand (4.2).
cards.back:
I = I̅
where I̅ is a positive constant which represents the autonomous (given or exogenous) investment in the economy in a given year.
cards.quote: We can write the ex ante investment demand as I = I̅ (4.2) where I̅ is a positive constant which represents the autonomous (given or exogenous) investment in the economy in a given year.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Formula: ex ante aggregate demand in an economy without a government.
cards.back: In an economy without a government, the ex ante aggregate demand for final goods is the sum total of the ex ante consumption expenditure and ex ante investment expenditure on such goods, viz. AD = C + I.
cards.quote: In an economy without a government, the ex ante aggregate demand for final goods is the sum total of the ex ante consumption expenditure and ex ante investment expenditure on such goods, viz. AD = C + I.

source.section: 4.2 Determination of Income in Two-Sector Model

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is total autonomous expenditure (A)?
cards.back: where A̅ = C̅ + I̅ is the total autonomous expenditure in the economy.
cards.quote: where A̅ = C̅ + I̅ is the total autonomous expenditure in the economy.

source.section: 4.2 Determination of Income in Two-Sector Model

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Ex ante supply is equal to ex ante demand only when the final goods market, and hence the economy, is in ____.
cards.back: Ex ante supply is equal to ex ante demand only when the final goods market, and hence the economy, is in equilibrium.
cards.quote: Ex ante supply is equal to ex ante demand only when the final goods market, and hence the economy, is in equilibrium.

source.section: 4.2 Determination of Income in Two-Sector Model

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Stocks will be piling up in the warehouses which we may consider as ____ of inventories.
cards.back: Stocks will be piling up in the warehouses which we may consider as unintended accumulation of inventories.
cards.quote: Stocks will be piling up in the warehouses which we may consider as unintended accumulation of inventories.

source.section: 4.2 Determination of Income in Two-Sector Model

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What are inventories (stocks)?
cards.back: inventories or stocks refers to that part of output produced which is not sold and therefore remains with the firm.
cards.quote: inventories or stocks refers to that part of output produced which is not sold and therefore remains with the firm.

source.section: 4.2 Determination of Income in Two-Sector Model

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: When is inventory investment positive, and when negative?
cards.back: It can be negative as well as positive: if there is a rise in inventory, it is positive inventory investment, while a depletion of inventory is negative inventory investment.
cards.quote: It can be negative as well as positive: if there is a rise in inventory, it is positive inventory investment, while a depletion of inventory is negative inventory investment.

source.section: 4.2 Determination of Income in Two-Sector Model

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Types of inventory investment (two reasons it takes place).
cards.back:
(i) the firm decides to keep some stocks for various reasons (this is called planned inventory investment)
(ii) the sales differ from the planned level of sales, in which case the firm has to add to/run down existing inventories (this is called unplanned inventory investment)
cards.quote: The inventory investment can take place due to two reasons: (i) the firm decides to keep some stocks for various reasons (this is called planned inventory investment) (ii) the sales differ from the planned level of sales, in which case the firm has to add to/run down existing inventories (this is called unplanned inventory investment).

source.section: 4.2 Determination of Income in Two-Sector Model

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Which fiscal variables summarise how the government affects aggregate demand?
cards.back: The major economic activities of the government that affect the aggregate demand for final goods and services can be summarized by the fiscal variables Tax (T) and Government Expenditure (G), both autonomous to our analysis.
cards.quote: The major economic activities of the government that affect the aggregate demand for final goods and services can be summarized by the fiscal variables Tax (T) and Government Expenditure (G), both autonomous to our analysis.

source.section: 4.2 Determination of Income in Two-Sector Model

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Formula: disposable income (Yd) when the government imposes taxes T.
cards.back: On the other hand, taxes imposed by the government take a part of the income away from the household, whose disposable income, therefore, becomes Yd = Y – T.
cards.quote: On the other hand, taxes imposed by the government take a part of the income away from the household, whose disposable income, therefore, becomes Yd = Y – T.

source.section: 4.2 Determination of Income in Two-Sector Model

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Without indirect taxes and subsidies, what does GDP become identically equal to?
cards.back: Observe also, that without the government imposing indirect taxes and subsidies, the total value of final goods and services produced in the economy, GDP, becomes identically equal to the National Income.
cards.quote: Observe also, that without the government imposing indirect taxes and subsidies, the total value of final goods and services produced in the economy, GDP, becomes identically equal to the National Income.

source.section: 4.2 Determination of Income in Two-Sector Model

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Steps in macroeconomic theory of equilibrium, in order.
cards.back:
at the first stage, we work out a macroeconomic equilibrium taking the price level as fixed.
At the second stage, we allow the price level to vary and again, analyse macroeconomic equilibrium.
cards.quote: In macroeconomic theory we proceed in two steps: at the first stage, we work out a macroeconomic equilibrium taking the price level as fixed. At the second stage, we allow the price level to vary and again, analyse macroeconomic equilibrium.

source.section: 4.3 Determination of Equilibrium Income in the Short Run

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Name the two justifications for taking the price level as fixed.
cards.back:
(i) at the first stage, we are assuming an economy with unused resources: machineries, buildings and labours. In such a situation, the law of diminishing returns will not apply; hence additional output can be produced without increasing marginal cost. Accordingly, price level does not vary even if the quantity produced changes
(ii) this is just a simplifying assumption which will be changed later.
cards.quote: (i) at the first stage, we are assuming an economy with unused resources: machineries, buildings and labours. In such a situation, the law of diminishing returns will not apply; hence additional output can be produced without increasing marginal cost. Accordingly, price level does not vary even if the quantity produced changes (ii) this is just a simplifying assumption which will be changed later.

source.section: 4.3 Determination of Equilibrium Income in the Short Run

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: In the two-sector model, what does it mean that investment I̅ is autonomous?
cards.back: In this model, I̅ is autonomous which means, it is the same no matter whatever is the level of income.
cards.quote: In this model, I̅ is autonomous which means, it is the same no matter whatever is the level of income.

source.section: 4.3.1 Macroeconomic Equilibrium with Price Level Fixed

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: The investment function was shown as I = I̅ Graphically, this is shown as a ____ at a height equal to I̅ above the horizontal axis.
cards.back: The investment function was shown as I = I̅ Graphically, this is shown as a horizontal line at a height equal to I̅ above the horizontal axis.
cards.quote: The investment function was shown as I = I̅ Graphically, this is shown as a horizontal line at a height equal to I̅ above the horizontal axis.

source.section: 4.3.1 Macroeconomic Equilibrium with Price Level Fixed

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What does the aggregate demand function show?
cards.back: The Aggregate Demand function shows the total demand (made up of consumption + investment) at each level of income.
cards.quote: The Aggregate Demand function shows the total demand (made up of consumption + investment) at each level of income.

source.section: 4.3.1 Macroeconomic Equilibrium with Price Level Fixed

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: The aggregate demand function is ____ to the consumption function i.e., they have the same ____ c.
cards.back: The aggregate demand function is parallel to the consumption function i.e., they have the same slope c.
cards.quote: The aggregate demand function is parallel to the consumption function i.e., they have the same slope c.

source.section: 4.3.1 Macroeconomic Equilibrium with Price Level Fixed

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Whatever is the level of GDP, that much will be supplied and price level has no role to play. This kind of supply situation is shown by a ____ line.
cards.back: Whatever is the level of GDP, that much will be supplied and price level has no role to play. This kind of supply situation is shown by a 45° line.
cards.quote: Whatever is the level of GDP, that much will be supplied and price level has no role to play. This kind of supply situation is shown by a 45° line.

source.section: 4.3.1 Macroeconomic Equilibrium with Price Level Fixed

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Graphically, which point is the equilibrium?
cards.back: The point where ex ante aggregate demand is equal to ex ante aggregate supply will be equilibrium.
cards.quote: The point where ex ante aggregate demand is equal to ex ante aggregate supply will be equilibrium.

source.section: 4.3.1 Macroeconomic Equilibrium with Price Level Fixed

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Algebraic method, two-sector model: what must equilibrium match, and what holds between ex ante AD and AS?
cards.back: Equilibrium requires that the plans of suppliers are matched by plans of those who provide final demands in the economy. Thus, in this situation, ex ante aggregate demand = ex ante aggregate supply,
cards.quote: Equilibrium requires that the plans of suppliers are matched by plans of those who provide final demands in the economy. Thus, in this situation, ex ante aggregate demand = ex ante aggregate supply,

source.section: 4.3.1 Macroeconomic Equilibrium with Price Level Fixed

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Name the two situations in which aggregate demand changes autonomously.
cards.back:
1. Change in consumption: this can happen due to (i) change in C̅ (ii) change in c
2. Change in investment
cards.quote: 1. Change in consumption: this can happen due to (i) change in C̅ (ii) change in c . 2. Change in investment: we have assumed that investment is autonomous.

source.section: 4.3.2 Effect of an Autonomous Change in Aggregate Demand on Income and Output

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is the interest rate, and how does it affect investment?
cards.back: Interest rate is the cost of investible funds, and at higher interest rates, firms tend to lower investment.
cards.quote: Another factor is interest rate: interest rate is the cost of investible funds, and at higher interest rates, firms tend to lower investment.

source.section: 4.3.2 Effect of an Autonomous Change in Aggregate Demand on Income and Output

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: C = 40 + 0.8Y, I = 10 gives Y = 250. If I rises to 20, what is the new equilibrium income?
cards.back: Now, let investment rise to 20. It can be seen that the new equilibrium will be 300.
cards.quote: Now, let investment rise to 20. It can be seen that the new equilibrium will be 300.

source.section: 4.3.2 Effect of an Autonomous Change in Aggregate Demand on Income and Output

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: How is the final goods output distributed among factors of production?
cards.back: In the absence of indirect taxes or subsidies, the total value of the final goods output is distributed among different factors of production – wages to labour, interest to capital, rent to land etc.
cards.quote: In the absence of indirect taxes or subsidies, the total value of the final goods output is distributed among different factors of production – wages to labour, interest to capital, rent to land etc.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Whatever is left over is appropriated by the entrepreneur and is called ____.
cards.back: Whatever is left over is appropriated by the entrepreneur and is called profit.
cards.quote: Whatever is left over is appropriated by the entrepreneur and is called profit.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Autonomous expenditure rises by 10 units, mpc 0.8. By how much does equilibrium income change?
cards.back: It was seen in the previous section that with a change in the autonomous expenditure of 10 units, the change in equilibrium income is equal to 50 units (from 250 to 300).
cards.quote: It was seen in the previous section that with a change in the autonomous expenditure of 10 units, the change in equilibrium income is equal to 50 units (from 250 to 300).

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Define the investment multiplier.
cards.back: The ratio of the total increment in equilibrium value of final goods output to the initial increment in autonomous expenditure is called the investment multiplier of the economy.
cards.quote: The ratio of the total increment in equilibrium value of final goods output to the initial increment in autonomous expenditure is called the investment multiplier of the economy.
cards.note: Bigger MPC means a bigger multiplier: 1/(1 - c) = 1/s. With c = 0.8 the multiplier is 5.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: How does the size of the investment multiplier depend on c (the mpc)?
cards.back:
A larger c (mpc) gives a larger multiplier.
As c becomes larger the multiplier increases.
cards.quote: Observe that the size of the multiplier depends on the value of c . As c becomes larger the multiplier increases.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: State the Paradox of Thrift.
cards.back: If all the people of the economy increase the proportion of income they save (i.e. if the mps of the economy increases) the total value of savings in the economy will not increase – it will either decline or remain unchanged. This result is known as the Paradox of Thrift – which states that as people become more thrifty they end up saving less or same as before.
cards.quote: If all the people of the economy increase the proportion of income they save (i.e. if the mps of the economy increases) the total value of savings in the economy will not increase – it will either decline or remain unchanged. This result is known as the Paradox of Thrift – which states that as people become more thrifty they end up saving less or same as before.
cards.note: If everyone saves more, income falls so much that total savings stay the same (10 in NCERT's example).

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Y = 250, S = 10. mpc falls 0.8 to 0.5, new Y = 100. What happens to total savings?
cards.back: Total value of savings in the economy has, therefore, remained unchanged.
cards.quote: Total value of savings in the economy has, therefore, remained unchanged.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Define the full employment level of income.
cards.back: Full employment level of income is that level of income where all the factors of production are fully employed in the production process.
cards.quote: Full employment level of income is that level of income where all the factors of production are fully employed in the production process.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Recall that equilibrium attained at the point of equality of Y and AD by itself does not signify ____ of resources.
cards.back: Recall that equilibrium attained at the point of equality of Y and AD by itself does not signify full employment of resources.
cards.quote: Recall that equilibrium attained at the point of equality of Y and AD by itself does not signify full employment of resources.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Equilibrium only means that if left to itself the level of income in the economy will not change even when there is ____ in the economy.
cards.back: Equilibrium only means that if left to itself the level of income in the economy will not change even when there is unemployment in the economy.
cards.quote: Equilibrium only means that if left to itself the level of income in the economy will not change even when there is unemployment in the economy.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is the situation of deficient demand?
cards.back: If it is less than the full employment of output, it is due to the fact that demand is not enough to employ all factors of production. This situation is called the situation of deficient demand. It leads to decline in prices in the long run.
cards.quote: If it is less than the full employment of output, it is due to the fact that demand is not enough to employ all factors of production. This situation is called the situation of deficient demand. It leads to decline in prices in the long run.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is the situation of excess demand?
cards.back: On the other hand, if the equilibrium level of output is more than the full employment level, it is due to the fact that the demand is more than the level of output produced at full employment level. This situation is called the situation of excess demand. It leads to rise in prices in the long run.
cards.quote: On the other hand, if the equilibrium level of output is more than the full employment level, it is due to the fact that the demand is more than the level of output produced at full employment level. This situation is called the situation of excess demand. It leads to rise in prices in the long run.
cards.note: Excess demand: output above full employment, prices tend to rise. Deficient demand: output below it, prices tend to fall.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: When, at a particular price level, ____ for final goods equals aggregate supply of final goods, the final goods or product market reaches its ____.
cards.back: When, at a particular price level, aggregate demand for final goods equals aggregate supply of final goods, the final goods or product market reaches its equilibrium.
cards.quote: When, at a particular price level, aggregate demand for final goods equals aggregate supply of final goods, the final goods or product market reaches its equilibrium.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: The rate of increase in ex ante consumption due to a unit increment in income is called ____.
cards.back: The rate of increase in ex ante consumption due to a unit increment in income is called marginal propensity to consume.
cards.quote: The rate of increase in ex ante consumption due to a unit increment in income is called marginal propensity to consume.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: In the fixed-price model, what is assumed about aggregate supply at the given price?
cards.back:
Aggregate supply is perfectly elastic at the given price.
We also assume that the aggregate supply is perfectly elastic at this price.
cards.quote: For simplicity we assume a constant final goods price and constant rate of interest over short run to determine the level of aggregate demand for final goods in the economy. We also assume that the aggregate supply is perfectly elastic at this price.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is the effective demand principle?
cards.back: Under such circumstances, aggregate output is determined solely by the level of aggregate demand. This is known as effective demand principle.
cards.quote: Under such circumstances, aggregate output is determined solely by the level of aggregate demand. This is known as effective demand principle.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Summary: an increase in autonomous spending raises aggregate output of final goods by a larger amount through what?
cards.back: An increase (decrease) in autonomous spending causes aggregate output of final goods to increase (decrease) by a larger amount through the multiplier process.
cards.quote: An increase (decrease) in autonomous spending causes aggregate output of final goods to increase (decrease) by a larger amount through the multiplier process.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What was Keynes's main idea about fiscal policy in The General Theory?
cards.back: One of Keynes's main ideas in The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money was that government fiscal policy should be used to stabilise the level of output and employment.
cards.quote: One of Keynes's main ideas in The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money was that government fiscal policy should be used to stabilise the level of output and employment.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Through changes in its ____, the government attempts to increase output and income and seeks to stabilise the ups and downs in the economy.
cards.back: Through changes in its expenditure and taxes, the government attempts to increase output and income and seeks to stabilise the ups and downs in the economy.
cards.quote: Through changes in its expenditure and taxes, the government attempts to increase output and income and seeks to stabilise the ups and downs in the economy.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What are lump-sum taxes?
cards.back: taxes that do not depend on income
cards.quote: We assume that the government imposes taxes that do not depend on income, called lump-sum taxes equal to T.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: How does the tax multiplier compare with the government expenditure multiplier in absolute value?
cards.back: we find that the tax multiplier is always one less in absolute value than the government expenditure multiplier.
cards.quote: we find that the tax multiplier is always one less in absolute value than the government expenditure multiplier.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What happens to output if a rise in government spending is matched by an equal rise in taxes?
cards.back: If an increase in government spending is matched by an equal increase in taxes, so that the budget remains balanced, output will rise by the amount of the increase in government spending.
cards.quote: If an increase in government spending is matched by an equal increase in taxes, so that the budget remains balanced, output will rise by the amount of the increase in government spending.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What does equilibrium income refer to in the multiplier process?
cards.back: The equilibrium income refers to the final income that one arrives at in a period sufficiently long for all the rounds of the multipliers to work themselves out.
cards.quote: The equilibrium income refers to the final income that one arrives at in a period sufficiently long for all the rounds of the multipliers to work themselves out.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Why does a rise in transfers raise output by less than an equal rise in government expenditure?
cards.back:
A part of any increase in transfer payments is saved.
output will rise by less than the amount by which it increases when government expenditure increases because a part of any increase in transfer payments is saved.
cards.quote: output will rise by less than the amount by which it increases when government expenditure increases because a part of any increase in transfer payments is saved.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is discretionary fiscal policy?
cards.back: This deliberate action to stabilise the economy is often referred to as discretionary fiscal policy to distinguish it from the inherent automatic stabilising properties of the fiscal system.
cards.quote: This deliberate action to stabilise the economy is often referred to as discretionary fiscal policy to distinguish it from the inherent automatic stabilising properties of the fiscal system.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Why is a proportional income tax called an automatic stabiliser?
cards.back:
It makes disposable income and spending less sensitive to GDP.
The proportional income tax, thus, acts as an automatic stabiliser – a shock absorber because it makes disposable income, and thus consumer spending, less sensitive to fluctuations in GDP.
cards.quote: The proportional income tax, thus, acts as an automatic stabiliser – a shock absorber because it makes disposable income, and thus consumer spending, less sensitive to fluctuations in GDP.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: How much of the fluctuation do built-in stabilisers reduce, and what takes care of the rest?
cards.back:
Only part; the rest needs deliberate policy initiative.
The built-in stabilisers, however, reduce only part of the fluctuation in the economy, the rest must be taken care of by deliberate policy initiative.
cards.quote: The built-in stabilisers, however, reduce only part of the fluctuation in the economy, the rest must be taken care of by deliberate policy initiative.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Proportional taxes reduce the autonomous expenditure multiplier because taxes reduce the ____ out of income.
cards.back: Proportional taxes reduce the autonomous expenditure multiplier because taxes reduce the marginal propensity to consume out of income.
cards.quote: Proportional taxes reduce the autonomous expenditure multiplier because taxes reduce the marginal propensity to consume out of income.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Which economic system appealed to Jawaharlal Nehru the most?
cards.back: There are different types of economic systems (see Box 2.1) and among them, socialism appealed to Jawaharlal Nehru the most.
cards.quote: There are different types of economic systems (see Box 2.1) and among them, socialism appealed to Jawaharlal Nehru the most.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: In this view, India would be a socialist society with a strong ____ but also with ____ and democracy
cards.back: In this view, India would be a socialist society with a strong public sector but also with private property and democracy
cards.quote: In this view, India would be a socialist society with a strong public sector but also with private property and democracy

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: The “Industrial Policy Resolution” of ____ and the Directive Principles of the Indian Constitution reflected this outlook.
cards.back: The “Industrial Policy Resolution” of 1948 and the Directive Principles of the Indian Constitution reflected this outlook.
cards.quote: The “Industrial Policy Resolution” of 1948 and the Directive Principles of the Indian Constitution reflected this outlook.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: When was the Planning Commission set up, and who was its Chairperson?
cards.back: In 1950, the Planning Commission was set up with the Prime Minister as its Chairperson.
