cards.quote: In 1950, the Planning Commission was set up with the Prime Minister as its Chairperson.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Which period did the first seven five year plans cover?
cards.back: Let us now see how the first seven five year plans, covering the period 1950-1990, attempted to attain these four goals and the extent to which they succeeded in doing so, with reference to agriculture, industry and trade.
cards.quote: Let us now see how the first seven five year plans, covering the period 1950-1990, attempted to attain these four goals and the extent to which they succeeded in doing so, with reference to agriculture, industry and trade.

source.section: 2.2 The Goals of Five Year Plans

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is a market economy (capitalism)?
cards.back: In a market economy, also called capitalism, only those consumer goods will be produced that are in demand, i.e., goods that can be sold profitably either in the domestic or in the foreign markets.
cards.quote: In a market economy, also called capitalism, only those consumer goods will be produced that are in demand, i.e., goods that can be sold profitably either in the domestic or in the foreign markets.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: In a capitalist society the goods produced are distributed among people not on the basis of what people need but on the basis of ____
cards.back: In a capitalist society the goods produced are distributed among people not on the basis of what people need but on the basis of Purchasing Power
cards.quote: In a capitalist society the goods produced are distributed among people not on the basis of what people need but on the basis of Purchasing Power

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: In a socialist society the ____ decides what goods are to be produced in accordance with the needs of society.
cards.back: In a socialist society the government decides what goods are to be produced in accordance with the needs of society.
cards.quote: In a socialist society the government decides what goods are to be produced in accordance with the needs of society.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: In principle, distribution under socialism is supposed to be based on what people ____ and not on what they can afford to purchase.
cards.back: In principle, distribution under socialism is supposed to be based on what people need and not on what they can afford to purchase.
cards.quote: In principle, distribution under socialism is supposed to be based on what people need and not on what they can afford to purchase.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Which countries does NCERT give as examples of economic activity governed by socialistic principles?
cards.back: In Cuba and China, for example, most of the economic activities are governed by the socialistic principles.
cards.quote: In Cuba and China, for example, most of the economic activities are governed by the socialistic principles.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is a mixed economy?
cards.back: Most economies are mixed economies, i.e. the government and the market together answer the three questions of what to produce, how to produce and how to distribute what is produced.
cards.quote: Most economies are mixed economies, i.e. the government and the market together answer the three questions of what to produce, how to produce and how to distribute what is produced.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is a plan?
cards.back: A plan spells out how the resources of a nation should be put to use.
cards.quote: A plan spells out how the resources of a nation should be put to use.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: From which country did India borrow the idea of five year plans?
cards.back: we borrowed this from the former Soviet Union, the pioneer in national planning
cards.quote: we borrowed this from the former Soviet Union, the pioneer in national planning

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is a perspective plan?
cards.back: Our plan documents upto the year 2017 not only specify the objectives to be attained in the five years of a plan but also what is to be achieved over a period of twenty years. This long-term plan is called “perspective plan”.
cards.quote: Our plan documents upto the year 2017 not only specify the objectives to be attained in the five years of a plan but also what is to be achieved over a period of twenty years. This long-term plan is called “perspective plan”.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: The goal of introducing modern technology may be in conflict with the goal of increasing ____ if the technology reduces the need for labour
cards.back: The goal of introducing modern technology may be in conflict with the goal of increasing employment if the technology reduces the need for labour
cards.quote: The goal of introducing modern technology may be in conflict with the goal of increasing employment if the technology reduces the need for labour

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Name the four goals of the five year plans.
cards.back:
growth
modernisation
self-reliance
equity
cards.quote: A plan should have some clearly specified goals. The goals of the five year plans were: growth, modernisation, self-reliance and equity.

source.section: 2.2 The Goals of Five Year Plans

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Due to ____, a choice has to be made in each plan about which of the goals is to be given primary importance.
cards.back: Due to limited resources, a choice has to be made in each plan about which of the goals is to be given primary importance.
cards.quote: Due to limited resources, a choice has to be made in each plan about which of the goals is to be given primary importance.

source.section: 2.2 The Goals of Five Year Plans

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Define growth as a goal of the five year plans.
cards.back: It refers to increase in the country’s capacity to produce the output of goods and services within the country.
cards.quote: Growth: It refers to increase in the country’s capacity to produce the output of goods and services within the country.

source.section: 2.2 The Goals of Five Year Plans

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: From which sectors is the GDP of a country derived?
cards.back:
agricultural sector
industrial sector
service sector
cards.quote: The GDP of a country is derived from the different sectors of the economy, namely the agricultural sector, the industrial sector and the service sector.

source.section: 2.2 The Goals of Five Year Plans

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What makes up the structural composition of the economy?
cards.back: The GDP of a country is derived from the different sectors of the economy, namely the agricultural sector, the industrial sector and the service sector. The contribution made by each of these sectors makes up the structural composition of the economy.
cards.quote: The GDP of a country is derived from the different sectors of the economy, namely the agricultural sector, the industrial sector and the service sector. The contribution made by each of these sectors makes up the structural composition of the economy.

source.section: 2.2 The Goals of Five Year Plans

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What was the service sector's share of GDP by 1990 compared with agriculture and industry?
cards.back: In India, the share of agriculture in the GDP was more than 50 per cent—as we would expect for a poor country. But by 1990 the share of the service sector was 40.59 per cent, more than that of agriculture or industry, like what we find in developed nations.
cards.quote: In India, the share of agriculture in the GDP was more than 50 per cent—as we would expect for a poor country. But by 1990 the share of the service sector was 40.59 per cent, more than that of agriculture or industry, like what we find in developed nations.

source.section: 2.2 The Goals of Five Year Plans

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is modernisation?
cards.back: Adoption of new technology is called modernisation.
cards.quote: Adoption of new technology is called modernisation.

source.section: 2.2 The Goals of Five Year Plans

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Modernisation does not refer only to the use of new technology but also to changes in ____
cards.back: Modernisation does not refer only to the use of new technology but also to changes in social outlook
cards.quote: Modernisation does not refer only to the use of new technology but also to changes in social outlook

source.section: 2.2 The Goals of Five Year Plans

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Why was self-reliance considered a necessity by the early plans?
cards.back: This policy was considered a necessity in order to reduce our dependence on foreign countries, especially for food.
cards.quote: This policy was considered a necessity in order to reduce our dependence on foreign countries, especially for food.

source.section: 2.2 The Goals of Five Year Plans

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Dependence on imported food supplies, foreign technology and foreign capital may make India’s ____ vulnerable to foreign interference in our policies
cards.back: Dependence on imported food supplies, foreign technology and foreign capital may make India’s sovereignty vulnerable to foreign interference in our policies
cards.quote: Dependence on imported food supplies, foreign technology and foreign capital may make India’s sovereignty vulnerable to foreign interference in our policies

source.section: 2.2 The Goals of Five Year Plans

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: The benefits of economic prosperity reach the ____ as well instead of being enjoyed only by the rich.
cards.back: The benefits of economic prosperity reach the poor sections as well instead of being enjoyed only by the rich.
cards.quote: The benefits of economic prosperity reach the poor sections as well instead of being enjoyed only by the rich.

source.section: 2.2 The Goals of Five Year Plans

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Which basic needs should every Indian be able to meet (equity)?
cards.back:
food
a decent house
education
health care
cards.quote: Every Indian should be able to meet his or her basic needs such as food, a decent house, education and health care

source.section: 2.2 The Goals of Five Year Plans

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Through which two measures did independent India's policy makers address growth and equity in agriculture?
cards.back: The policy makers of independent India had to address these issues which they did through land reforms and promoting the use of “High Yielding Variety” (HYV) seeds which ushered in a revolution in Indian agriculture.
cards.quote: The policy makers of independent India had to address these issues which they did through land reforms and promoting the use of “High Yielding Variety” (HYV) seeds which ushered in a revolution in Indian agriculture.

source.section: 2.2 The Goals of Five Year Plans

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What do land reforms primarily refer to?
cards.back: Equity in agriculture called for land reforms which primarily refer to change in the ownership of landholdings.
cards.quote: Equity in agriculture called for land reforms which primarily refer to change in the ownership of landholdings.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: From which country did low agricultural productivity force India to import food?
cards.back: The low productivity of the agricultural sector forced India to import food from the United States of America (U.S.A.).
cards.quote: The low productivity of the agricultural sector forced India to import food from the United States of America (U.S.A.).

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Just a year after independence, steps were taken to ____ intermediaries and to make the tillers the owners of land.
cards.back: Just a year after independence, steps were taken to abolish intermediaries and to make the tillers the owners of land.
cards.quote: Just a year after independence, steps were taken to abolish intermediaries and to make the tillers the owners of land.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Ownership of land would give ____ (see Box 2.5) to the tillers to invest in making improvements
cards.back: Ownership of land would give incentives (see Box 2.5) to the tillers to invest in making improvements
cards.quote: Ownership of land would give incentives (see Box 2.5) to the tillers to invest in making improvements

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: The policy of “land to the tiller” is based on the idea that the cultivators will take more interest — they will have more ____ — in increasing output
cards.back: The policy of “land to the tiller” is based on the idea that the cultivators will take more interest — they will have more incentive — in increasing output
cards.quote: The policy of “land to the tiller” is based on the idea that the cultivators will take more interest — they will have more incentive — in increasing output

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is land ceiling?
cards.back: Land ceiling was another policy to promote equity in the agricultural sector. This means fixing the maximum size of land which could be owned by an individual.
cards.quote: Land ceiling was another policy to promote equity in the agricultural sector. This means fixing the maximum size of land which could be owned by an individual.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: The purpose of land ceiling was to reduce the ____ of land ownership in a few hands.
cards.back: The purpose of land ceiling was to reduce the concentration of land ownership in a few hands.
cards.quote: The purpose of land ceiling was to reduce the concentration of land ownership in a few hands.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: How many tenants came into direct contact with the government after intermediaries were abolished?
cards.back: The abolition of intermediaries meant that some 200 lakh tenants came into direct contact with the government — they were thus freed from being exploited by the zamindars.
cards.quote: The abolition of intermediaries meant that some 200 lakh tenants came into direct contact with the government — they were thus freed from being exploited by the zamindars.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Why abolition of intermediaries did not fully serve equity: three reasons (zamindars, tenants, labourers).
cards.back:
continued to own large areas of land by making use of some loopholes in the legislation
there were cases where tenants were evicted and the landowners claimed to be self-cultivators (the actual tillers), claiming ownership of the land
the poorest of the agricultural labourers (such as sharecroppers and landless labourers) did not benefit from land reforms
cards.quote: continued to own large areas of land by making use of some loopholes in the legislation; there were cases where tenants were evicted and the landowners claimed to be self-cultivators (the actual tillers), claiming ownership of the land; and even when the tillers got ownership of land, the poorest of the agricultural labourers (such as sharecroppers and landless labourers) did not benefit from land reforms.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: How did big landlords escape the land ceiling legislation?
cards.back: The big landlords challenged the legislation in the courts, delaying its implementation. They used this delay to register their lands in the name of close relatives, thereby escaping from the legislation.
cards.quote: The big landlords challenged the legislation in the courts, delaying its implementation. They used this delay to register their lands in the name of close relatives, thereby escaping from the legislation.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: In which states were land reforms successful, and why?
cards.back: Land reforms were successful in Kerala and West Bengal because these states had governments committed to the policy of land to the tiller.
cards.quote: Land reforms were successful in Kerala and West Bengal because these states had governments committed to the policy of land to the tiller.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is the green revolution?
cards.back: The stagnation in agriculture during the colonial rule was permanently broken by the green revolution. This refers to the large increase in production of food grains resulting from the use of high yielding variety (HYV) seeds especially for wheat and rice.
cards.quote: The stagnation in agriculture during the colonial rule was permanently broken by the green revolution. This refers to the large increase in production of food grains resulting from the use of high yielding variety (HYV) seeds especially for wheat and rice.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What did the use of HYV seeds require?
cards.back:
fertiliser and pesticide in the correct quantities
regular supply of water
cards.quote: The use of these seeds required the use of fertiliser and pesticide in the correct quantities as well as regular supply of water

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: First phase of the green revolution: which period, and which states used HYV seeds?
cards.back: in the first phase of the green revolution (approximately mid 1960s upto mid 1970s), the use of HYV seeds was restricted to the more affluent states such as Punjab, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu.
cards.quote: in the first phase of the green revolution (approximately mid 1960s upto mid 1970s), the use of HYV seeds was restricted to the more affluent states such as Punjab, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Second phase of the green revolution: which period, and what changed?
cards.back: In the second phase of the green revolution (mid-1970s to mid-1980s), the HYV technology spread to a larger number of states and benefited more variety of crops.
cards.quote: In the second phase of the green revolution (mid-1970s to mid-1980s), the HYV technology spread to a larger number of states and benefited more variety of crops.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: The spread of green revolution technology enabled India to achieve ____ in food grains
cards.back: The spread of green revolution technology enabled India to achieve self-sufficiency in food grains
cards.quote: The spread of green revolution technology enabled India to achieve self-sufficiency in food grains

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is marketed surplus?
cards.back: The portion of agricultural produce which is sold in the market by the farmers is called marketed surplus.
cards.quote: The portion of agricultural produce which is sold in the market by the farmers is called marketed surplus.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What happened to food grain prices relative to other items because of marketed surplus in the green revolution?
cards.back: As a result, the price of food grains declined relative to other items of consumption.
cards.quote: A good proportion of the rice and wheat produced during the green revolution period (available as marketed surplus) was sold by the farmers in the market. As a result, the price of food grains declined relative to other items of consumption.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What did the green revolution enable the government to build from procured food grains, and for what use?
cards.back: The green revolution enabled the government to procure sufficient amount of food grains to build a stock which could be used in times of food shortage.
cards.quote: The green revolution enabled the government to procure sufficient amount of food grains to build a stock which could be used in times of food shortage.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Name the two risks of the green revolution technology.
cards.back:
the possibility that it would increase the disparities between small and big farmers
the HYV crops were also more prone to attack by pests
cards.quote: One such risk was the possibility that it would increase the disparities between small and big farmers—since only the big farmers could afford the required inputs, thereby reaping most of the benefits of the green revolution. Moreover, the HYV crops were also more prone to attack by pests and the small farmers who adopted this technology could lose everything in a pest attack.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: The government provided loans at a low interest rate to small farmers and ____ fertilisers
cards.back: The government provided loans at a low interest rate to small farmers and subsidised fertilisers
cards.quote: The government provided loans at a low interest rate to small farmers and subsidised fertilisers

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Why were subsidies considered necessary for adopting the new HYV technology in agriculture?
cards.back:
To provide an incentive for adoption by farmers, small farmers in particular
it was necessary to use subsidies to provide an incentive for adoption of the new HYV technology by farmers in general and small farmers in particular
cards.quote: it was necessary to use subsidies to provide an incentive for adoption of the new HYV technology by farmers in general and small farmers in particular

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Arguments against continuing fertiliser subsidies (NCERT's reasons).
cards.back:
once the technology is found profitable and is widely adopted, subsidies should be phased out since their purpose has been served
a substantial amount of fertiliser subsidy also benefits the fertiliser industry
among farmers, the subsidy largely benefits the farmers in the more prosperous regions
it is a huge burden on the government’s finances
cards.quote: Some economists believe that once the technology is found profitable and is widely adopted, subsidies should be phased out since their purpose has been served. Further, subsidies are meant to benefit the farmers but a substantial amount of fertiliser subsidy also benefits the fertiliser industry; and among farmers, the subsidy largely benefits the farmers in the more prosperous regions. Therefore, it is argued that there is no case for continuing with fertiliser subsidies; it does not benefit the target group and it is a huge burden on the government’s finances

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Arguments for continuing agricultural subsidies (NCERT's reasons).
cards.back:
farming in India continues to be a risky business
Most farmers are very poor and they will not be able to afford the required inputs without subsidies
Eliminating subsidies will increase the inequality between rich and poor farmers and violate the goal of equity
cards.quote: On the other hand, some believe that the government should continue with agricultural subsidies because farming in India continues to be a risky business. Most farmers are very poor and they will not be able to afford the required inputs without subsidies. Eliminating subsidies will increase the inequality between rich and poor farmers and violate the goal of equity.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What share of India's population was still employed in agriculture as late as 1990?
cards.back: On the negative side, some 65 per cent of the country’s population continued to be employed in agriculture even as late as 1990.
cards.quote: On the negative side, some 65 per cent of the country’s population continued to be employed in agriculture even as late as 1990.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: How did the share of population depending on agriculture change between 1950 and 1990?
cards.back: In India, between 1950 and 1990, the proportion of GDP contributed by agriculture declined significantly but not the population depending on it (67.5 per cent in 1950 to 64.9 per cent by 1990).
cards.quote: In India, between 1950 and 1990, the proportion of GDP contributed by agriculture declined significantly but not the population depending on it (67.5 per cent in 1950 to 64.9 per cent by 1990).

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Why did the share of population in agriculture stay high in 1950-1990 although its share of GDP fell?
cards.back: The industrial sector and the service sector did not absorb the people working in the agricultural sector
cards.quote: The industrial sector and the service sector did not absorb the people working in the agricultural sector

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Industry provides employment which is more ____ than the employment in agriculture
cards.back: Industry provides employment which is more stable than the employment in agriculture
cards.quote: Industry provides employment which is more stable than the employment in agriculture

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: At independence, industry was largely confined to which two industries, and where were the two iron and steel firms?
cards.back: largely confined to cotton textiles and jute. There were two well-managed iron and steel firms — one in Jamshedpur and the other in Kolkata — but, obviously, we needed to expand the industrial base with a variety of industries if the economy was to grow.
cards.quote: largely confined to cotton textiles and jute. There were two well-managed iron and steel firms — one in Jamshedpur and the other in Kolkata — but, obviously, we needed to expand the industrial base with a variety of industries if the economy was to grow.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Besides capital, what was not big enough to encourage industrialists to start major projects?
cards.back:
The market
nor was the market big enough to encourage industrialists to undertake major projects even if they had the capital to do so.
cards.quote: nor was the market big enough to encourage industrialists to undertake major projects even if they had the capital to do so.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What did the government controlling the 'commanding heights of the economy' mean?
cards.back: This meant that the government would have complete control of those industries that were vital for the economy.
cards.quote: In addition, the decision to develop the Indian economy on socialist lines led to the policy of the government controlling the commanding heights of the economy, as the Second Five Year plan put it. This meant that the government would have complete control of those industries that were vital for the economy.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Under the commanding heights policy, how were the policies of the private sector to relate to those of the public sector?
cards.back: The policies of the private sector would have to be complimentary to those of the public sector, with the public sector leading the way.
cards.quote: The policies of the private sector would have to be complimentary to those of the public sector, with the public sector leading the way.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: The Industrial Policy Resolution of 1956 was adopted. This resolution formed the basis of the ____
cards.back: The Industrial Policy Resolution of 1956 was adopted. This resolution formed the basis of the Second Five Year Plan
cards.quote: The Industrial Policy Resolution of 1956 was adopted. This resolution formed the basis of the Second Five Year Plan

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Three categories of industries under the Industrial Policy Resolution 1956.
cards.back:
The first category comprised industries which would be exclusively owned by the government
the second category consisted of industries in which the private sector could supplement the efforts of the public sector, with the government taking the sole responsibility for starting new units
the third category consisted of the remaining industries which were to be in the private sector
cards.quote: This resolution classified industries into three categories. The first category comprised industries which would be exclusively owned by the government; the second category consisted of industries in which the private sector could supplement the efforts of the public sector, with the government taking the sole responsibility for starting new units; the third category consisted of the remaining industries which were to be in the private sector.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: No new industry was allowed unless a ____ was obtained from the government.
cards.back: No new industry was allowed unless a license was obtained from the government.
cards.quote: No new industry was allowed unless a license was obtained from the government.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: How did industrial licensing promote regional equality?
cards.back: This policy was used for promoting industry in backward regions; it was easier to obtain a license if the industrial unit was established in an economically backward area. In addition, such units were given certain concessions such as tax benefits and electricity at a lower tariff. The purpose of this policy was to promote regional equality.
cards.quote: This policy was used for promoting industry in backward regions; it was easier to obtain a license if the industrial unit was established in an economically backward area. In addition, such units were given certain concessions such as tax benefits and electricity at a lower tariff. The purpose of this policy was to promote regional equality.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Even an existing industry had to obtain a license for expanding output or for ____ production (producing a new variety of goods).
cards.back: Even an existing industry had to obtain a license for expanding output or for diversifying production (producing a new variety of goods).
cards.quote: Even an existing industry had to obtain a license for expanding output or for diversifying production (producing a new variety of goods).

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Which committee (1955) noted that small-scale industries could promote rural development?
cards.back: In 1955, the Village and Small-Scale Industries Committee, also called the Karve Committee, noted the possibility of using small-scale industries for promoting rural development.
cards.quote: In 1955, the Village and Small-Scale Industries Committee, also called the Karve Committee, noted the possibility of using small-scale industries for promoting rural development.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: How is a small-scale industry defined?
cards.back: A “small-scale industry” is defined with reference to the maximum investment allowed on the assets of a unit.
cards.quote: A “small-scale industry” is defined with reference to the maximum investment allowed on the assets of a unit.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Small-scale industries are more “labour ____” i.e., they use more labour than the large-scale industries
cards.back: Small-scale industries are more “labour intensive” i.e., they use more labour than the large-scale industries
cards.quote: Small-scale industries are more “labour intensive” i.e., they use more labour than the large-scale industries

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: How were small-scale industries shielded from large firms?
cards.back:
the production of a number of products was reserved for the small-scale industry
lower excise duty
bank loans at lower interest rates
cards.quote: For this purpose, the production of a number of products was reserved for the small-scale industry; the criterion of reservation being the ability of these units to manufacture the goods. They were also given concessions such as lower excise duty and bank loans at lower interest rates.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is import substitution?
cards.back: Technically, this strategy is called import substitution. This policy aimed at replacing or substituting imports with domestic production.
cards.quote: Technically, this strategy is called import substitution. This policy aimed at replacing or substituting imports with domestic production.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is the technical name of the inward looking trade strategy of the first seven plans?
cards.back:
Import substitution
what is commonly called an inward looking trade strategy. Technically, this strategy is called import substitution.
cards.quote: what is commonly called an inward looking trade strategy. Technically, this strategy is called import substitution.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Name the two forms of protection from imports.
cards.back:
tariffs
quotas
cards.quote: Protection from imports took two forms: tariffs and quotas.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Tariffs vs quotas: what each is.
cards.back: Tariffs are a tax on imported goods; they make imported goods more expensive and discourage their use. Quotas specify the quantity of goods which can be imported.
cards.quote: Tariffs are a tax on imported goods; they make imported goods more expensive and discourage their use. Quotas specify the quantity of goods which can be imported.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is the effect of tariffs and quotas on imports and on domestic firms?
cards.back: The effect of tariffs and quotas is that they restrict imports and, therefore, protect the domestic firms from foreign competition.
cards.quote: The effect of tariffs and quotas is that they restrict imports and, therefore, protect the domestic firms from foreign competition.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: On what notion was the policy of protection based?
cards.back: The policy of protection was based on the notion that industries of developing countries were not in a position to compete against the goods produced by more developed economies.
cards.quote: The policy of protection was based on the notion that industries of developing countries were not in a position to compete against the goods produced by more developed economies.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Nor was any serious thought given to promote exports until the ____.
cards.back: Nor was any serious thought given to promote exports until the mid-1980s.
cards.quote: Nor was any serious thought given to promote exports until the mid-1980s.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: How did industry's share of GDP change between 1950-51 and 1990-91?
cards.back: The proportion of GDP contributed by the industrial sector increased in the period from 13 per cent in 1950-51 to 24.6 per cent in 1990-91.
cards.quote: The proportion of GDP contributed by the industrial sector increased in the period from 13 per cent in 1950-51 to 24.6 per cent in 1990-91.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What annual growth rate did the industrial sector achieve during the first seven plans?
cards.back: The six per cent annual growth rate of the industrial sector during the period is commendable.
cards.quote: The six per cent annual growth rate of the industrial sector during the period is commendable.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: No longer was Indian industry restricted largely to cotton textiles and jute; in fact, the industrial sector became well ____ by 1990
cards.back: No longer was Indian industry restricted largely to cotton textiles and jute; in fact, the industrial sector became well diversified by 1990
cards.quote: No longer was Indian industry restricted largely to cotton textiles and jute; in fact, the industrial sector became well diversified by 1990

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: The promotion of ____ gave opportunities to those people who did not have the capital to start large firms to get into business.
cards.back: The promotion of small-scale industries gave opportunities to those people who did not have the capital to start large firms to get into business.
cards.quote: The promotion of small-scale industries gave opportunities to those people who did not have the capital to start large firms to get into business.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Which areas of indigenous industry did protection from foreign competition help develop?
cards.back: Protection from foreign competition enabled the development of indigenous industries in the areas of electronics and automobile sectors which otherwise could not have developed.
cards.quote: Protection from foreign competition enabled the development of indigenous industries in the areas of electronics and automobile sectors which otherwise could not have developed.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Which service does NCERT give as an example of a monopoly the public sector kept after it was no longer required?
cards.back: It is now widely held that state enterprises continued to produce certain goods and services (often monopolising them) although this was no longer required. An example is the provision of telecommunication service. This industry continued to be reserved for the Public Sector even after it was realised that private sector firms could also provide it.
cards.quote: It is now widely held that state enterprises continued to produce certain goods and services (often monopolising them) although this was no longer required. An example is the provision of telecommunication service. This industry continued to be reserved for the Public Sector even after it was realised that private sector firms could also provide it.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Why were some private firms on the verge of closure nationalised?
cards.back: (indeed, quite a few of the public sector firms were originally private firms which were on the verge of closure due to losses; they were then nationalised to protect the jobs of the workers).
cards.quote: (indeed, quite a few of the public sector firms were originally private firms which were on the verge of closure due to losses; they were then nationalised to protect the jobs of the workers).

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: How did big industrialists misuse the need to obtain a license?
cards.back: The need to obtain a license to start an industry was misused by industrial houses; a big industrialist would get a license not for starting a new firm but to prevent competitors from starting new firms.
cards.quote: The need to obtain a license to start an industry was misused by industrial houses; a big industrialist would get a license not for starting a new firm but to prevent competitors from starting new firms.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: The excessive regulation of what came to be called the permit license ____ prevented certain firms from becoming more efficient.
cards.back: The excessive regulation of what came to be called the permit license raj prevented certain firms from becoming more efficient.
cards.quote: The excessive regulation of what came to be called the permit license raj prevented certain firms from becoming more efficient.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: The producers were aware that they had a ____ market; so they had no incentive to improve the quality of their goods.
cards.back: The producers were aware that they had a captive market; so they had no incentive to improve the quality of their goods.
cards.quote: The producers were aware that they had a captive market; so they had no incentive to improve the quality of their goods.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What, on the view of a few economists, is the public sector meant to promote instead of earning profits?
cards.back: The public sector is not meant for earning profits but to promote the welfare of the nation
cards.quote: The public sector is not meant for earning profits but to promote the welfare of the nation

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: In which year did the government introduce a new economic policy?
cards.back: Owing to all these conflicts, economists called for a change in our policy. This, alongwith other problems, led the government to introduce a new economic policy in 1991.
cards.quote: Owing to all these conflicts, economists called for a change in our policy. This, alongwith other problems, led the government to introduce a new economic policy in 1991.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Achievements of the first seven plans (NCERT's conclusion).
cards.back:
Our industries became far more diversified compared to the situation at independence
India became self-sufficient in food production thanks to the green revolution
Land reforms resulted in abolition of the hated zamindari system
cards.quote: Our industries became far more diversified compared to the situation at independence. India became self-sufficient in food production thanks to the green revolution. Land reforms resulted in abolition of the hated zamindari system.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Shortcomings of the first seven plans (NCERT's conclusion).
cards.back:
many economists became dissatisfied with the performance of many public sector enterprises
Excessive government regulation prevented growth of entrepreneurship
Indian producers were protected against foreign competition and this did not give them the incentive to improve the quality of goods that they produced
Indian policies were “inward oriented” that failed to develop a strong export sector
cards.quote: In industrial sector, many economists became dissatisfied with the performance of many public sector enterprises. Excessive government regulation prevented growth of entrepreneurship. In the name of self-reliance, Indian producers were protected against foreign competition and this did not give them the incentive to improve the quality of goods that they produced. Indian policies were “inward oriented” that failed to develop a strong export sector.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: After independence, what economic model did India adopt, combining the best features of socialism and capitalism?
cards.back: After independence, India envisaged an economic system which combines the best features of socialism and capitalism — this culminated in the mixed economy model.
cards.quote: After independence, India envisaged an economic system which combines the best features of socialism and capitalism — this culminated in the mixed economy model.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: The major policy initiatives in agriculture sector were ____ and green revolution.
cards.back: The major policy initiatives in agriculture sector were land reforms and green revolution.
cards.quote: The major policy initiatives in agriculture sector were land reforms and green revolution.

cards.subject: economics
cards.chapter: Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence
cards.front: What was the sole purpose of the British colonial rule in India?
cards.back: The sole purpose of the British colonial rule in India was to reduce the country to being a raw material supplier for Great Britain's own rapidly expanding modern industrial base.
cards.quote: The sole purpose of the British colonial rule in India was to reduce the country to being a raw material supplier for Great Britain's own rapidly expanding modern industrial base.
cards.note: Colonial rule treated India as a source of raw materials for Britain's industry.

cards.subject: economics
cards.chapter: Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence
cards.front: India was particularly well known for its ____ in the fields of cotton and silk textiles, metal and precious stone works etc.
cards.back: India was particularly well known for its handicraft industries in the fields of cotton and silk textiles, metal and precious stone works etc.
cards.quote: India was particularly well known for its handicraft industries in the fields of cotton and silk textiles, metal and precious stone works etc.

source.section: 1.2 Low Level of Economic Development under the Colonial Rule

cards.subject: economics
cards.chapter: Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence
cards.front: What is muslin?
cards.back: Muslin is a type of cotton textile which had its origin in Bengal, particularly, places in and around Dhaka (spelled during the pre-independence period as Dacca), now the capital city of Bangladesh.
cards.quote: Muslin is a type of cotton textile which had its origin in Bengal, particularly, places in and around Dhaka (spelled during the pre-independence period as Dacca), now the capital city of Bangladesh.

cards.subject: economics
cards.chapter: Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence
cards.front: The finest variety of muslin was called ____.
cards.back: The finest variety of muslin was called malmal.
cards.quote: The finest variety of muslin was called malmal.

cards.subject: economics
cards.chapter: Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence
cards.front: What were the colonial government's economic policies in India concerned with more than India's development?
cards.back: The economic policies pursued by the colonial government in India were concerned more with the protection and promotion of the economic interests of their home country than with the development of the Indian economy.
cards.quote: The economic policies pursued by the colonial government in India were concerned more with the protection and promotion of the economic interests of their home country than with the development of the Indian economy.

source.section: 1.2 Low Level of Economic Development under the Colonial Rule

cards.note: Colonial policy served Britain's interests, not India's development.

cards.subject: economics
cards.chapter: Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence
cards.front: What fundamental change did the colonial government's economic policies bring about in the structure of the Indian economy?
cards.back: Such policies brought about a fundamental change in the structure of the Indian economy — transforming the country into supplier of raw materials and consumer of finished industrial products from Britain.
cards.quote: Such policies brought about a fundamental change in the structure of the Indian economy — transforming the country into supplier of raw materials and consumer of finished industrial products from Britain.

source.section: 1.2 Low Level of Economic Development under the Colonial Rule

cards.subject: economics
cards.chapter: Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence
cards.front: Name the 5 notable estimators of India's national and per capita income in the colonial period.
cards.back:
Dadabhai Naoroji
William Digby
Findlay Shirras
V.K.R.V. Rao
R.C. Desai
cards.quote: Among the notable estimators — Dadabhai Naoroji, William Digby, Findlay Shirras, V.K.R.V. Rao and R.C. Desai — it was Rao, whose estimates during the colonial period was considered very significant.

source.section: 1.2 Low Level of Economic Development under the Colonial Rule

cards.subject: economics
cards.chapter: Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence
cards.front: Among the estimators of colonial India's income, whose estimates were considered very significant?
cards.back: it was Rao, whose estimates during the colonial period was considered very significant.
cards.quote: it was Rao, whose estimates during the colonial period was considered very significant.

source.section: 1.2 Low Level of Economic Development under the Colonial Rule

cards.subject: economics
cards.chapter: Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence
cards.front: India, first half of the twentieth century: how much was the growth of aggregate real output and of per capita output per year?
cards.back: most studies did find that the country's growth of aggregate real output during the first half of the twentieth century was less than two per cent coupled with a meagre half per cent growth in per capita output per year.
cards.quote: most studies did find that the country's growth of aggregate real output during the first half of the twentieth century was less than two per cent coupled with a meagre half per cent growth in per capita output per year.

source.section: 1.2 Low Level of Economic Development under the Colonial Rule

cards.subject: economics
cards.chapter: Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence
cards.front: What mainly caused the stagnation in India's colonial agricultural sector?
cards.back:
Land settlement systems introduced by the colonial government
This stagnation in the agricultural sector was caused mainly because of the various systems of land settlement that were introduced by the colonial government.
cards.quote: This stagnation in the agricultural sector was caused mainly because of the various systems of land settlement that were introduced by the colonial government.
cards.note: Main cause of agricultural stagnation: the colonial land settlement systems.

cards.subject: economics
cards.chapter: Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence
cards.front: Under which system in the then Bengal Presidency did agricultural profit go to the zamindars instead of the cultivators?
cards.back: Particularly, under the zamindari system which was implemented in the then Bengal Presidency comprising parts of India's present-day eastern states, the profit accruing out of the agriculture sector went to the zamindars instead of the cultivators.
cards.quote: Particularly, under the zamindari system which was implemented in the then Bengal Presidency comprising parts of India's present-day eastern states, the profit accruing out of the agriculture sector went to the zamindars instead of the cultivators.

cards.subject: economics
cards.chapter: Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence
cards.front: What was the main interest of the zamindars, regardless of the economic condition of the cultivators?
cards.back: The main interest of the zamindars was only to collect rent regardless of the economic condition of the cultivators; this caused immense misery and social tension among the latter.
cards.quote: The main interest of the zamindars was only to collect rent regardless of the economic condition of the cultivators; this caused immense misery and social tension among the latter.

cards.subject: economics
cards.chapter: Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence
cards.front: There was, of course, some evidence of a relatively higher yield of ____ in certain areas of the country due to ____.
cards.back: There was, of course, some evidence of a relatively higher yield of cash crops in certain areas of the country due to commercialisation of agriculture.
cards.quote: There was, of course, some evidence of a relatively higher yield of cash crops in certain areas of the country due to commercialisation of agriculture.

cards.subject: economics
cards.chapter: Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence
cards.front: What was the two-fold motive behind the systematic deindustrialisation of India?
cards.back:
to reduce India to the status of a mere exporter of important raw materials for the upcoming modern industries in Britain
to turn India into a sprawling market for the finished products of those industries
cards.quote: The intention was, first, to reduce India to the status of a mere exporter of important raw materials for the upcoming modern industries in Britain and, second, to turn India into a sprawling market for the finished products of those industries so that their continued expansion could be ensured to the maximum advantage of their home country — Britain.

cards.subject: economics
cards.chapter: Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence
cards.front: What did the decline of the indigenous handicraft industries create in India, besides a new demand in the consumer market?
cards.back: the decline of the indigenous handicraft industries created not only massive unemployment in India but also a new demand in the Indian consumer market, which was now deprived of the supply of locally made goods.
cards.quote: the decline of the indigenous handicraft industries created not only massive unemployment in India but also a new demand in the Indian consumer market, which was now deprived of the supply of locally made goods.

cards.subject: economics
cards.chapter: Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence
cards.front: During the ____, modern industry began to take root in India but its progress remained very slow.
cards.back: During the second half of the nineteenth century, modern industry began to take root in India but its progress remained very slow.
cards.quote: During the second half of the nineteenth century, modern industry began to take root in India but its progress remained very slow.
blanks: second half of the nineteenth century

cards.subject: economics
cards.chapter: Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence
cards.front: Cotton textile mills vs jute mills: the difference on ownership and location.
cards.back: The cotton textile mills, mainly dominated by Indians, were located in the western parts of the country, namely, Maharashtra and Gujarat, while the jute mills dominated by the foreigners were mainly concentrated in Bengal.
cards.quote: The cotton textile mills, mainly dominated by Indians, were located in the western parts of the country, namely, Maharashtra and Gujarat, while the jute mills dominated by the foreigners were mainly concentrated in Bengal.

cards.subject: economics
cards.chapter: Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence
cards.front: In which year was the Tata Iron and Steel Company (TISCO) incorporated?
cards.back: The Tata Iron and Steel Company (TISCO) was incorporated in 1907.
cards.quote: The Tata Iron and Steel Company (TISCO) was incorporated in 1907.

cards.subject: economics
cards.chapter: Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence
cards.front: Name the modern industries that came up in colonial India, in the order they appeared.
cards.back:
cotton and jute textile mills
iron and steel industries
sugar, cement, paper etc.
cards.quote: Initially, this development was confined to the setting up of cotton and jute textile mills. The cotton textile mills, mainly dominated by Indians, were located in the western parts of the country, namely, Maharashtra and Gujarat, while the jute mills dominated by the foreigners were mainly concentrated in Bengal. Subsequently, the iron and steel industries began coming up in the beginning of the twentieth century. The Tata Iron and Steel Company (TISCO) was incorporated in 1907. A few other industries in the fields of sugar, cement, paper etc. came up after the Second World War.

cards.subject: economics
cards.chapter: Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence
cards.front: What is a capital goods industry?
cards.back: Capital goods industry means industries which can produce machine tools which are, in turn, used for producing articles for current consumption.
cards.quote: Capital goods industry means industries which can produce machine tools which are, in turn, used for producing articles for current consumption.

cards.subject: economics
cards.chapter: Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence
cards.front: Which industry was hardly present in colonial India, holding back further industrialisation?
cards.back:
Capital goods industry
there was hardly any capital goods industry to help promote further industrialisation in India.
cards.quote: there was hardly any capital goods industry to help promote further industrialisation in India.

cards.subject: economics
cards.chapter: Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence
cards.front: Another significant drawback of the new industrial sector was the very limited area of operation of the ____.
cards.back: Another significant drawback of the new industrial sector was the very limited area of operation of the public sector.
cards.quote: Another significant drawback of the new industrial sector was the very limited area of operation of the public sector.

cards.subject: economics
cards.chapter: Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence
cards.front: Name the areas to which the public sector remained confined in the colonial period.
cards.back:
railways
power generation
communications
ports
some other departmental undertakings
cards.quote: This sector remained confined only to the railways, power generation, communications, ports and some other departmental undertakings.

cards.subject: economics
cards.chapter: Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence
cards.front: What aspects of India's foreign trade did the colonial restrictive policies of production, trade and tariff adversely affect?
cards.back: the restrictive policies of commodity production, trade and tariff pursued by the colonial government adversely affected the structure, composition and volume of India's foreign trade.
cards.quote: the restrictive policies of commodity production, trade and tariff pursued by the colonial government adversely affected the structure, composition and volume of India's foreign trade.

cards.subject: economics
cards.chapter: Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence
cards.front: Colonial India's exports vs imports: what each consisted of.
cards.back: India became an exporter of primary products such as raw silk, cotton, wool, sugar, indigo, jute etc. and an importer of finished consumer goods like cotton, silk and woollen clothes and capital goods like light machinery produced in the factories of Britain.
cards.quote: India became an exporter of primary products such as raw silk, cotton, wool, sugar, indigo, jute etc. and an importer of finished consumer goods like cotton, silk and woollen clothes and capital goods like light machinery produced in the factories of Britain.

cards.subject: economics
cards.chapter: Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence
cards.front: Britain maintained a ____ over India's exports and imports.
cards.back: Britain maintained a monopoly control over India's exports and imports.
cards.quote: Britain maintained a monopoly control over India's exports and imports.

cards.subject: economics
cards.chapter: Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence
cards.front: ____ of India's foreign trade was restricted to Britain while the rest was allowed with a few other countries like China, Ceylon (Sri Lanka) and ____.
cards.back: more than half of India's foreign trade was restricted to Britain while the rest was allowed with a few other countries like China, Ceylon (Sri Lanka) and Persia (Iran).
cards.quote: more than half of India's foreign trade was restricted to Britain while the rest was allowed with a few other countries like China, Ceylon (Sri Lanka) and Persia (Iran).

cards.subject: economics
cards.chapter: Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence
cards.front: The opening of the ____ further intensified British control over India's foreign trade
cards.back: The opening of the Suez Canal further intensified British control over India's foreign trade
cards.quote: The opening of the Suez Canal further intensified British control over India's foreign trade

cards.subject: economics
cards.chapter: Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence
cards.front: What is the Suez Canal?
cards.back: Suez Canal is an artificial waterway running from north to south across the Isthmus of Suez in north-eastern Egypt.
cards.quote: Suez Canal is an artificial waterway running from north to south across the Isthmus of Suez in north-eastern Egypt.

source.section: Box 1.3: Trade Through the Suez Canal

cards.subject: economics
cards.chapter: Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence
cards.front: In which year did the Suez Canal open, and what effect did it have on the Indian market?
cards.back: Its opening in 1869 reduced the cost of transportation and made access to the Indian market easier.
cards.quote: Its opening in 1869 reduced the cost of transportation and made access to the Indian market easier.

source.section: Box 1.3: Trade Through the Suez Canal

cards.subject: economics
cards.chapter: Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence
cards.front: The most important characteristic of India's foreign trade throughout the colonial period was the generation of a large ____.
cards.back: The most important characteristic of India's foreign trade throughout the colonial period was the generation of a large export surplus.
cards.quote: The most important characteristic of India's foreign trade throughout the colonial period was the generation of a large export surplus.

cards.subject: economics
cards.chapter: Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence
cards.front: Colonial India's export surplus did not bring which metals into India?
cards.back:
Gold or silver
this export surplus did not result in any flow of gold or silver into India.
cards.quote: this export surplus did not result in any flow of gold or silver into India.

cards.subject: economics
cards.chapter: Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence
cards.front: Name the 3 uses of India's export surplus that led to the drain of Indian wealth.
cards.back:
the expenses incurred by an office set up by the colonial government in Britain
expenses on war, again fought by the British government
the import of invisible items
cards.quote: Rather, this was used to make payments for the expenses incurred by an office set up by the colonial government in Britain, expenses on war, again fought by the British government, and the import of invisible items, all of which led to the drain of Indian wealth.
cards.note: Export surplus paid Britain's costs instead of bringing in gold or silver: the drain of wealth.

cards.subject: economics
cards.chapter: Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence
cards.front: In which year was the first census of British India carried out?
cards.back: Various details about the population of British India were first collected through a census in 1881.
cards.quote: Various details about the population of British India were first collected through a census in 1881.

cards.subject: economics
cards.chapter: Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence
cards.front: Which year marks the shift from the first to the second stage of India's demographic transition?
cards.back: Before 1921, India was in the first stage of demographic transition. The second stage of transition began after 1921.
cards.quote: Before 1921, India was in the first stage of demographic transition. The second stage of transition began after 1921.

cards.subject: economics
cards.chapter: Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence
cards.front: The overall literacy level was less than ____ per cent. Out of this, the female literacy level was at a negligible low of about ____ per cent.
cards.back: The overall literacy level was less than 16 per cent. Out of this, the female literacy level was at a negligible low of about seven per cent.
cards.quote: The overall literacy level was less than 16 per cent. Out of this, the female literacy level was at a negligible low of about seven per cent.

cards.subject: economics
cards.chapter: Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence
cards.front: What was India's infant mortality rate per thousand in the colonial period?
cards.back:
About 218 per thousand
the infant mortality rate was quite alarming—about 218 per thousand
cards.quote: the infant mortality rate was quite alarming—about 218 per thousand

cards.subject: economics
cards.chapter: Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence
cards.front: Life expectancy was also very low — ____ years
cards.back: Life expectancy was also very low — 32 years
cards.quote: Life expectancy was also very low — 32 years

cards.subject: economics
cards.chapter: Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence
cards.front: What prevailed in India during the colonial period, worsening the profile of India's population?
cards.back: there is no doubt that extensive poverty prevailed in India during the colonial period which contributed to the worsening profile of India's population of the time.
cards.quote: there is no doubt that extensive poverty prevailed in India during the colonial period which contributed to the worsening profile of India's population of the time.

cards.subject: economics
cards.chapter: Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence
cards.front: What is meant by the occupational structure of an economy?
cards.back: the occupational structure of India, i.e., distribution of working persons across different industries and sectors
cards.quote: the occupational structure of India, i.e., distribution of working persons across different industries and sectors

cards.subject: economics
cards.chapter: Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence
cards.front: How did India's occupational structure change during the colonial period?
cards.back: During the colonial period, the occupational structure of India, i.e., distribution of working persons across different industries and sectors, showed little sign of change.
cards.quote: During the colonial period, the occupational structure of India, i.e., distribution of working persons across different industries and sectors, showed little sign of change.

cards.subject: economics
cards.chapter: Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence
cards.front: Colonial period: what share of India's workforce was in agriculture, and what in manufacturing and services?
cards.back: the largest share of workforce, which usually remained at a high of 70-75 per cent while the manufacturing and the services sectors accounted for only 10 and 15-20 per cent respectively.
cards.quote: the largest share of workforce, which usually remained at a high of 70-75 per cent while the manufacturing and the services sectors accounted for only 10 and 15-20 per cent respectively.
cards.note: Agriculture 70-75 per cent; manufacturing 10 per cent; services 15-20 per cent of the workforce.

cards.subject: economics
cards.chapter: Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence
cards.front: What was the real motive behind the colonial development of railways, ports, water transport, posts and telegraphs?
cards.back: Under the colonial regime, basic infrastructure such as railways, ports, water transport, posts and telegraphs did develop. However, the real motive behind this development was not to provide basic amenities to the people but to subserve various colonial interests.
cards.quote: Under the colonial regime, basic infrastructure such as railways, ports, water transport, posts and telegraphs did develop. However, the real motive behind this development was not to provide basic amenities to the people but to subserve various colonial interests.

cards.subject: economics
cards.chapter: Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence
cards.front: There always remained an acute shortage of ____ to reach out to the rural areas during the rainy season.
cards.back: There always remained an acute shortage of all-weather roads to reach out to the rural areas during the rainy season.
cards.quote: There always remained an acute shortage of all-weather roads to reach out to the rural areas during the rainy season.

cards.subject: economics
cards.chapter: Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence
cards.front: The British introduced the railways in India in ____ and it is considered as one of their most important contributions.
cards.back: The British introduced the railways in India in 1850 and it is considered as one of their most important contributions.
cards.quote: The British introduced the railways in India in 1850 and it is considered as one of their most important contributions.

cards.subject: economics
cards.chapter: Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence
cards.front: Name the 2 important ways in which the railways affected the structure of the Indian economy.
cards.back:
enabled people to undertake long distance travel and thereby break geographical and cultural barriers
fostered commercialisation of Indian agriculture which adversely affected the self-sufficiency of the village economies in India
cards.quote: The railways affected the structure of the Indian economy in two important ways. On the one hand it enabled people to undertake long distance travel and thereby break geographical and cultural barriers while, on the other hand, it fostered commercialisation of Indian agriculture which adversely affected the self-sufficiency of the village economies in India.

cards.subject: economics
cards.chapter: Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence
cards.front: The introduction of the expensive system of electric telegraph in India, similarly, served the purpose of ____.
cards.back: The introduction of the expensive system of electric telegraph in India, similarly, served the purpose of maintaining law and order.
cards.quote: The introduction of the expensive system of electric telegraph in India, similarly, served the purpose of maintaining law and order.

cards.subject: economics
cards.chapter: Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence
cards.front: The agricultural sector was already saddled with ____ and ____.
cards.back: The agricultural sector was already saddled with surplus labour and extremely low productivity.
cards.quote: The agricultural sector was already saddled with surplus labour and extremely low productivity.

cards.subject: economics
cards.chapter: Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence
cards.front: The industrial sector was crying for ____, diversification, capacity building and ____.
cards.back: The industrial sector was crying for modernisation, diversification, capacity building and increased public investment.
cards.quote: The industrial sector was crying for modernisation, diversification, capacity building and increased public investment.

cards.subject: economics
cards.chapter: Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence
cards.front: Foreign trade was oriented to feed the ____ in Britain.
cards.back: Foreign trade was oriented to feed the Industrial Revolution in Britain.
cards.quote: Foreign trade was oriented to feed the Industrial Revolution in Britain.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What do we mean by goods?
cards.back: physical, tangible objects used to satisfy people's wants and needs.
cards.quote: physical, tangible objects used to satisfy people's wants and needs.
cards.note: Goods are tangible things that satisfy wants.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Food and clothes are examples of goods. The tasks doctors and teachers perform for us are examples of what?
cards.back: As compared to food items and clothes, which are examples of goods, we can think of the tasks that doctors and teachers perform for us as examples of services.
cards.quote: As compared to food items and clothes, which are examples of goods, we can think of the tasks that doctors and teachers perform for us as examples of services.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Name the two approaches that explain consumer behaviour (NCERT).
cards.back:
(i) Cardinal Utility Analysis
(ii) Ordinal Utility Analysis
cards.quote: This chapter presents two different approaches that explain consumer behaviour (i) Cardinal Utility Analysis and (ii) Ordinal Utility Analysis.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What does NCERT mean by an individual in economics?
cards.back: By individual, we mean an individual decision making unit. A decision making unit can be a single person or a group like a household, a firm or any other organisation.
cards.quote: By individual, we mean an individual decision making unit. A decision making unit can be a single person or a group like a household, a firm or any other organisation.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Any combination of the amount of the two goods will be called a ____ or, in short, a bundle.
cards.back:
consumption bundle
Any combination of the amount of the two goods will be called a consumption bundle or, in short, a bundle.
cards.quote: Any combination of the amount of the two goods will be called a consumption bundle or, in short, a bundle.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What does NCERT mean by a resource?
cards.back: By resource, we mean those goods and services which are used to produce other goods and services, e.g. land, labour, tools and machinery, etc.
cards.quote: By resource, we mean those goods and services which are used to produce other goods and services, e.g. land, labour, tools and machinery, etc.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is the utility of a commodity?
cards.back: Utility of a commodity is its want-satisfying capacity.
cards.quote: Utility of a commodity is its want-satisfying capacity.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is the nature of utility, and why can two people get different utility from the same commodity?
cards.back: Utility is subjective. Different individuals can get different levels of utility from the same commodity.
cards.quote: Utility is subjective. Different individuals can get different levels of utility from the same commodity.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Everyone faces ____ of resources, and therefore, has to use the limited resources in the best possible way to fulfill her needs.
cards.back: Everyone faces scarcity of resources, and therefore, has to use the limited resources in the best possible way to fulfill her needs.
cards.quote: Everyone faces scarcity of resources, and therefore, has to use the limited resources in the best possible way to fulfill her needs.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: A room heater gives different utility in Ladakh and Chennai, and in summer and winter. What does this show?
cards.back: Also, utility that one individual gets from the commodity can change with change in place and time. For example, utility from the use of a room heater will depend upon whether the individual is in Ladakh or Chennai (place) or whether it is summer or winter (time).
cards.quote: Also, utility that one individual gets from the commodity can change with change in place and time. For example, utility from the use of a room heater will depend upon whether the individual is in Ladakh or Chennai (place) or whether it is summer or winter (time).

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is cardinal utility analysis?
cards.back: Cardinal utility analysis assumes that level of utility can be expressed in numbers.
cards.quote: Cardinal utility analysis assumes that level of utility can be expressed in numbers.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is total utility (TU)?
cards.back: Total utility of a fixed quantity of a commodity (TU) is the total satisfaction derived from consuming the given amount of some commodity x.
cards.quote: Total utility of a fixed quantity of a commodity (TU) is the total satisfaction derived from consuming the given amount of some commodity x.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: The ____ of the limited resources and the ____ of the final mix of goods and services are two of the basic economic problems faced by the society.
cards.back: The allocation of the limited resources and the distribution of the final mix of goods and services are two of the basic economic problems faced by the society.
cards.quote: The allocation of the limited resources and the distribution of the final mix of goods and services are two of the basic economic problems faced by the society.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is marginal utility (MU)?
cards.back: Marginal utility (MU) is the change in total utility due to consumption of one additional unit of a commodity.
cards.quote: Marginal utility (MU) is the change in total utility due to consumption of one additional unit of a commodity.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What gives rise to the problem of choice in an economy?
cards.back:
The scarcity of resources
it is the scarcity of resources that gives rise to the problem of choice.
cards.quote: it is the scarcity of resources that gives rise to the problem of choice.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Formula: marginal utility of the nth unit (MUn).
cards.back: MUn = TUn - TUn-1, where subscript n refers to the nth unit of the commodity
cards.quote: In general, MUn = TUn - TUn-1, where subscript n refers to the nth unit of the commodity

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: 4 bananas give 28 units of total utility and 5 bananas give 30 units. What is the marginal utility of the 5th banana?
cards.back: Clearly, consumption of the 5th banana has caused total utility to increase by 2 units (30 units minus 28 units). Therefore, marginal utility of the 5th banana is 2 units.
cards.quote: For example, suppose 4 bananas give us 28 units of total utility and 5 bananas give us 30 units of total utility. Clearly, consumption of the 5th banana has caused total utility to increase by 2 units (30 units minus 28 units). Therefore, marginal utility of the 5th banana is 2 units.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Name the 3 central problems of an economy.
cards.back:
What is produced and in what quantities?
How are these goods produced?
For whom are these goods produced?
cards.quote: What is produced and in what quantities? Every society must decide on how much of each of the many possible goods and services it will produce. Whether to produce more of food, clothing, housing or to have more of luxury goods. Whether to have more agricultural goods or to have industrial products and services. Whether to use more resources in education and health or to use more resources in building military services. Whether to have more of basic education or more of higher education. Whether to have more of consumption goods or to have investment goods (like machine) which will boost production and consumption tomorrow. How are these goods produced? Every society has to decide on how much of which of the resources to use in the production of each of the different goods and services. Whether to use more labour or more machines. Which of the available technologies to adopt in the production of each of the goods? For whom are these goods produced?

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is produced and in what quantities: what must every society decide?
cards.back:
How much of each of the many possible goods and services to produce
Every society must decide on how much of each of the many possible goods and services it will produce.
cards.quote: Every society must decide on how much of each of the many possible goods and services it will produce.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Formula: total utility from n units (TUn) in terms of marginal utilities.
cards.back: TUn = MU1 + MU2 + ... + MUn-1 + MUn
cards.quote: TUn = MU1 + MU2 + ... + MUn-1 + MUn
cards.note: TU of n units is the sum of the marginal utilities of the first to the nth unit.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Every society has to decide on how much of which of the ____ to use in the production of each of the different goods and services.
cards.back: Every society has to decide on how much of which of the resources to use in the production of each of the different goods and services.
cards.quote: Every society has to decide on how much of which of the resources to use in the production of each of the different goods and services.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What does the central problem 'for whom are goods produced' ask about the economy's produce?
cards.back:
How it should be distributed among the individuals in the economy
How should the produce of the economy be distributed among the individuals in the economy?
cards.quote: How should the produce of the economy be distributed among the individuals in the economy?

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is marginal utility (MU) at the level of consumption where total utility (TU) stops changing?
cards.back: MU becomes zero at a level when TU remains constant. In the example, TU does not change at 5th unit of consumption and therefore MU5= 0.
cards.quote: MU becomes zero at a level when TU remains constant. In the example, TU does not change at 5th unit of consumption and therefore MU5= 0.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: State the Law of Diminishing Marginal Utility.
cards.back: marginal utility from consuming each additional unit of a commodity declines as its consumption increases, while keeping consumption of other commodities constant.
cards.quote: marginal utility from consuming each additional unit of a commodity declines as its consumption increases, while keeping consumption of other commodities constant.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: The ____ of scarce resources and the ____ of the final goods and services are the central problems of any economy.
