cards.back: The allocation of scarce resources and the distribution of the final goods and services are the central problems of any economy.
cards.quote: The allocation of scarce resources and the distribution of the final goods and services are the central problems of any economy.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is demand for a commodity?
cards.back: The quantity of a commodity that a consumer is willing to buy and is able to afford, given prices of goods and income of the consumer, is called demand for that commodity.
cards.quote: The quantity of a commodity that a consumer is willing to buy and is able to afford, given prices of goods and income of the consumer, is called demand for that commodity.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is the production possibility set of an economy?
cards.back: The collection of all possible combinations of the goods and services that can be produced from a given amount of resources and a given stock of technological knowledge is called the production possibility set of the economy.
cards.quote: The collection of all possible combinations of the goods and services that can be produced from a given amount of resources and a given stock of technological knowledge is called the production possibility set of the economy.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Define the demand curve as in the cardinal utility analysis of a single commodity.
cards.back: Demand curve is a graphic presentation of various quantities of a commodity that a consumer is willing to buy at different prices of the same commodity, while holding constant prices of other related commodities and income of the consumer.
cards.quote: Demand curve is a graphic presentation of various quantities of a commodity that a consumer is willing to buy at different prices of the same commodity, while holding constant prices of other related commodities and income of the consumer.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is the production possibility frontier?
cards.back: The production possibility frontier gives the combinations of corn and cotton that can be produced when the resources of the economy are fully utilised.
cards.quote: The production possibility frontier gives the combinations of corn and cotton that can be produced when the resources of the economy are fully utilised.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What does a point lying strictly below the production possibility frontier represent?
cards.back:
Underemployed or wastefully utilised resources
Note that a point lying strictly below the production possibility frontier represents a combination of corn and cotton that will be produced when all or some of the resources are either underemployed or are utilised in a wasteful fashion.
cards.quote: Note that a point lying strictly below the production possibility frontier represents a combination of corn and cotton that will be produced when all or some of the resources are either underemployed or are utilised in a wasteful fashion.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Which law of utility explains why demand curves have a negative slope?
cards.back: the law of diminishing marginal utility explains why demand curves have a negative slope.
cards.quote: the law of diminishing marginal utility explains why demand curves have a negative slope.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is the opportunity cost of an additional unit of a good?
cards.back: Thus, there is always a cost of having a little more of one good in terms of the amount of the other good that has to be forgone.
cards.quote: Thus, there is always a cost of having a little more of one good in terms of the amount of the other good that has to be forgone.
cards.note: Opportunity cost is the amount of the other good given up to get a little more of one good.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is the major drawback of cardinal utility analysis?
cards.back: Cardinal utility analysis is simple to understand, but suffers from a major drawback in the form of quantification of utility in numbers.
cards.quote: Cardinal utility analysis is simple to understand, but suffers from a major drawback in the form of quantification of utility in numbers.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: By what other name is opportunity cost sometimes called?
cards.back:
Economic cost
Because of its importance in economics, sometimes, opportunity cost is also called the economic cost.
cards.quote: Because of its importance in economics, sometimes, opportunity cost is also called the economic cost.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: In real life a consumer never expresses utility in numbers; what can she do at the most (ordinal analysis)?
cards.back: In real life, we never express utility in the form of numbers. At the most, we can rank various alternative combinations in terms of having more or less utility.
cards.quote: In real life, we never express utility in the form of numbers. At the most, we can rank various alternative combinations in terms of having more or less utility.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is an indifference curve?
cards.back: An indifference curve is a locus of all points representing bundles among which the consumer is indifferent.
cards.quote: An indifference curve is a locus of all points representing bundles among which the consumer is indifferent.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: To whom is the concept of opportunity cost applicable?
cards.back:
The individual as well as the society
Note that the concept of opportunity cost is applicable to the individual as well as the society.
cards.quote: Note that the concept of opportunity cost is applicable to the individual as well as the society.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is the marginal rate of substitution (MRS)?
cards.back: The amount of mangoes that the consumer has to forego, in order to get an additional banana, her total utility level being the same, is called marginal rate of substitution (MRS).
cards.quote: The amount of mangoes that the consumer has to forego, in order to get an additional banana, her total utility level being the same, is called marginal rate of substitution (MRS).

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: In what two ways can the basic problems of an economy be solved?
cards.back:
By the market, or by planning by a central authority
Basic problems can be solved either by the free interaction of the individuals pursuing their own objectives as is done in the market or in a planned manner by some central authority like the government.
cards.quote: Basic problems can be solved either by the free interaction of the individuals pursuing their own objectives as is done in the market or in a planned manner by some central authority like the government.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is a centrally planned economy?
cards.back: In a centrally planned economy, the government or the central authority plans all the important activities in the economy.
cards.quote: In a centrally planned economy, the government or the central authority plans all the important activities in the economy.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Formula: MRS = | ΔY / ΔX |. What does it mean, and what is MRS if ΔY / ΔX = −3 / 1?
cards.back: MRS =| ∆Y / ∆X | means that MRS equals only the magnitude of the expression ∆Y / ∆X . If ∆Y / ∆X = −3 / 1 it means MRS=3.
cards.quote: MRS =| ∆Y / ∆X | means that MRS equals only the magnitude of the expression ∆Y / ∆X . If ∆Y / ∆X = −3 / 1 it means MRS=3.
cards.note: Y = mangoes, X = bananas: MRS is the mangoes given up per extra banana, taken as a positive number.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is the tendency of the MRS to fall as the quantity of bananas increases called?
cards.back:
Law of Diminishing Marginal Rate of Substitution
This tendency for the MRS to fall with increase in quantity of bananas is known as Law of Diminishing Marginal Rate of Substitution.
cards.quote: This tendency for the MRS to fall with increase in quantity of bananas is known as Law of Diminishing Marginal Rate of Substitution.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is a market economy?
cards.back: In contrast to a centrally planned economy, in a market economy, all economic activities are organised through the market.
cards.quote: In contrast to a centrally planned economy, in a market economy, all economic activities are organised through the market.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: The law of Diminishing Marginal Rate of Substitution causes an indifference curve to be ____ to the origin.
cards.back: The law of Diminishing Marginal Rate of Substitution causes an indifference curve to be **convex** to the origin.
cards.quote: The law of Diminishing Marginal Rate of Substitution causes an indifference curve to be convex to the origin.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is a market, as studied in economics?
cards.back: In other words, a market is a set of arrangements where economic agents can freely exchange their endowments or products with each other.
cards.quote: In other words, a market is a set of arrangements where economic agents can freely exchange their endowments or products with each other.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What are perfect substitutes?
cards.back: Perfect Substitutes are the goods which can be used in place of each other, and provide exactly the same level of utility to the consumer.
cards.quote: Perfect Substitutes are the goods which can be used in place of each other, and provide exactly the same level of utility to the consumer.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Indifference curve depicting two commodities which are perfect substitutes is a ____.
cards.back: Indifference curve depicting two commodities which are perfect substitutes is a **straight line**.
cards.quote: Indifference curve depicting two commodities which are perfect substitutes is a straight line.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What are monotonic preferences?
cards.back: Consumer's preferences are assumed to be such that between any two bundles (x1, x2) and (y1, y2), if (x1, x2) has more of at least one of the goods and no less of the other good compared to (y1, y2), then the consumer prefers (x1, x2) to (y1, y2). Preferences of this kind are called monotonic preferences.
cards.quote: Consumer's preferences are assumed to be such that between any two bundles (x1, x2) and (y1, y2), if (x1, x2) has more of at least one of the goods and no less of the other good compared to (y1, y2), then the consumer prefers (x1, x2) to (y1, y2). Preferences of this kind are called monotonic preferences.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is an indifference map?
cards.back: The consumer’s preferences over all the bundles can be represented by a family of indifference curves as shown in Figure 2.5. This is called an indifference map of the consumer.
cards.quote: The consumer’s preferences over all the bundles can be represented by a family of indifference curves as shown in Figure 2.5. This is called an indifference map of the consumer.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: In a market system, how are the central problems of how much and what to produce solved?
cards.back:
Through coordination brought about by the price signals
in a market system, the central problems regarding how much and what to produce are solved through the coordination of economic activities brought about by the price signals.
cards.quote: in a market system, the central problems regarding how much and what to produce are solved through the coordination of economic activities brought about by the price signals.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Define a mixed economy (the form every real economy takes).
cards.back: In reality, all economies are mixed economies where some important decisions are taken by the government and the economic activities are by and large conducted through the market.
cards.quote: In reality, all economies are mixed economies where some important decisions are taken by the government and the economic activities are by and large conducted through the market.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: In which direction does an indifference curve slope from left to right, and what does this mean for bananas and mangoes?
cards.back: An indifference curve slopes downwards from left to right, which means that in order to have more of bananas, the consumer has to forego some mangoes.
cards.quote: An indifference curve slopes downwards from left to right, which means that in order to have more of bananas, the consumer has to forego some mangoes.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: As long as marginal utility of a commodity is ____, an individual will always prefer more of that commodity
cards.back: As long as marginal utility of a commodity is **positive**, an individual will always prefer more of that commodity
cards.quote: As long as marginal utility of a commodity is positive, an individual will always prefer more of that commodity

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Can two indifference curves intersect each other? What would intersecting curves lead to?
cards.back: Thus, it is clear that intersecting indifference curves will lead to conflicting results. Thus, two indifference curves cannot intersect each other.
cards.quote: Thus, it is clear that intersecting indifference curves will lead to conflicting results. Thus, two indifference curves cannot intersect each other.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is a consumer's budget set?
cards.back: The budget set is thus the collection of all bundles that the consumer can buy with her income at the prevailing market prices.
cards.quote: The budget set is thus the collection of all bundles that the consumer can buy with her income at the prevailing market prices.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Name the two broad branches under which economics has traditionally been studied.
cards.back:
Microeconomics
Macroeconomics
cards.quote: Traditionally, the subject matter of economics has been studied under two broad branches: Microeconomics and Macroeconomics.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is microeconomics? In microeconomics, we study...
cards.back: the behaviour of individual economic agents in the markets for different goods and services and try to figure out how prices and quantities of goods and services are determined through the interaction of individuals in these markets.
cards.quote: the behaviour of individual economic agents in the markets for different goods and services and try to figure out how prices and quantities of goods and services are determined through the interaction of individuals in these markets.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Formula: the consumer's budget constraint (income M, prices p1 and p2).
cards.back: p1x1 + p2x2 ≤ M
cards.quote: In other words, the consumer can buy any bundle (x1, x2) such that p1x1 + p2x2 ≤ M (2.1)
cards.note: The bundle (x1, x2) must cost no more than the income M.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is the budget line?
cards.back: The budget line represents all bundles which cost the consumer her entire income. The budget line is negatively sloping.
cards.quote: The budget line represents all bundles which cost the consumer her entire income. The budget line is negatively sloping.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Microeconomics vs macroeconomics: the difference in what is studied.
cards.back: Thus, instead of studying the different markets as is done in microeconomics, in macroeconomics, we try to study the behaviour of aggregate or macro measures of the performance of the economy.
cards.quote: Thus, instead of studying the different markets as is done in microeconomics, in macroeconomics, we try to study the behaviour of aggregate or macro measures of the performance of the economy.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Formula: slope of the budget line, with bananas (price p1) on the horizontal axis and mangoes (price p2) on the vertical axis
cards.back: The slope of the budget line is – p1/p2.
cards.quote: The slope of the budget line is – p1/p2.
cards.note: p1 = price of bananas (horizontal axis), p2 = price of mangoes (vertical axis).

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: On a budget line, with banana price p1 and mango price p2, how many mangoes go for one extra banana?
cards.back: she will have to give up p1/p2 quantities of mangoes
cards.quote: Therefore, if the consumer wants to have an extra quantity of bananas when she is spending all her money, she will have to give up p1/p2 quantities of mangoes.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: On the budget line (bananas on the horizontal axis), what does the horizontal intercept represent?
cards.back: The horizontal intercept represents the bundle that the consumer can buy if she spends her entire income on bananas.
cards.quote: The horizontal intercept represents the bundle that the consumer can buy if she spends her entire income on bananas.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: If income changes and prices stay the same, what happens to the slope of the budget line?
cards.back: Note that the slope of the new budget line is the same as the slope of the budget line prior to the change in the consumer’s income.
cards.quote: Note that the slope of the new budget line is the same as the slope of the budget line prior to the change in the consumer’s income.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: When income rises (M' > M) with prices unchanged, how does the budget line shift?
cards.back: if M' > M, the vertical as well as horizontal intercepts increase, there is a parallel outward shift of the budget line.
cards.quote: if M' > M, the vertical as well as horizontal intercepts increase, there is a parallel outward shift of the budget line.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: When income falls (M' < M) with prices unchanged, how does the budget line shift?
cards.back: if the income goes down, i.e. if M' < M, both intercepts decrease, and hence, there is a parallel inward shift of the budget line.
cards.quote: if the income goes down, i.e. if M' < M, both intercepts decrease, and hence, there is a parallel inward shift of the budget line.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: If the price of bananas increases, ie if p'1> p1, the absolute value of the slope of the budget line increases, and the budget line becomes ____
cards.back: If the price of bananas increases, ie if p'1> p1, the absolute value of the slope of the budget line increases, and the budget line becomes **steeper**
cards.quote: If the price of bananas increases, ie if p'1> p1, the absolute value of the slope of the budget line increases, and the budget line becomes steeper

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: If the price of bananas decreases, i.e., p'1< p1, the absolute value of the slope of the budget line decreases and hence, the budget line becomes ____
cards.back: If the price of bananas decreases, i.e., p'1< p1, the absolute value of the slope of the budget line decreases and hence, the budget line becomes **flatter**
cards.quote: If the price of bananas decreases, i.e., p'1< p1, the absolute value of the slope of the budget line decreases and hence, the budget line becomes flatter

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: The optimum bundle of the consumer is located at the point where the budget line is ____ to one of the indifference curves.
cards.back: The optimum bundle of the consumer is located at the point where the budget line is **tangent** to one of the indifference curves.
cards.quote: The optimum bundle of the consumer is located at the point where the budget line is tangent to one of the indifference curves.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: At the optimum bundle, where the budget line touches an indifference curve, which two slopes are equal?
cards.back:
MRS (slope of indifference curve) = price ratio (slope of budget line)
the absolute value of the slope of the indifference curve (MRS) and that of the budget line (price ratio) are same at that point.
cards.quote: the absolute value of the slope of the indifference curve (MRS) and that of the budget line (price ratio) are same at that point.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: The slope of the ____ is the rate at which the consumer is willing to substitute one good for the other.
cards.back: The slope of the **indifference curve** is the rate at which the consumer is willing to substitute one good for the other.
cards.quote: The slope of the indifference curve is the rate at which the consumer is willing to substitute one good for the other.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: The slope of the ____ is the rate at which the consumer is able to substitute one good for the other in the market.
cards.back: The slope of the **budget line** is the rate at which the consumer is able to substitute one good for the other in the market.
cards.quote: The slope of the budget line is the rate at which the consumer is able to substitute one good for the other in the market.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Who is a rational individual in economics?
cards.back: A rational individual clearly knows what is good or what is bad for her, and in any given situation, she always tries to achieve the best for herself.
cards.quote: A rational individual clearly knows what is good or what is bad for her, and in any given situation, she always tries to achieve the best for herself.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: From the available bundles, which one does a rational consumer always choose?
cards.back: From the bundles which are available to her, a rational consumer always chooses the one which gives her maximum satisfaction.
cards.quote: From the bundles which are available to her, a rational consumer always chooses the one which gives her maximum satisfaction.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: The rational consumer's problem is to move to a point on the ____ possible indifference curve given her budget set.
cards.back: The rational consumer's problem is to move to a point on the **highest** possible indifference curve given her budget set.
cards.quote: The rational consumer's problem is to move to a point on the highest possible indifference curve given her budget set.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: With monotonic preferences, is the consumer's optimum (most preferred) bundle below, on or above the budget line?
cards.back: Therefore, the optimum (most preferred) bundle of the consumer would be on the budget line.
cards.quote: Therefore, the optimum (most preferred) bundle of the consumer would be on the budget line.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Formula: the consumer's demand for a good as a function of its price.
cards.back:
X = f (P)
where X denotes the quantity and P denotes the price of the good.
cards.quote: The consumer's demand for a good as a function of its price can be written as X = f (P) (2.12) where X denotes the quantity and P denotes the price of the good.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: The graphical representation of the demand function is called the ____.
cards.back:
demand curve
The graphical representation of the demand function is called the demand curve.
cards.quote: The graphical representation of the demand function is called the demand curve.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Name the two effects that explain the negative slope of the demand curve.
cards.back:
substitution effect
income effect
cards.quote: The negative slope of the demand curve can also be explained in terms of the two effects namely, substitution effect and income effect that come into play when price of a commodity changes.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is the income effect of a price change (when bananas become cheaper)?
cards.back: as price of bananas drops, consumer’s purchasing power increases, which further increases demand for bananas (and mangoes). This is the income effect of a price change, resulting in further increase in demand for bananas.
cards.quote: as price of bananas drops, consumer’s purchasing power increases, which further increases demand for bananas (and mangoes). This is the income effect of a price change, resulting in further increase in demand for bananas.
cards.note: This is the income effect of a price change.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: State the Law of Demand.
cards.back: Law of Demand states that other things being equal, there is a negative relation between demand for a commodity and its price.
cards.quote: Law of Demand states that other things being equal, there is a negative relation between demand for a commodity and its price.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What are normal goods?
cards.back: For most goods, the quantity that a consumer chooses, increases as the consumer's income increases and decreases as the consumer's income decreases. Such goods are called normal goods.
cards.quote: For most goods, the quantity that a consumer chooses, increases as the consumer's income increases and decreases as the consumer's income decreases. Such goods are called normal goods.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What are inferior goods?
cards.back: However, there are some goods the demands for which move in the opposite direction of the income of the consumer. Such goods are called inferior goods.
cards.quote: However, there are some goods the demands for which move in the opposite direction of the income of the consumer. Such goods are called inferior goods.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Which low quality food items does NCERT give as an example of inferior goods?
cards.back: Examples of inferior goods include low quality food items like coarse cereals.
cards.quote: Examples of inferior goods include low quality food items like coarse cereals.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is a Giffen good?
cards.back: if the income effect is stronger than the substitution effect, the demand for the good would be positively related to its price. Such a good is called a Giffen good.
cards.quote: if the income effect is stronger than the substitution effect, the demand for the good would be positively related to its price. Such a good is called a Giffen good.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What are complementary goods? Give examples.
cards.back: Goods which are consumed together are called complementary goods. Examples of goods which are complement to each other include tea and sugar, shoes and socks, pen and ink, etc.
cards.quote: Goods which are consumed together are called complementary goods. Examples of goods which are complement to each other include tea and sugar, shoes and socks, pen and ink, etc.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: In general, the demand for a good moves in the ____ direction of the price of its complementary goods.
cards.back: In general, the demand for a good moves in the **opposite** direction of the price of its complementary goods.
cards.quote: In general, the demand for a good moves in the opposite direction of the price of its complementary goods.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Substitute goods: which pair does NCERT give, and what happens to demand for tea if the price of coffee rises?
cards.back: goods like tea and coffee are not consumed together. In fact, they are substitutes for each other. Since tea is a substitute for coffee, if the price of coffee increases, the consumers can shift to tea, and hence, the consumption of tea is likely to go up.
cards.quote: goods like tea and coffee are not consumed together. In fact, they are substitutes for each other. Since tea is a substitute for coffee, if the price of coffee increases, the consumers can shift to tea, and hence, the consumption of tea is likely to go up.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: In which direction does the demand for a good usually move relative to the price of its substitutes?
cards.back: The demand for a good usually moves in the direction of the price of its substitutes.
cards.quote: The demand for a good usually moves in the direction of the price of its substitutes.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: For normal goods, the demand curve shifts ____ and for inferior goods, the demand curve shifts ____.
cards.back: For normal goods, the demand curve shifts **rightward** and for inferior goods, the demand curve shifts **leftward**.
cards.quote: For normal goods, the demand curve shifts rightward and for inferior goods, the demand curve shifts leftward.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: If there is an increase in the price of a ____ good, the demand curve shifts ____.
cards.back: If there is an increase in the price of a **substitute** good, the demand curve shifts **rightward**.
cards.quote: If there is an increase in the price of a substitute good, the demand curve shifts rightward.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: If the price of a complementary good increases, in which direction does the demand curve shift?
cards.back: if there is an increase in the price of a complementary good, the demand curve shifts leftward.
cards.quote: if there is an increase in the price of a complementary good, the demand curve shifts leftward.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: If the consumer's preferences change in ____ of a good, the demand curve for such a good shifts ____.
cards.back: If the consumer's preferences change in **favour** of a good, the demand curve for such a good shifts **rightward**.
cards.quote: If the consumer's preferences change in favour of a good, the demand curve for such a good shifts rightward.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What happens to the demand curve when the consumer's preferences change unfavourably?
cards.back: the demand curve shifts leftward due to an unfavourable change in the preferences of the consumer.
cards.quote: the demand curve shifts leftward due to an unfavourable change in the preferences of the consumer.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Why is the demand curve for ice-creams likely to shift rightward in summer?
cards.back: The demand curve for ice-creams, for example, is likely to shift rightward in the summer because of preference for ice-creams goes up in summer.
cards.quote: The demand curve for ice-creams, for example, is likely to shift rightward in the summer because of preference for ice-creams goes up in summer.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: When does a shift in the demand curve (not a movement along it) take place?
cards.back: It may be mentioned that shift in demand curve takes place when there is a change in some factor, other than the price of the commodity.
cards.quote: It may be mentioned that shift in demand curve takes place when there is a change in some factor, other than the price of the commodity.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Any change in the price leads to ____ along the demand curve.
cards.back: Any change in the price leads to **movements** along the demand curve.
cards.quote: Any change in the price leads to movements along the demand curve.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is the market demand for a good at a particular price?
cards.back: The market demand for a good at a particular price is the total demand of all consumers taken together.
cards.quote: The market demand for a good at a particular price is the total demand of all consumers taken together.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: How is market demand at price p′ found when consumer 1 demands q1′ and consumer 2 demands q2′?
cards.back: the market demand of the good at p′ is q1′ + q′2.
cards.quote: Suppose at price p′, the demand of consumer 1 is q1′ and that of consumer 2 is q′2. Then, the market demand of the good at p′ is q1′ + q′2.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is the method of adding individual demand curves horizontally to get the market demand curve called?
cards.back: graphically by adding up the individual demand curves horizontally as shown in Figure 2.18. This method of adding two curves is called horizontal summation.
cards.quote: graphically by adding up the individual demand curves horizontally as shown in Figure 2.18. This method of adding two curves is called horizontal summation.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is price elasticity of demand?
cards.back: Price elasticity of demand is a measure of the responsiveness of the demand for a good to changes in its price.
cards.quote: Price elasticity of demand is a measure of the responsiveness of the demand for a good to changes in its price.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Types of price elasticity of demand by the value of eD.
cards.back:
eD is estimated to be less than one and the demand for the good is said to be inelastic at that price.
the estimated eD is more than one. The demand for the good is said to be elastic at that price.
eD is estimated to be equal to one and the demand for the good is said to be Unitary-elastic at that price.
cards.quote: When the percentage change in quantity demanded is less than the percentage change in market price, eD is estimated to be less than one and the demand for the good is said to be inelastic at that price. Demand for essential goods is often found to be inelastic. When the percentage change in quantity demanded is more than the percentage change in market price, the demand is said to be highly responsive to changes in market price and the estimated eD is more than one. The demand for the good is said to be elastic at that price. Demand for luxury goods is seen to be highly responsive to changes in their market prices and eD >1. When the percentage change in quantity demanded equals the percentage change in its market price, eD is estimated to be equal to one and the demand for the good is said to be Unitary-elastic at that price.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Is demand for essential goods often found to be elastic or inelastic?
cards.back: Demand for essential goods is often found to be inelastic.
cards.quote: Demand for essential goods is often found to be inelastic.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Demand for ____ goods is seen to be highly responsive to changes in their market prices and eD >1.
cards.back: Demand for **luxury** goods is seen to be highly responsive to changes in their market prices and eD >1.
cards.quote: Demand for luxury goods is seen to be highly responsive to changes in their market prices and eD >1.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Note that the price elasticity of demand is a ____ number since the demand for a good is negatively related to the price of a good.
cards.back: Note that the price elasticity of demand is a **negative** number since the demand for a good is negatively related to the price of a good.
cards.quote: Note that the price elasticity of demand is a negative number since the demand for a good is negatively related to the price of a good.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: For simplicity, we will always refer to the ____ value of the elasticity.
cards.back: For simplicity, we will always refer to the **absolute** value of the elasticity.
cards.quote: For simplicity, we will always refer to the absolute value of the elasticity.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: How does elasticity vary along a straight line demand curve (at the axes, at the midpoint, left and right of it)?
cards.back: Elasticity is 0 at the point where the demand curve meets the horizontal axis and it is ∞ at the point where the demand curve meets the vertical axis. At the midpoint of the demand curve, the elasticity is 1, at any point to the left of the midpoint, it is greater than 1 and at any point to the right, it is less than 1.
cards.quote: Elasticity is 0 at the point where the demand curve meets the horizontal axis and it is ∞ at the point where the demand curve meets the vertical axis. At the midpoint of the demand curve, the elasticity is 1, at any point to the left of the midpoint, it is greater than 1 and at any point to the right, it is less than 1.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is the price elasticity of demand |eD| of a vertical demand curve?
cards.back: A price never leads to a change in the demand for such a demand curve and |eD| is always 0. Therefore, a vertical demand curve is perfectly inelastic.
cards.quote: A price never leads to a change in the demand for such a demand curve and |eD| is always 0. Therefore, a vertical demand curve is perfectly inelastic.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is the price elasticity of demand of a horizontal demand curve?
cards.back: At any other price, quantity demanded drops to zero and therefore ed = ∞. A horizontal demand curve is perfectly elastic.
cards.quote: At any other price, quantity demanded drops to zero and therefore ed = ∞. A horizontal demand curve is perfectly elastic.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Which demand curve shape has |eD| = 1 at every point, and what is such a curve called?
cards.back: Figure 2.20(c) depicts a demand curve which has the shape of a rectangular hyperbola. This demand curve has a property that a percentage change in price along the demand curve always leads to equal percentage change in quantity. Therefore, |eD| = 1 at every point on this demand curve. This demand curve is called the unitary elastic demand curve.
cards.quote: Figure 2.20(c) depicts a demand curve which has the shape of a rectangular hyperbola. This demand curve has a property that a percentage change in price along the demand curve always leads to equal percentage change in quantity. Therefore, |eD| = 1 at every point on this demand curve. This demand curve is called the unitary elastic demand curve.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: On what does the price elasticity of demand for a good depend?
cards.back:
the nature of the good
the availability of close substitutes of the good
cards.quote: The price elasticity of demand for a good depends on the nature of the good and the availability of close substitutes of the good.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: When is the demand for a good likely to be elastic, as far as substitutes are concerned?
cards.back: The demand for a good is likely to be elastic if close substitutes are easily available.
cards.quote: The demand for a good is likely to be elastic if close substitutes are easily available.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: If close substitutes are not available easily, the demand for a good is likely to be ____.
cards.back: If close substitutes are not available easily, the demand for a good is likely to be **inelastic**.
cards.quote: If close substitutes are not available easily, the demand for a good is likely to be inelastic.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is the expenditure on a good equal to?
cards.back: The expenditure on a good is equal to the demand for the good times its price.
cards.quote: The expenditure on a good is equal to the demand for the good times its price.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: How does expenditure on a good change with its price for price-elastic, price-inelastic and unit-elastic goods?
cards.back:
The expenditure on the good would change in the opposite direction as the price change if and only if the percentage change in quantity is greater than the percentage change in price, ie if the good is price-elastic
The expenditure on the good would change in the same direction as the price change if and only if the percentage change in quantity is less than the percentage change in price, i.e., if the good is price inelastic
The expenditure on the good would remain unchanged if and only if the percentage change in quantity is equal to the percentage change in price, i.e., if the good is unit-elastic
cards.quote: The expenditure on the good would change in the opposite direction as the price change if and only if the percentage change in quantity is greater than the percentage change in price, ie if the good is price-elastic (see rows 2 and 4 in table 2.5). The expenditure on the good would change in the same direction as the price change if and only if the percentage change in quantity is less than the percentage change in price, i.e., if the good is price inelastic (see rows 1 and 5 in table 2.5). The expenditure on the good would remain unchanged if and only if the percentage change in quantity is equal to the percentage change in price, i.e., if the good is unit-elastic

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: The elasticity of demand is a ____ number.
cards.back: The elasticity of demand is a **pure** number.
cards.quote: The elasticity of demand is a pure number.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Define equilibrium in a perfectly competitive market.
cards.back: An equilibrium is defined as a situation where the plans of all consumers and firms in the market match and the market clears.
cards.quote: An equilibrium is defined as a situation where the plans of all consumers and firms in the market match and the market clears.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: The price at which equilibrium is reached is called ____ and the quantity bought and sold at this price is called ____.
cards.back: The price at which equilibrium is reached is called equilibrium price and the quantity bought and sold at this price is called equilibrium quantity.
cards.quote: The price at which equilibrium is reached is called equilibrium price and the quantity bought and sold at this price is called equilibrium quantity.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Formula: the condition for (p*, q*) to be an equilibrium.
cards.back: Therefore, (p*, q*) is an equilibrium if qD(p*) = qS(p*)
cards.quote: Therefore, (p*, q*) is an equilibrium if qD(p*) = qS(p*)
cards.note: qD is market demand, qS is market supply and p* is the equilibrium price: equilibrium holds where demand equals supply.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is excess supply?
cards.back: If at a price, market supply is greater than market demand, we say that there is an excess supply in the market at that price
cards.quote: If at a price, market supply is greater than market demand, we say that there is an excess supply in the market at that price

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is excess demand?
cards.back: if market demand exceeds market supply at a price, it is said that excess demand exists in the market at that price
cards.quote: if market demand exceeds market supply at a price, it is said that excess demand exists in the market at that price

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Equilibrium in a perfectly competitive market can be defined alternatively as ____ situation.
cards.back: Equilibrium in a perfectly competitive market can be defined alternatively as zero excess demand-zero excess supply situation.
cards.quote: Equilibrium in a perfectly competitive market can be defined alternatively as zero excess demand-zero excess supply situation.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Whose name is linked with the ‘Invisible Hand’ that changes price when a perfectly competitive market is out of balance?
cards.back: From the time of Adam Smith (1723-1790), it has been maintained that in a perfectly competitive market an ‘Invisible Hand’ is at play which changes price whenever there is imbalance in the market.
cards.quote: From the time of Adam Smith (1723-1790), it has been maintained that in a perfectly competitive market an ‘Invisible Hand’ is at play which changes price whenever there is imbalance in the market.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What should the ‘Invisible Hand’ do to prices under excess demand and under excess supply?
cards.back: this ‘Invisible Hand’ should raise the prices in case of ‘excess demand’ and lower the prices in case of ‘excess supply’
cards.quote: Our intuition also tells us that this ‘Invisible Hand’ should raise the prices in case of ‘excess demand’ and lower the prices in case of ‘excess supply’.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Graphically, an equilibrium is a point where the market supply curve ____ the market demand curve
cards.back: Graphically, an equilibrium is a point where the market supply curve intersects the market demand curve
cards.quote: Graphically, an equilibrium is a point where the market supply curve intersects the market demand curve

source.section: Market Equilibrium: Fixed Number of Firms

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: With equilibrium price p* in a market, what is there at any price greater than p*, and at any price lower than p*?
cards.back: At any price greater than p*, there will be excess supply, and at any price lower than p*,there will be excess demand.
cards.quote: At any price greater than p*, there will be excess supply, and at any price lower than p*,there will be excess demand.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is a price ceiling?
cards.back: The government-imposed upper limit on the price of a good or service is called price ceiling.
cards.quote: The government-imposed upper limit on the price of a good or service is called price ceiling.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: On which items is a price ceiling generally imposed (NCERT's examples)?
cards.back: Price ceiling is generally imposed on necessary items like wheat, rice, kerosene, sugar
cards.quote: Price ceiling is generally imposed on necessary items like wheat, rice, kerosene, sugar

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: ____ are issued to the consumers so that no individual can buy more than a certain amount of wheat
cards.back: Ration coupons are issued to the consumers so that no individual can buy more than a certain amount of wheat
cards.quote: Ration coupons are issued to the consumers so that no individual can buy more than a certain amount of wheat

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Ration shops which are also called ____
cards.back: Ration shops which are also called fair price shops
cards.quote: Ration shops which are also called fair price shops

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Name the adverse consequences on consumers of a price ceiling accompanied by rationing.
cards.back:
(a) Each consumer has to stand in long queues to buy the good from ration shops.
(b) Since all consumers will not be satisfied by the quantity of the goods that they get from the fair price shop, some of them will be willing to pay higher price for it. This may result in the creation of black market.
cards.quote: In general, price ceiling accompanied by rationing of the goods may have the following adverse consequences on the consumers: (a) Each consumer has to stand in long queues to buy the good from ration shops. (b) Since all consumers will not be satisfied by the quantity of the goods that they get from the fair price shop, some of them will be willing to pay higher price for it. This may result in the creation of black market.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is the government-imposed lower limit on the price that may be charged for a good or service called?
cards.back: particular good or service is called price floor.
cards.quote: particular good or service is called price floor.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Name NCERT's well-known examples of imposing a price floor.
cards.back: examples of imposition of price floor are agricultural price support programmes and the minimum wage legislation.
cards.quote: examples of imposition of price floor are agricultural price support programmes and the minimum wage legislation.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: In an agricultural price support programme, how is the floor normally set relative to the market-determined price?
cards.back: the floor is normally set at a level higher than the market-determined price for these goods.
cards.quote: the floor is normally set at a level higher than the market-determined price for these goods.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Through the ____, the government ensures that the wage rate of the labourers does not fall below a particular level
cards.back: Through the minimum wage legislation, the government ensures that the wage rate of the labourers does not fall below a particular level
cards.quote: Through the minimum wage legislation, the government ensures that the wage rate of the labourers does not fall below a particular level

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: In agricultural support, what must the government do to stop price falling because of excess supply?
cards.back: In the case of agricultural support, to prevent price from falling because of excess supply, government needs to buy the surplus at the predetermined price.
cards.quote: In the case of agricultural support, to prevent price from falling because of excess supply, government needs to buy the surplus at the predetermined price.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: In a perfectly competitive market, equilibrium occurs where ____.
cards.back: In a perfectly competitive market, equilibrium occurs where market demand equals market supply.
cards.quote: In a perfectly competitive market, equilibrium occurs where market demand equals market supply.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: The equilibrium price and quantity are determined at the ____ of the market demand and market supply curves when there is fixed number of firms.
cards.back: The equilibrium price and quantity are determined at the intersection of the market demand and market supply curves when there is fixed number of firms.
cards.quote: The equilibrium price and quantity are determined at the intersection of the market demand and market supply curves when there is fixed number of firms.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What does the imposition of a price ceiling below the equilibrium price lead to?
cards.back: Imposition of price ceiling below the equilibrium price leads to an excess demand.
cards.quote: Imposition of price ceiling below the equilibrium price leads to an excess demand.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What does the imposition of a price floor above the equilibrium price lead to?
cards.back: Imposition of price floor above the equilibrium price leads to an excess supply.
cards.quote: Imposition of price floor above the equilibrium price leads to an excess supply.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is money?
cards.back: Money is the commonly accepted medium of exchange.
cards.quote: Money is the commonly accepted medium of exchange.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Define barter exchange.
cards.back: Economic exchanges without the mediation of money are referred to as barter exchanges.
cards.quote: Economic exchanges without the mediation of money are referred to as barter exchanges.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: A person has surplus rice and wants clothing but finds no one to swap with. Which barter difficulty is this?
cards.back:
double coincidence of wants
If she is not lucky enough she may not be able to find another person who has the diametrically opposite demand for rice with a surplus of clothing to offer in exchange.
cards.quote: However, they presume the rather improbable double coincidence of wants. Consider, for example, an individual who has a surplus of rice which she wishes to exchange for clothing. If she is not lucky enough she may not be able to find another person who has the diametrically opposite demand for rice with a surplus of clothing to offer in exchange.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: As explained above, the first and foremost role of money is that it acts as a ____.
cards.back: As explained above, the first and foremost role of money is that it acts as a medium of exchange.
cards.quote: As explained above, the first and foremost role of money is that it acts as a medium of exchange.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Money also acts as a convenient ____. The value of all goods and services can be expressed in monetary units.
cards.back: Money also acts as a convenient unit of account. The value of all goods and services can be expressed in monetary units.
cards.quote: Money also acts as a convenient unit of account. The value of all goods and services can be expressed in monetary units.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: If the general price level rises, what happens to the purchasing power of money?
cards.back: Thus if prices of all commodities increase in terms of money i.e., there is a general increase in the price level, the value of money in terms of any commodity must have decreased – in the sense that a unit of money can now purchase less of any commodity. We call it a deterioration in the purchasing power of money.
cards.quote: Thus if prices of all commodities increase in terms of money i.e., there is a general increase in the price level, the value of money in terms of any commodity must have decreased – in the sense that a unit of money can now purchase less of any commodity. We call it a deterioration in the purchasing power of money.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Why is money easier than perishable goods for carrying wealth forward?
cards.back: Money is not perishable and its storage costs are also considerably lower. It is also acceptable to anyone at any point of time.
cards.quote: Money is not perishable and its storage costs are also considerably lower. It is also acceptable to anyone at any point of time.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Which function of money lets individuals keep wealth for future use?
cards.back: Thus money can act as a store of value for individuals. Wealth can be stored in the form of money for future use.
cards.quote: Thus money can act as a store of value for individuals. Wealth can be stored in the form of money for future use.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: For money to act as a store of value, what must be true of its value?
cards.back: However, to perform this function well, the value of money must be sufficiently stable.
cards.quote: Wealth can be stored in the form of money for future use. However, to perform this function well, the value of money must be sufficiently stable.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Why are assets like gold, landed property, houses or bonds less suitable than money as a store of value?
cards.back: It may be noted that any asset other than money can also act as a store of value, e.g. gold, landed property, houses or even bonds (to be introduced shortly). However, they may not be easily convertible to other commodities and do not have universal acceptability.
cards.quote: It may be noted that any asset other than money can also act as a store of value, e.g. gold, landed property, houses or even bonds (to be introduced shortly). However, they may not be easily convertible to other commodities and do not have universal acceptability.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What does money comprise in a modern economy?
cards.back: In a modern economy, money comprises cash and bank deposits.
cards.quote: In a modern economy, money comprises cash and bank deposits.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Types of institutions that create the money supply.
cards.back:
central bank of the economy
commercial banking system
cards.quote: These are created by a system comprising two types of institutions: central bank of the economy and the commercial banking system.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: When did India get its central bank, and what is it called?
cards.back: India got its central bank in 1935. Its name is the ‘Reserve Bank of India’.
cards.quote: India got its central bank in 1935. Its name is the ‘Reserve Bank of India’.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Name the functions of the central bank.
cards.back:
It issues the currency of the country.
It controls money supply of the country through various methods, like bank rate, open market operations and variations in reserve ratios.
It acts as a banker to the government.
It is the custodian of the foreign exchange reserves of the economy.
It also acts as a bank to the banking system
cards.quote: Central bank has several important functions. It issues the currency of the country. It controls money supply of the country through various methods, like bank rate, open market operations and variations in reserve ratios. It acts as a banker to the government. It is the custodian of the foreign exchange reserves of the economy. It also acts as a bank to the banking system, which is discussed in detail later.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is high-powered money?
cards.back: This currency issued by the central bank can be held by the public or by the commercial banks, and is called the ‘high-powered money’ or ‘reserve money’ or ‘monetary base’ as it acts as a basis for credit creation.
cards.quote: This currency issued by the central bank can be held by the public or by the commercial banks, and is called the ‘high-powered money’ or ‘reserve money’ or ‘monetary base’ as it acts as a basis for credit creation.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What do commercial banks do with the deposits they accept?
cards.back: They accept deposits from the public and lend out part of these funds to those who want to borrow.
cards.quote: They accept deposits from the public and lend out part of these funds to those who want to borrow.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is the ‘spread’ of a commercial bank?
cards.back: The interest rate paid by the banks to depositors is lower than the rate charged from the borrowers. This difference between these two types of interest rates, called the ‘spread’ is the profit appropriated by the bank.
cards.quote: The interest rate paid by the banks to depositors is lower than the rate charged from the borrowers. This difference between these two types of interest rates, called the ‘spread’ is the profit appropriated by the bank.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Between whom do commercial banks mediate?
cards.back: Commercial banks mediate between individuals or firms with excess funds and lend to those who need funds.
cards.quote: Commercial banks mediate between individuals or firms with excess funds and lend to those who need funds.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Why must a bank not lend out all its funds?
cards.back: Since banks earn interest from loans they make, any bank would like to lend the maximum possible. However, being able to repay depositors on demand is crucial to the bank’s survival.
cards.quote: Since banks earn interest from loans they make, any bank would like to lend the maximum possible. However, being able to repay depositors on demand is crucial to the bank’s survival.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Why can banks lend?
cards.back: Banks can lend simply because they do not expect all the depositors to withdraw what they have deposited at the same time.
cards.quote: Banks can lend simply because they do not expect all the depositors to withdraw what they have deposited at the same time.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: When the banks lend to any person, a ____ is opened in that person’s name.
cards.back: When the banks lend to any person, a new deposit is opened in that person’s name.
cards.quote: When the banks lend to any person, a new deposit is opened in that person’s name.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is a balance sheet?
cards.back: Balance sheet is a record of assets and liabilities of any firm.
cards.quote: Balance sheet is a record of assets and liabilities of any firm.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: On which sides of a balance sheet are assets and liabilities conventionally recorded?
cards.back: Conventionally, the assets of the firm are recorded on the left hand side and liabilities on the right hand side.
cards.quote: Conventionally, the assets of the firm are recorded on the left hand side and liabilities on the right hand side.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Accounting rules say that both sides of the balance sheet must be equal or total assets must be equal to the ____.
cards.back: Accounting rules say that both sides of the balance sheet must be equal or total assets must be equal to the total liabilities.
cards.quote: Accounting rules say that both sides of the balance sheet must be equal or total assets must be equal to the total liabilities.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What are assets?
cards.back: Assets are things a firm owns or what a firm can claim from others.
cards.quote: Assets are things a firm owns or what a firm can claim from others.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What are reserves of a commercial bank?
cards.back: Reserves are deposits which commercial banks keep with the Central bank, Reserve Bank of India (RBI) and its cash.
cards.quote: Reserves are deposits which commercial banks keep with the Central bank, Reserve Bank of India (RBI) and its cash.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: In what forms are a bank’s reserves kept?
cards.back: These reserves are kept partly as cash and partly in the form of financial instruments (bonds and treasury bills) issued by the RBI.
cards.quote: These reserves are kept partly as cash and partly in the form of financial instruments (bonds and treasury bills) issued by the RBI.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Formula: assets of a bank
cards.back: Assets = Reserves + Loans
cards.quote: Similarly, commercial banks like State Bank of India (SBI) keep their deposits with RBI and these are called Reserves. Assets = Reserves + Loans

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What are liabilities of a firm, and the main liability of a bank?
cards.back: Liabilities for any firm are its debts or what it owes to others. For a bank, the main liability is the deposits which people keep with it.
cards.quote: Liabilities for any firm are its debts or what it owes to others. For a bank, the main liability is the deposits which people keep with it.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Formula: net worth
cards.back: Net Worth = Assets – Liabilities
cards.quote: Hence if assets are greater than liabilities, they are recorded on the right hand side as Net Worth. Net Worth = Assets – Liabilities

source.section: 3.3.1 Balance Sheet of a Fictional Bank

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: By what names is the legal minimum reserve ratio known?
cards.back: This is called the ‘Required Reserve Ratio’ or the ‘Reserve Ratio’ or ‘Cash Reserve Ratio’ (CRR).
cards.quote: This is called the ‘Required Reserve Ratio’ or the ‘Reserve Ratio’ or ‘Cash Reserve Ratio’ (CRR).

source.section: 3.3.2 Limits to Credit Creation and Money Multiplier

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is the Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR)?
cards.back: Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) = Percentage of deposits which a bank must keep as cash reserves with the bank.
cards.quote: Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) = Percentage of deposits which a bank must keep as cash reserves with the bank.

source.section: 3.3.2 Limits to Credit Creation and Money Multiplier

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is the Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR)?
cards.back: Apart from the CRR, banks are also required to keep some reserves in liquid form in the short term. This ratio is called Statutory Liquidity Ratio or SLR.
cards.quote: Apart from the CRR, banks are also required to keep some reserves in liquid form in the short term. This ratio is called Statutory Liquidity Ratio or SLR.

source.section: 3.3.2 Limits to Credit Creation and Money Multiplier

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What does the statutory requirement of the reserve ratio do to the amount of credit banks can create?
cards.back: The statutory requirement of the reserve ratio acts as a limit to the amount of credit that banks can create.
cards.quote: The statutory requirement of the reserve ratio acts as a limit to the amount of credit that banks can create.

source.section: 3.3.2 Limits to Credit Creation and Money Multiplier

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: With a 20 per cent reserve ratio, deposits of what amount can reserves of Rs 100 support?
cards.back: The required reserves will be Rs 100 only when the total deposits become Rs 500. This is because for deposits of Rs 500, cash reserves would have to be Rs 100 (20 per cent of 500 = 100).
cards.quote: The required reserves will be Rs 100 only when the total deposits become Rs 500. This is because for deposits of Rs 500, cash reserves would have to be Rs 100 (20 per cent of 500 = 100).

source.section: 3.3.2 Limits to Credit Creation and Money Multiplier

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is the RBI’s role as the ‘lender of last resort’?
cards.back: This role of RBI, that of being ready to lend to banks at all times is another important function of the central bank, and due to this central bank is said to be the lender of last resort.
cards.quote: This role of RBI, that of being ready to lend to banks at all times is another important function of the central bank, and due to this central bank is said to be the lender of last resort.

source.section: 3.4 Policy Tools to Control Money Supply

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Types of tools the central bank uses to control money supply.
cards.back:
Quantitative tools, control the extent of money supply by changing the CRR, or bank rate or open market operations.
Qualitative tools include persuasion by the Central bank in order to make commercial banks discourage or encourage lending which is done through moral suasion, margin requirement, etc.
cards.quote: The tools used by the Central bank to control money supply can be quantitative or qualitative. Quantitative tools, control the extent of money supply by changing the CRR, or bank rate or open market operations. Qualitative tools include persuasion by the Central bank in order to make commercial banks discourage or encourage lending which is done through moral suasion, margin requirement, etc.

source.section: 3.4 Policy Tools to Control Money Supply

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Which two qualitative tools of money control does NCERT name (persuasion of banks on lending)?
cards.back:
moral suasion
margin requirement
cards.quote: Qualitative tools include persuasion by the Central bank in order to make commercial banks discourage or encourage lending which is done through moral suasion, margin requirement, etc.

source.section: 3.4 Policy Tools to Control Money Supply

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What happens to bank lending, deposits and money supply when the central bank changes the reserve ratio?
cards.back: It should be evident by now that if the Central bank changes the reserve ratio, this would lead to changes in lending by the banks which, in turn, would impact the deposits and hence, the money supply.
cards.quote: It should be evident by now that if the Central bank changes the reserve ratio, this would lead to changes in lending by the banks which, in turn, would impact the deposits and hence, the money supply.

source.section: 3.4 Policy Tools to Control Money Supply

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What are Open Market Operations?
cards.back: Open Market Operations refers to buying and selling of bonds issued by the Government in the open market. This purchase and sale is entrusted to the Central bank on behalf of the Government.
cards.quote: Open Market Operations refers to buying and selling of bonds issued by the Government in the open market. This purchase and sale is entrusted to the Central bank on behalf of the Government.

source.section: 3.4 Policy Tools to Control Money Supply

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: RBI buying vs selling a government bond: effect on money supply.
cards.back:
When RBI buys a Government bond in the open market, it pays for it by giving a cheque. This cheque increases the total amount of reserves in the economy and thus increases the money supply.
Selling of a bond by RBI (to private individuals or institutions) leads to reduction in quantity of reserves and hence the money supply.
cards.quote: When RBI buys a Government bond in the open market, it pays for it by giving a cheque. This cheque increases the total amount of reserves in the economy and thus increases the money supply. Selling of a bond by RBI (to private individuals or institutions) leads to reduction in quantity of reserves and hence the money supply.

source.section: 3.4 Policy Tools to Control Money Supply

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Types of open market operations.
cards.back:
outright
repo
cards.quote: There are two types of open market operations: outright and repo.

source.section: 3.4 Policy Tools to Control Money Supply

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What are outright open market operations?
cards.back: Outright open market operations are permanent in nature: when the central bank buys these securities (thus injecting money into the system), it is without any promise to sell them later.
cards.quote: Outright open market operations are permanent in nature: when the central bank buys these securities (thus injecting money into the system), it is without any promise to sell them later.

source.section: 3.4 Policy Tools to Control Money Supply

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is a repurchase agreement (repo)?
cards.back: When the central bank buys the security, this agreement of purchase also has specification about date and price of resale of this security. This type of agreement is called a repurchase agreement or repo.
cards.quote: when the central bank buys the security, this agreement of purchase also has specification about date and price of resale of this security. This type of agreement is called a repurchase agreement or repo.

source.section: 3.4 Policy Tools to Control Money Supply

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is the repo rate?
cards.back: This type of agreement is called a repurchase agreement or repo. The interest rate at which the money is lent in this way is called the repo rate.
cards.quote: This type of agreement is called a repurchase agreement or repo. The interest rate at which the money is lent in this way is called the repo rate.

source.section: 3.4 Policy Tools to Control Money Supply

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is a reverse repurchase agreement (reverse repo)?
cards.back: Instead of outright sale of securities the central bank may sell the securities through an agreement which has a specification about the date and price at which it will be repurchased. This type of agreement is called a reverse repurchase agreement or reverse repo.
cards.quote: instead of outright sale of securities the central bank may sell the securities through an agreement which has a specification about the date and price at which it will be repurchased. This type of agreement is called a reverse repurchase agreement or reverse repo.

source.section: 3.4 Policy Tools to Control Money Supply

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is the reverse repo rate?
cards.back: This type of agreement is called a reverse repurchase agreement or reverse repo. The rate at which the money is withdrawn in this manner is called the reverse repo rate.
cards.quote: This type of agreement is called a reverse repurchase agreement or reverse repo. The rate at which the money is withdrawn in this manner is called the reverse repo rate.

source.section: 3.4 Policy Tools to Control Money Supply

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Which RBI operations are now the main tool of its monetary policy?
cards.back: The Reserve Bank of India conducts repo and reverse repo operations at various maturities: overnight, 7-day, 14-day, etc. This type of operations have now become the main tool of monetary policy of the Reserve Bank of India.
cards.quote: The Reserve Bank of India conducts repo and reverse repo operations at various maturities: overnight, 7-day, 14-day, etc. This type of operations have now become the main tool of monetary policy of the Reserve Bank of India.

source.section: 3.4 Policy Tools to Control Money Supply

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is the Bank Rate in India?
cards.back: The RBI can influence money supply by changing the rate at which it gives loans to the commercial banks. This rate is called the Bank Rate in India.
cards.quote: The RBI can influence money supply by changing the rate at which it gives loans to the commercial banks. This rate is called the Bank Rate in India.

source.section: 3.4 Policy Tools to Control Money Supply

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: How does a rise in the bank rate affect money supply?
cards.back: By increasing the bank rate, loans taken by commercial banks become more expensive; this reduces the reserves held by the commercial bank and hence decreases money supply. A fall in the bank rate can increase the money supply.
cards.quote: By increasing the bank rate, loans taken by commercial banks become more expensive; this reduces the reserves held by the commercial bank and hence decreases money supply. A fall in the bank rate can increase the money supply.

source.section: 3.4 Policy Tools to Control Money Supply

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Who issues currency notes and who issues coins in India?
cards.back: In India currency notes are issued by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), which is the monetary authority in India. However, coins are issued by the Government of India.
cards.quote: In India currency notes are issued by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), which is the monetary authority in India. However, coins are issued by the Government of India.

source.section: The Supply of Money: Various Measures

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What are demand deposits and time deposits?
cards.back: Such deposits are called demand deposits as they are payable by the bank on demand from the account-holder. Other deposits, e.g. fixed deposits, have a fixed period to maturity and are referred to as time deposits.
cards.quote: Such deposits are called demand deposits as they are payable by the bank on demand from the account-holder. Other deposits, e.g. fixed deposits, have a fixed period to maturity and are referred to as time deposits.

source.section: The Supply of Money: Various Measures

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: From what do currency notes and coins derive their value?
cards.back: The value of the currency notes and coins is derived from the guarantee provided by the issuing authority of these items.
cards.quote: The value of the currency notes and coins is derived from the guarantee provided by the issuing authority of these items.

source.section: The Supply of Money: Various Measures

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is fiat money?
cards.back: Currency notes and coins are therefore called fiat money. They do not have intrinsic value like a gold or silver coin.
cards.quote: Currency notes and coins are therefore called fiat money. They do not have intrinsic value like a gold or silver coin.

source.section: The Supply of Money: Various Measures

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is a legal tender?
cards.back: They are also called legal tenders as they cannot be refused by any citizen of the country for settlement of any kind of transaction. Cheques drawn on savings or current accounts, however, can be refused by anyone as a mode of payment. Hence, demand deposits are not legal tenders.
cards.quote: They are also called legal tenders as they cannot be refused by any citizen of the country for settlement of any kind of transaction. Cheques drawn on savings or current accounts, however, can be refused by anyone as a mode of payment. Hence, demand deposits are not legal tenders.

source.section: The Supply of Money: Various Measures

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is money supply?
cards.back: Money supply, like money demand, is a stock variable. The total stock of money in circulation among the public at a particular point of time is called money supply.
cards.quote: Money supply, like money demand, is a stock variable. The total stock of money in circulation among the public at a particular point of time is called money supply.

source.section: The Supply of Money: Various Measures

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Which four alternative measures of money supply does RBI publish?
cards.back: RBI publishes figures for four alternative measures of money supply, viz. M1, M2, M3 and M4.
cards.quote: RBI publishes figures for four alternative measures of money supply, viz. M1, M2, M3 and M4.

source.section: The Supply of Money: Various Measures

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Formula: M1
cards.back: M1 = CU + DD
cards.quote: M1 = CU + DD

source.section: The Supply of Money: Various Measures

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Formula: M2
cards.back: M2 = M1 + Savings deposits with Post Office savings banks
cards.quote: M2 = M1 + Savings deposits with Post Office savings banks

source.section: The Supply of Money: Various Measures

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Formula: M3
cards.back: M3 = M1 + Net time deposits of commercial banks
cards.quote: M3 = M1 + Net time deposits of commercial banks

source.section: The Supply of Money: Various Measures

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Formula: M4
cards.back: M4 = M3 + Total deposits with Post Office savings organisations (excluding National Savings Certificates)
cards.quote: M4 = M3 + Total deposits with Post Office savings organisations (excluding National Savings Certificates)

source.section: The Supply of Money: Various Measures

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: In M1 = CU + DD, what are CU and DD?
cards.back: where, CU is currency (notes plus coins) held by the public and DD is net demand deposits held by commercial banks.
cards.quote: where, CU is currency (notes plus coins) held by the public and DD is net demand deposits held by commercial banks.

source.section: The Supply of Money: Various Measures

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What does the word ‘net’ mean in net demand deposits?
cards.back: The word ‘net’ implies that only deposits of the public held by the banks are to be included in money supply. The interbank deposits, which a commercial bank holds in other commercial banks, are not to be regarded as part of money supply.
cards.quote: The word ‘net’ implies that only deposits of the public held by the banks are to be included in money supply. The interbank deposits, which a commercial bank holds in other commercial banks, are not to be regarded as part of money supply.

source.section: The Supply of Money: Various Measures

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Which measures of money supply are narrow money and which are broad money?
cards.back:
M1 and M2 are known as narrow money.
M3 and M4 are known as broad money.
cards.quote: M1 and M2 are known as narrow money. M3 and M4 are known as broad money.

source.section: The Supply of Money: Various Measures

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Rank M1 to M4 by liquidity. Which is most and which is least liquid?
cards.back: These measures are in decreasing order of liquidity. M1 is most liquid and easiest for transactions whereas M4 is least liquid of all.
cards.quote: These measures are in decreasing order of liquidity. M1 is most liquid and easiest for transactions whereas M4 is least liquid of all.

source.section: The Supply of Money: Various Measures

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Which is the most commonly used measure of money supply?
cards.back: M3 is the most commonly used measure of money supply.
cards.quote: M3 is the most commonly used measure of money supply.

source.section: The Supply of Money: Various Measures

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Exchange of commodities without the mediation of money is called Barter Exchange. It suffers from lack of ____.
cards.back: Exchange of commodities without the mediation of money is called Barter Exchange. It suffers from lack of double coincidence of wants.
cards.quote: Exchange of commodities without the mediation of money is called Barter Exchange. It suffers from lack of double coincidence of wants.
