cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What does the supply of money consist of?
cards.back: Supply of money, on the other hand, consists of currency notes and coins, demand and time deposits held by commercial banks, etc.
cards.quote: Supply of money, on the other hand, consists of currency notes and coins, demand and time deposits held by commercial banks, etc.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: In India, which institution regulates the supply of money and acts as the monetary authority?
cards.back: In India, the supply of money is regulated by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) which acts as the monetary authority of the country.
cards.quote: In India, the supply of money is regulated by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) which acts as the monetary authority of the country.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: RBI regulates money supply by controlling the stock of ____, the ____ and ____ of the commercial banks.
cards.back: RBI regulates money supply by controlling the stock of high powered money, the bank rate and reserve requirements of the commercial banks.
cards.quote: RBI regulates money supply by controlling the stock of high powered money, the bank rate and reserve requirements of the commercial banks.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is a final good?
cards.back: Such an item that is meant for final use and will not pass through any more stages of production or transformations is called a final good.
cards.quote: Such an item that is meant for final use and will not pass through any more stages of production or transformations is called a final good.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What are consumption goods (consumer goods)?
cards.back: Goods like food and clothing, and services like recreation that are consumed when purchased by their ultimate consumers are called consumption goods or consumer goods.
cards.quote: Goods like food and clothing, and services like recreation that are consumed when purchased by their ultimate consumers are called consumption goods or consumer goods.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What are capital goods?
cards.back: Then there are other goods that are of durable character which are used in the production process. These are tools, implements and machines.
cards.quote: Then there are other goods that are of durable character which are used in the production process. These are tools, implements and machines.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What are consumer durables (final goods like television sets, automobiles, home computers)?
cards.back: They are not extinguished by immediate or even short period consumption; they have a relatively long life as compared to articles such as food or even clothing. They also undergo wear and tear with gradual use and often need repairs and replacements of parts, i.e., like machines they also need to be preserved, maintained and renewed. That is why we call these goods consumer durables.
cards.quote: They are not extinguished by immediate or even short period consumption; they have a relatively long life as compared to articles such as food or even clothing. They also undergo wear and tear with gradual use and often need repairs and replacements of parts, i.e., like machines they also need to be preserved, maintained and renewed. That is why we call these goods consumer durables.
cards.note: Durable final goods bought for consumption, such as television sets, automobiles and home computers.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What are intermediate goods?
cards.back: These are intermediate goods, mostly used as raw material or inputs for production of other commodities. These are not final goods.
cards.quote: These are intermediate goods, mostly used as raw material or inputs for production of other commodities. These are not final goods.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Why are only final goods counted, not intermediate goods?
cards.back: the value of the final goods already includes the value of the intermediate goods that have entered into their production as inputs. Counting them separately will lead to the error of double counting.
cards.quote: the value of the final goods already includes the value of the intermediate goods that have entered into their production as inputs. Counting them separately will lead to the error of double counting.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What are flows?
cards.back: Thus income, or output, or profits are concepts that make sense only when a time period is specified. These are called flows because they occur in a period of time.
cards.quote: Thus income, or output, or profits are concepts that make sense only when a time period is specified. These are called flows because they occur in a period of time.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What are stocks (for example, the buildings or machines in a factory)?
cards.back: The buildings or machines in a factory are there irrespective of the specific time period. There can be addition to, or deduction from, these if a new machine is added or a machine falls in disuse and is not replaced. These are called stocks. Stocks are defined at a particular point of time.
cards.quote: The buildings or machines in a factory are there irrespective of the specific time period. There can be addition to, or deduction from, these if a new machine is added or a machine falls in disuse and is not replaced. These are called stocks. Stocks are defined at a particular point of time.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Stock vs flow: the tank filled by a tap
cards.back: The amount of water which is flowing into the tank from the tap per minute is a flow. But how much water there is in the tank at a particular point of time is a stock concept.
cards.quote: The amount of water which is flowing into the tank from the tap per minute is a flow. But how much water there is in the tank at a particular point of time is a stock concept.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is gross investment?
cards.back: that part of our final output that comprises of capital goods constitutes gross investment of an economy
cards.quote: that part of our final output that comprises of capital goods constitutes gross investment of an economy

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Formula: net investment
cards.back: Net Investment = Gross investment – Depreciation
cards.quote: Net Investment = Gross investment – Depreciation
cards.note: Net investment is the new addition to the capital stock (new capital formation).

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Formula: annual depreciation of a capital good
cards.back: it is the cost of the good divided by number of years of its useful life
cards.quote: it is the cost of the good divided by number of years of its useful life
cards.note: Depreciation = cost of the capital good ÷ years of its useful life.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: In a year, what is the trade-off between producing consumer goods and capital goods?
cards.back: In a specific time period, say in a year, the total production of final goods can thus be either in the form of consumption or investment. This implies that there is a trade-off. If an economy, produces more of consumer goods, it is producing less of capital goods and vice-versa.
cards.quote: In a specific time period, say in a year, the total production of final goods can thus be either in the form of consumption or investment. This implies that there is a trade-off. If an economy, produces more of consumer goods, it is producing less of capital goods and vice-versa.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Simply put, how does the circular flow work through the market?
cards.back: Simply put, the firms’ demand for factors of production to run the production process creates payments to the public. In turn, the public’s demand for goods and services creates payments to the firms and enables the sale of the products they produce.
cards.quote: Simply put, the firms’ demand for factors of production to run the production process creates payments to the public. In turn, the public’s demand for goods and services creates payments to the firms and enables the sale of the products they produce.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Name the four contributions in production and the remuneration for each.
cards.back:
contribution made by human labour, remuneration for which is called wage
contribution made by capital, remuneration for which is called interest
contribution made by entrepreneurship, remuneration of which is profit
contribution made by fixed natural resources (called ‘land’), remuneration for which is called rent.
cards.quote: (a) contribution made by human labour, remuneration for which is called wage (b) contribution made by capital, remuneration for which is called interest (c) contribution made by entrepreneurship, remuneration of which is profit (d) contribution made by fixed natural resources (called ‘land’), remuneration for which is called rent.

source.section: Circular Flow of Income and Methods of Calculating National Income

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: In the simple circular-flow economy, what do households not do?
cards.back: we have assumed that the households do not save, they do not pay taxes to the government – since there is no government, and neither do they buy imported goods since there is no external trade in this simple economy.
cards.quote: we have assumed that the households do not save, they do not pay taxes to the government – since there is no government, and neither do they buy imported goods since there is no external trade in this simple economy.

source.section: Circular Flow of Income and Methods of Calculating National Income

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Define the income method of calculating national income.
cards.back: Measuring the sum total of all factor payments will be called income method.
cards.quote: measuring the sum total of all factor payments will be called income method.

source.section: Circular Flow of Income and Methods of Calculating National Income

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Observe that the aggregate spending of the economy must be equal to the aggregate ____ earned by the factors of production
cards.back: Observe that the aggregate spending of the economy must be equal to the aggregate income earned by the factors of production
cards.quote: Observe that the aggregate spending of the economy must be equal to the aggregate income earned by the factors of production

source.section: Circular Flow of Income and Methods of Calculating National Income

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: For any economy, how do the annual production estimates from the three methods compare?
cards.back: No matter how complicated an economic system may be, the annual production of goods and services estimated through each of the three methods is the same.
cards.quote: No matter how complicated an economic system may be, the annual production of goods and services estimated through each of the three methods is the same.

source.section: Circular Flow of Income and Methods of Calculating National Income

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Wheat worth Rs 50 is bought by bakers for bread worth Rs 200. What mistake occurs if bread is added in full?
cards.back: If we do not do this we shall commit the mistake of ‘double counting’. This is because Rs 50 worth of wheat will be counted twice.
cards.quote: If we do not do this we shall commit the mistake of ‘double counting’. This is because Rs 50 worth of wheat will be counted twice.

source.section: The Product or Value Added Method

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is value added?
cards.back: The term that is used to denote the net contribution made by a firm is called its value added.
cards.quote: The term that is used to denote the net contribution made by a firm is called its value added.

source.section: The Product or Value Added Method

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Wages, interest, profits and rents paid out by the firm must add up to the ____ of the firm.
cards.back: Wages, interest, profits and rents paid out by the firm must add up to the value added of the firm.
cards.quote: Wages, interest, profits and rents paid out by the firm must add up to the value added of the firm.

source.section: The Product or Value Added Method

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Depreciation is also known by what other name?
cards.back: We have already introduced the concept of depreciation, which is also known as consumption of fixed capital.
cards.quote: We have already introduced the concept of depreciation, which is also known as consumption of fixed capital.

source.section: The Product or Value Added Method

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Gross value added vs net value added: how is each obtained?
cards.back: If we include depreciation in value added then the measure of value added that we obtain is called Gross Value Added. If we deduct the value of depreciation from gross value added we obtain Net Value Added.
cards.quote: If we include depreciation in value added then the measure of value added that we obtain is called Gross Value Added. If we deduct the value of depreciation from gross value added we obtain Net Value Added.

source.section: The Product or Value Added Method

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Firm: output Rs 100, intermediate goods Rs 20, capital consumption Rs 10. Find GVA and NVA.
cards.back: The gross value added of the firm will be, Rs 100 – Rs 20 = Rs 80 per year. The net value added will be, Rs 100 – Rs 20 – Rs 10 = Rs 70 per year.
cards.quote: The gross value added of the firm will be, Rs 100 – Rs 20 = Rs 80 per year. The net value added will be, Rs 100 – Rs 20 – Rs 10 = Rs 70 per year.

source.section: The Product or Value Added Method

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is inventory (in economics)?
cards.back: In economics, the stock of unsold finished goods, or semi-finished goods, or raw materials which a firm carries from one year to the next is called inventory. Inventory is a stock variable.
cards.quote: In economics, the stock of unsold finished goods, or semi-finished goods, or raw materials which a firm carries from one year to the next is called inventory. Inventory is a stock variable.

source.section: The Product or Value Added Method

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Formula: change of inventories of a firm during a year
cards.back: the change of inventories of a firm during a year ≡ production of the firm during the year – sale of the firm during the year
cards.quote: the change of inventories of a firm during a year ≡ production of the firm during the year – sale of the firm during the year

source.section: The Product or Value Added Method

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is investment?
cards.back: Addition to the stock of capital of a firm is known as investment.
cards.quote: Addition to the stock of capital of a firm is known as investment.

source.section: The Product or Value Added Method

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Name the three major categories of investment.
cards.back:
First is the rise in the value of inventories of a firm over a year which is treated as investment expenditure undertaken by the firm.
The second category of investment is the fixed business investment, which is defined as the addition to the machinery, factory buildings and equipment employed by the firms.
The last category of investment is the residential investment, which refers to the addition of housing facilities.
cards.quote: There can be three major categories of investment. First is the rise in the value of inventories of a firm over a year which is treated as investment expenditure undertaken by the firm. The second category of investment is the fixed business investment, which is defined as the addition to the machinery, factory buildings and equipment employed by the firms. The last category of investment is the residential investment, which refers to the addition of housing facilities.

source.section: The Product or Value Added Method

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What causes unplanned accumulation of inventories?
cards.back: In case of an unexpected fall in sales, the firm will have unsold stock of goods which it had not anticipated. Hence there will be unplanned accumulation of inventories.
cards.quote: In case of an unexpected fall in sales, the firm will have unsold stock of goods which it had not anticipated. Hence there will be unplanned accumulation of inventories.

source.section: The Product or Value Added Method

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Formula: gross value added of firm i (GVAi)
cards.back: Gross value added of firm, i (GVAi) ≡ Gross value of the output produced by the firm i (Qi) – Value of intermediate goods used by the firm (Zi)
cards.quote: Gross value added of firm, i (GVAi) ≡ Gross value of the output produced by the firm i (Qi) – Value of intermediate goods used by the firm (Zi)

source.section: The Product or Value Added Method

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Formula: net value added of firm i
cards.back: Net value added of the firm i ≡ GVAi – Depreciation of the firm i (Di)
cards.quote: Net value added of the firm i ≡ GVAi – Depreciation of the firm i (Di)

source.section: The Product or Value Added Method

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Define GDP by the product method (sum of gross value added).
cards.back: If we sum the gross value added of all the firms of the economy in a year, we get a measure of the value of aggregate amount of goods and services produced by the economy in a year (just as we had done in the wheat-bread example). Such an estimate is called Gross Domestic Product (GDP). Thus GDP ≡ Sum total of gross value added of all the firms in the economy.
cards.quote: If we sum the gross value added of all the firms of the economy in a year, we get a measure of the value of aggregate amount of goods and services produced by the economy in a year (just as we had done in the wheat-bread example). Such an estimate is called Gross Domestic Product (GDP). Thus GDP ≡ Sum total of gross value added of all the firms in the economy.

source.section: The Product or Value Added Method

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is the expenditure method of calculating GDP?
cards.back: An alternative way to calculate the GDP is by looking at the demand side of the products. This method is referred to as the expenditure method.
cards.quote: An alternative way to calculate the GDP is by looking at the demand side of the products. This method is referred to as the expenditure method.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is final expenditure?
cards.back: Final expenditure is that part of expenditure which is undertaken not for intermediate purposes.
cards.quote: Final expenditure is that part of expenditure which is undertaken not for intermediate purposes.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Why is expenditure on investment goods included in GDP but expenditure on intermediate goods is not?
cards.back: The reason is that investment goods remain with the firm, whereas intermediate goods are consumed in the process of production
cards.quote: The reason is that investment goods remain with the firm, whereas intermediate goods are consumed in the process of production

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Name the final expenditures received by a firm (C, I, G, X).
cards.back: Sum total of final consumption, investment, government and exports expenditures received by the firm i
cards.quote: RVi ≡ Sum total of final consumption, investment, government and exports expenditures received by the firm i ≡ Ci + Ii + Gi + Xi

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: In GDP ≡ C + I + G + X – M, what do X and M denote?
cards.back: X denotes aggregate expenditure by the foreigners on the exports of the economy. M ≡ Cm + Im + Gm is the aggregate imports expenditure incurred by the economy.
cards.quote: X denotes aggregate expenditure by the foreigners on the exports of the economy. M ≡ Cm + Im + Gm is the aggregate imports expenditure incurred by the economy.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is macroeconomics?
cards.back: In macroeconomics, on the other hand, we try to get an understanding of the economy as a whole by focusing our attention on aggregate measures such as total output, employment and aggregate price level.
cards.quote: In macroeconomics, on the other hand, we try to get an understanding of the economy as a whole by focusing our attention on aggregate measures such as total output, employment and aggregate price level.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: In GDP ≡ C + I + G + X – M, which of the five variables on the right hand side is the most unstable?
cards.back: It may be noted that out of the five variables on the right hand side, investment expenditure, I, is the most unstable.
cards.quote: It may be noted that out of the five variables on the right hand side, investment expenditure, I, is the most unstable.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: As we mentioned in the beginning, the sum of final expenditures in the economy must be equal to the incomes received by all the ____ taken together
cards.back: As we mentioned in the beginning, the sum of final expenditures in the economy must be equal to the incomes received by all the factors of production taken together
cards.quote: As we mentioned in the beginning, the sum of final expenditures in the economy must be equal to the incomes received by all the factors of production taken together

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Formula: the identity linking the expenditure and income methods of GDP
cards.back: C + I + G + X – M ≡ W + P + In + R
cards.quote: C + I + G + X – M ≡ W + P + In + R
cards.note: GDP ≡ ΣGVAi ≡ C + I + G + X – M ≡ W + P + In + R (identity 2.6).

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Formula: value added (VA)
cards.back: value added (VA) = Sales – Intermediate Goods
cards.quote: value added (VA) = Sales – Intermediate Goods

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Define gross value added (GVA).
cards.back: it is the value of total output produced in the economy less the value of intermediate consumption (the output which is used in production of output further, and not used in final consumption).
cards.quote: it is the value of total output produced in the economy less the value of intermediate consumption (the output which is used in production of output further, and not used in final consumption).

source.section: Factor Cost, Basic Prices and Market Prices

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Production taxes vs product taxes: when are they paid, and examples
cards.back: Production taxes and subsidies are paid or received in relation to production and are independent of the volume of production such as land revenues, stamp and registration fee. Product taxes and subsidies, on the other hand, are paid or received per unit or product, e.g., excise tax, service tax, export and import duties etc.
cards.quote: Production taxes and subsidies are paid or received in relation to production and are independent of the volume of production such as land revenues, stamp and registration fee. Product taxes and subsidies, on the other hand, are paid or received per unit or product, e.g., excise tax, service tax, export and import duties etc.

source.section: Factor Cost, Basic Prices and Market Prices

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: In order to arrive at the market prices, we have to add to the factor cost the total ____ less total ____.
cards.back: In order to arrive at the market prices, we have to add to the factor cost the total indirect taxes less total subsidies.
cards.quote: In order to arrive at the market prices, we have to add to the factor cost the total indirect taxes less total subsidies.

source.section: Factor Cost, Basic Prices and Market Prices

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What do basic prices include and not include?
cards.back: The basic prices lie in between: they include the production taxes (less production subsidies) but not product taxes (less product subsidies).
cards.quote: The basic prices lie in between: they include the production taxes (less production subsidies) but not product taxes (less product subsidies).

source.section: Factor Cost, Basic Prices and Market Prices

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: In order to arrive at market prices we have to add ____ (less product subsidies) to the basic prices.
cards.back: In order to arrive at market prices we have to add product taxes (less product subsidies) to the basic prices.
cards.quote: In order to arrive at market prices we have to add product taxes (less product subsidies) to the basic prices.

source.section: Factor Cost, Basic Prices and Market Prices

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Formula: GVA at basic prices (from GVA at factor cost)
cards.back: GVA at factor costs + Net production taxes = GVA at basic prices
cards.quote: GVA at factor costs + Net production taxes = GVA at basic prices

source.section: Factor Cost, Basic Prices and Market Prices

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Formula: GVA at market prices (from GVA at basic prices)
cards.back: GVA at basic prices + Net product taxes = GVA at market prices
cards.quote: GVA at basic prices + Net product taxes = GVA at market prices

source.section: Factor Cost, Basic Prices and Market Prices

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What does Gross Domestic Product measure?
cards.back: Gross Domestic Product measures the aggregate production of final goods and services taking place within the domestic economy during a year.
cards.quote: Gross Domestic Product measures the aggregate production of final goods and services taking place within the domestic economy during a year.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Formula: GNP in terms of GDP
cards.back: GNP ≡ GDP + Net factor income from abroad
cards.quote: GNP ≡ GDP + Net factor income from abroad

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Define net factor income from abroad (NFIA).
cards.back: (Net factor income from abroad = Factor income earned by the domestic factors of production employed in the rest of the world – Factor income earned by the factors of production of the rest of the world employed in the domestic economy).
cards.quote: (Net factor income from abroad = Factor income earned by the domestic factors of production employed in the rest of the world – Factor income earned by the factors of production of the rest of the world employed in the domestic economy).

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Define depreciation.
cards.back: A part of the capital goods produced this year goes for replacement of existing capital goods and is not an addition to the stock of capital goods already existing and its value needs to be subtracted from gross investment for arriving at the measure for net investment. This deletion, which is made from the value of gross investment in order to accommodate regular wear and tear of capital, is called depreciation.
cards.quote: A part of the capital goods produced this year goes for replacement of existing capital goods and is not an addition to the stock of capital goods already existing and its value needs to be subtracted from gross investment for arriving at the measure for net investment. This deletion, which is made from the value of gross investment in order to accommodate regular wear and tear of capital, is called depreciation.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Define Net National Product (NNP).
cards.back: If we deduct depreciation from GNP the measure of aggregate income that we obtain is called Net National Product (NNP).
cards.quote: If we deduct depreciation from GNP the measure of aggregate income that we obtain is called Net National Product (NNP).

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Formula: NNP
cards.back: NNP ≡ GNP – Depreciation
cards.quote: NNP ≡ GNP – Depreciation

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: NNP at factor cost is also called what?
cards.back: The measure that we obtain by doing so is called Net National Product at factor cost or National Income.
cards.quote: The measure that we obtain by doing so is called Net National Product at factor cost or National Income.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Formula: NNP at factor cost (National Income)
cards.back: NNP at factor cost ≡ National Income (NI ) ≡ NNP at market prices – (Indirect taxes – Subsidies) ≡ NNP at market prices – Net indirect taxes
cards.quote: NNP at factor cost ≡ National Income (NI ) ≡ NNP at market prices – (Indirect taxes – Subsidies) ≡ NNP at market prices – Net indirect taxes

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What are Undistributed Profits (UP)?
cards.back: a part of profit is not distributed among the factors of production. This is called Undistributed Profits (UP).
cards.quote: a part of profit is not distributed among the factors of production. This is called Undistributed Profits (UP).

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Formula: Personal Income (PI)
cards.back: Personal Income (PI) ≡ NI – Undistributed profits – Net interest payments made by households – Corporate tax + Transfer payments to the households from the government and firms.
cards.quote: Personal Income (PI) ≡ NI – Undistributed profits – Net interest payments made by households – Corporate tax + Transfer payments to the households from the government and firms.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Define Personal Disposable Income (PDI).
cards.back: If we deduct the Personal Tax Payments (income tax, for example) and Non-tax Payments (such as fines) from PI, we obtain what is known as the Personal Disposable Income.
cards.quote: If we deduct the Personal Tax Payments (income tax, for example) and Non-tax Payments (such as fines) from PI, we obtain what is known as the Personal Disposable Income.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Formula: Personal Disposable Income (PDI)
cards.back: Personal Disposable Income (PDI ) ≡ PI – Personal tax payments – Non-tax payments
cards.quote: Personal Disposable Income (PDI ) ≡ PI – Personal tax payments – Non-tax payments

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Formula: National Disposable Income
cards.back: National Disposable Income = Net National Product at market prices + Other current transfers from the rest of the world
cards.quote: National Disposable Income = Net National Product at market prices + Other current transfers from the rest of the world

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Does GDP include production by non-residents or foreign-owned firms in the country?
cards.back: All production done by the national residents or the non-residents in a country gets included, regardless of whether that production is owned by a local company or a foreign entity.
cards.quote: All production done by the national residents or the non-residents in a country gets included, regardless of whether that production is owned by a local company or a foreign entity.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Formula: GDP at market prices by the expenditure method
cards.back: GDPMP = C + I + G + X − M
cards.quote: GDPMP = C + I + G + X − M
cards.note: C consumption, I investment, G government expenditure, X exports, M imports.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Market prices vs factor cost: whose price is each?
cards.back: Market prices are the prices as paid by the consumers Market prices also include product taxes and subsides. The term factor cost refers to the prices of products as received by the producers.
cards.quote: Market prices are the prices as paid by the consumers Market prices also include product taxes and subsides. The term factor cost refers to the prices of products as received by the producers.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Factor cost is equal to market prices, minus ____.
cards.back: Factor cost is equal to market prices, minus net indirect taxes.
cards.quote: Factor cost is equal to market prices, minus net indirect taxes.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Formula: GDP at factor cost (NIT = net indirect taxes)
cards.back:
GDPFC = GDPMP − NIT
Factor cost is equal to market prices, minus net indirect taxes.
cards.quote: Thus, factor cost is equal to market prices, minus net indirect taxes. GDP at factor cost measures money value of output produced by the firms within the domestic boundaries of a country in a year. GDPFC = GDPMP − NIT
cards.note: NIT is net indirect taxes (indirect taxes less subsidies).

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Formula: NDP at market prices
cards.back: NDPMP = GDPMP − Dep.
cards.quote: NDPMP = GDPMP − Dep.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Formula: Private Income
cards.back: Private Income = Factor income from net domestic product accruing to the private sector + National debt interest + Net factor income from abroad + Current transfers from government + Other net transfers from the rest of the world.
cards.quote: Private Income = Factor income from net domestic product accruing to the private sector + National debt interest + Net factor income from abroad + Current transfers from government + Other net transfers from the rest of the world.

source.section: National Disposable Income and Private Income

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Formula: NDP at factor cost
cards.back: NDPFC = NDPMP - Net Product Taxes - Net Production Taxes
cards.quote: NDPFC = NDPMP - Net Product Taxes - Net Production Taxes

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What does GNP refer to?
cards.back: GNP refers to all the economic output produced by a nation’s normal residents, whether they are located within the national boundary or abroad.
cards.quote: GNP refers to all the economic output produced by a nation’s normal residents, whether they are located within the national boundary or abroad.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Formula: GNP at market prices
cards.back: GNPMP = GDPMP + NFIA
cards.quote: GNPMP = GDPMP + NFIA

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Formula: GNP at factor cost
cards.back: GNPFC = GNPMP - Net Product Taxes - Net Production Taxes
cards.quote: GNPFC = GNPMP - Net Product Taxes - Net Production Taxes

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Formula: NNP at market prices (from GNP)
cards.back: NNPMP = GNPMP − Depreciation
cards.quote: NNPMP = GNPMP − Depreciation

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Formula: NNP at market prices (from NDP)
cards.back: NNPMP = NDPMP + NFIA
cards.quote: NNPMP = NDPMP + NFIA

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Formula: GVA at basic prices (from GVA at market prices)
cards.back: GVAMP - Net Product Taxes
cards.quote: GVAMP - Net Product Taxes

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Formula: GVA at factor cost (from GVA at basic prices)
cards.back: GVA at basic prices - Net Production Taxes
cards.quote: GVA at basic prices - Net Production Taxes

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is real GDP?
cards.back: Real GDP is calculated in a way such that the goods and services are evaluated at some constant set of prices (or constant prices).
cards.quote: Real GDP is calculated in a way such that the goods and services are evaluated at some constant set of prices (or constant prices).

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is nominal GDP?
cards.back: Nominal GDP, on the other hand, is simply the value of GDP at the current prevailing prices.
cards.quote: Nominal GDP, on the other hand, is simply the value of GDP at the current prevailing prices.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is the base year in calculating real GDP?
cards.back: The base year (the year whose prices are being used to calculate the real GDP)
cards.quote: the base year (the year whose prices are being used to calculate the real GDP)

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is the GDP deflator?
cards.back: The ratio of nominal to real GDP is a well known index of prices. This is called GDP Deflator.
cards.quote: The ratio of nominal to real GDP is a well known index of prices. This is called GDP Deflator.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Formula: GDP deflator (GDP = nominal GDP, gdp = real GDP)
cards.back: Thus if GDP stands for nominal GDP and gdp stands for real GDP then, GDP deflator = GDP/gdp
cards.quote: Thus if GDP stands for nominal GDP and gdp stands for real GDP then, GDP deflator = GDP/gdp

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: GDP and welfare, reason 1: distribution of GDP
cards.back: Distribution of GDP – how uniform is it: If the GDP of the country is rising, the welfare may not rise as a consequence. This is because the rise in GDP may be concentrated in the hands of very few individuals or firms.
cards.quote: Distribution of GDP – how uniform is it: If the GDP of the country is rising, the welfare may not rise as a consequence. This is because the rise in GDP may be concentrated in the hands of very few individuals or firms.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: GDP rises from Rs 1,000 to Rs 1,010 yet 90% of people earn less. Is GDP a good welfare index?
cards.back: 90 per cent of the people are worse off though the GDP of the country has gone up. If we relate welfare improvement in the country to the percentage of people who are better off, then surely GDP is not a good index.
cards.quote: 90 per cent of the people are worse off though the GDP of the country has gone up. If we relate welfare improvement in the country to the percentage of people who are better off, then surely GDP is not a good index.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: GDP and welfare, reason 2: non-monetary exchanges
cards.back: Many activities in an economy are not evaluated in monetary terms. For example, the domestic services women perform at home are not paid for.
cards.quote: Many activities in an economy are not evaluated in monetary terms. For example, the domestic services women perform at home are not paid for.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Define externalities.
cards.back: Externalities refer to the benefits (or harms) a firm or an individual causes to another for which they are not paid (or penalised).
cards.quote: Externalities refer to the benefits (or harms) a firm or an individual causes to another for which they are not paid (or penalised).

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: If GDP is used as a welfare measure, what does a negative or a positive externality do to it?
cards.back: Therefore, if we take GDP as a measure of welfare of the economy we shall be overestimating the actual welfare. This was an example of negative externality. There can be cases of positive externalities as well. In such cases, GDP will underestimate the actual welfare of the economy.
cards.quote: Therefore, if we take GDP as a measure of welfare of the economy we shall be overestimating the actual welfare. This was an example of negative externality. There can be cases of positive externalities as well. In such cases, GDP will underestimate the actual welfare of the economy.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Name the three methods of calculating national income (aggregate value of goods and services).
cards.back:
measuring the aggregate value of factor payments (income method)
measuring the aggregate value of goods and services produced by the firms (product method)
measuring the aggregate value of spending received by the firms (expenditure method)
cards.quote: (a) measuring the aggregate value of factor payments (income method) (b) measuring the aggregate value of goods and services produced by the firms (product method) (c) measuring the aggregate value of spending received by the firms (expenditure method)

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: In the product method, to avoid ____, we need to deduct the value of intermediate goods
cards.back: In the product method, to avoid double counting, we need to deduct the value of intermediate goods
cards.quote: In the product method, to avoid double counting, we need to deduct the value of intermediate goods

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is production?
cards.back: Production is the process by which inputs are transformed into ‘output’.
cards.quote: Production is the process by which inputs are transformed into ‘output’.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: In order to acquire inputs a firm has to pay for them. This is called the ____.
cards.back: cost of production. In order to acquire inputs a firm has to pay for them. This is called the cost of production.
cards.quote: In order to acquire inputs a firm has to pay for them. This is called the cost of production.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is a firm's profit?
cards.back: The difference between the revenue and cost is called the firm's profit.
cards.quote: The difference between the revenue and cost is called the firm's profit.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: We assume that the objective of a firm is to earn the ____ that it can.
cards.back: We assume that the objective of a firm is to earn the maximum profit that it can.
cards.quote: We assume that the objective of a firm is to earn the maximum profit that it can.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Define the production function of a firm.
cards.back: The production function of a firm is a relationship between inputs used and output produced by the firm. For various quantities of inputs used, it gives the maximum quantity of output that can be produced.
cards.quote: The production function of a firm is a relationship between inputs used and output produced by the firm. For various quantities of inputs used, it gives the maximum quantity of output that can be produced.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What does a production function deal with, as it takes the maximum output for any level of inputs?
cards.back:
Only the efficient use of inputs.
Since by definition we are taking the maximum output for any level of inputs, a production function deals only with the efficient use of inputs.
cards.quote: Since by definition we are taking the maximum output for any level of inputs, a production function deals only with the efficient use of inputs.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: ____ implies that it is not possible to get any more output from the same level of inputs.
cards.back: Efficiency implies that it is not possible to get any more output from the same level of inputs.
cards.quote: Efficiency implies that it is not possible to get any more output from the same level of inputs.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: A production function is defined for a given ____.
cards.back: A production function is defined for a given technology.
cards.quote: A production function is defined for a given technology.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Define total revenue (TR) of a firm.
cards.back: total revenue (TR) of the firm is defined as the market price of the good (p) multiplied by the firm's output (q).
cards.quote: total revenue (TR) of the firm is defined as the market price of the good (p) multiplied by the firm's output (q).

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: If the technology improves, the maximum levels of output obtainable for different input combinations increase. We then have a ____.
cards.back: If the technology improves, the maximum levels of output obtainable for different input combinations increase. We then have a new production function.
cards.quote: If the technology improves, the maximum levels of output obtainable for different input combinations increase. We then have a new production function.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What are factors of production?
cards.back: The inputs that a firm uses in the production process are called factors of production.
cards.quote: The inputs that a firm uses in the production process are called factors of production.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Formula: total revenue (TR) of a firm.
cards.back:
TR = p × q
Let q be the quantity of the good produced, and therefore sold, by the firm at price p.
cards.quote: Let q be the quantity of the good produced, and therefore sold, by the firm at price p. Then, total revenue (TR) of the firm is defined as the market price of the good (p) multiplied by the firm's output (q). Hence, TR = p × q

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Why is the TR curve of a price-taking firm (TR = p × q) a straight line?
cards.back: the equation ‘TR = p × q’ is that of a straight line because p is constant.
cards.quote: Moreover, the equation ‘TR = p × q’ is that of a straight line because p is constant.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Formula: the production function with labour (L) and capital (K)
cards.back:
q = f(L,K)
where, L is labour and K is capital and q is the maximum output that can be produced.
cards.quote: We may write the production function as q = f(L,K) (3.1) where, L is labour and K is capital and q is the maximum output that can be produced.
cards.note: q = maximum output that can be produced; L = labour; K = capital.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Define the short run.
cards.back: In the short run, at least one of the factor – labour or capital – cannot be varied, and therefore, remains fixed.
cards.quote: In the short run, at least one of the factor – labour or capital – cannot be varied, and therefore, remains fixed.

source.section: 3.2 The Short Run and the Long Run

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is the slope of a price-taking firm's total revenue curve?
cards.back: Therefore, the slope of the straight line is Aq1/Oq1 = p.
cards.quote: Therefore, the slope of the straight line is Aq1/Oq1 = p.
cards.note: The slope of the TR curve equals the market price.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Define average revenue (AR) of a firm.
cards.back: The average revenue (AR) of a firm is defined as total revenue per unit of output.
cards.quote: The average revenue (AR) of a firm is defined as total revenue per unit of output.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What are the fixed factor and the variable factor?
cards.back: The factor that remains fixed is called the fixed factor whereas the other factor which the firm can vary is called the variable factor.
cards.quote: The factor that remains fixed is called the fixed factor whereas the other factor which the firm can vary is called the variable factor.

source.section: 3.2 The Short Run and the Long Run

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Define the long run.
cards.back: In the long run, all factors of production can be varied. A firm in order to produce different levels of output in the long run may vary both the inputs simultaneously. So, in the long run, there is no fixed factor.
cards.quote: In the long run, all factors of production can be varied. A firm in order to produce different levels of output in the long run may vary both the inputs simultaneously. So, in the long run, there is no fixed factor.

source.section: 3.2 The Short Run and the Long Run

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: We define a period as long run or short run simply by looking at ____ or not.
cards.back: We define a period as long run or short run simply by looking at whether all the inputs can be varied or not.
cards.quote: We define a period as long run or short run simply by looking at whether all the inputs can be varied or not.
blanks: whether all the inputs can be varied

source.section: 3.2 The Short Run and the Long Run

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Define marginal revenue (MR) of a firm.
cards.back: The marginal revenue (MR) of a firm is defined as the increase in total revenue for a unit increase in the firm's output.
cards.quote: The marginal revenue (MR) of a firm is defined as the increase in total revenue for a unit increase in the firm's output.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is Total Product (TP) of a variable input?
cards.back: Suppose we vary a single input and keep all other inputs constant. Then for different levels of that input, we get different levels of output. This relationship between the variable input and output, keeping all other inputs constant, is often referred to as Total Product (TP) of the variable input.
cards.quote: Suppose we vary a single input and keep all other inputs constant. Then for different levels of that input, we get different levels of output. This relationship between the variable input and output, keeping all other inputs constant, is often referred to as Total Product (TP) of the variable input.

source.section: 3.3 Total Product, Average Product and Marginal Product

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Define average product.
cards.back: Average product is defined as the output per unit of variable input.
cards.quote: Average product is defined as the output per unit of variable input.

source.section: 3.3 Total Product, Average Product and Marginal Product

cards.note: APL = TPL / L (average product of labour = total product of labour divided by labour).

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Formula: MR of a price-taking firm when output changes from q1 to q2.
cards.quote: Consider the situation when the firm's output changes from q1 to q2. Given the market price p, MR = (pq2 –pq1)/ (q2 –q1) = [p (q2 –q1)]/ (q2 –q1) =p

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Under perfect competition, how are MR, AR and market price (p) related?
cards.back: Thus, for the perfectly competitive firm, MR=AR=p
cards.quote: Thus, for the perfectly competitive firm, MR=AR=p

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Formula: average product of labour (APL)
cards.back: APL = TPL / L
cards.quote: APL = TPL / L

source.section: 3.3 Total Product, Average Product and Marginal Product

cards.note: TPL is total product of labour; L is the units of labour.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Define marginal product of an input.
cards.back: Marginal product of an input is defined as the change in output per unit of change in the input when all other inputs are held constant.
cards.quote: Marginal product of an input is defined as the change in output per unit of change in the input when all other inputs are held constant.

source.section: 3.3 Total Product, Average Product and Marginal Product

cards.note: MPL = change in TPL divided by change in L.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Formula: marginal product of the Lth unit of labour (MPL)
cards.back: MPL= (TP at L units) – (TP at L – 1 unit)
cards.quote: MPL= (TP at L units) – (TP at L – 1 unit)

source.section: 3.3 Total Product, Average Product and Marginal Product

cards.note: MP of the Lth unit = TP at L units minus TP at (L - 1) units.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: How do profits behave when MR is greater than MC, and when MR is less than MC?
cards.back: as long as marginal revenue is greater than marginal cost, profits are increasing. By the same logic, as long as marginal revenue is less than marginal cost, profits will fall.
cards.quote: as long as marginal revenue is greater than marginal cost, profits are increasing. By the same logic, as long as marginal revenue is less than marginal cost, profits will fall.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: For any level of an input, the sum of marginal products of every preceeding unit of that input gives the ____.
cards.back: For any level of an input, the sum of marginal products of every preceeding unit of that input gives the total product.
cards.quote: For any level of an input, the sum of marginal products of every preceeding unit of that input gives the total product.

source.section: 3.3 Total Product, Average Product and Marginal Product

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Formula: the level of output at which profits are maximum.
cards.back:
MR = MC
profits are maximum at the level of output (which we have called q0)
cards.quote: profits are maximum at the level of output (which we have called q0) for which MR = MC

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Average product of an input at any level of employment is the average of all ____ up to that level.
cards.back: Average product of an input at any level of employment is the average of all marginal products up to that level.
cards.quote: Average product of an input at any level of employment is the average of all marginal products up to that level.

source.section: 3.3 Total Product, Average Product and Marginal Product

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: For a price-taking firm, what condition defines the profit maximizing level of output?
cards.back: the firm's profit maximizing output becomes the level of output at which P=MC.
cards.quote: So the firm's profit maximizing output becomes the level of output at which P=MC.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Average and marginal products are often referred to as average and marginal ____, respectively, to the variable input.
cards.back: Average and marginal products are often referred to as average and marginal returns, respectively, to the variable input.
cards.quote: Average and marginal products are often referred to as average and marginal returns, respectively, to the variable input.

source.section: 3.3 Total Product, Average Product and Marginal Product

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: State the law of variable proportions.
cards.back: Law of variable proportions say that the marginal product of a factor input initially rises with its employment level. But after reaching a certain level of employment, it starts falling.
cards.quote: Law of variable proportions say that the marginal product of a factor input initially rises with its employment level. But after reaching a certain level of employment, it starts falling.

source.section: 3.4 The Law of Diminishing Marginal Product and the Law of Variable Proportions

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What is the law of variable proportions also called?
cards.back:
The law of diminishing marginal product.
This tendency of the MP to first increase and then fall is called the law of variable proportions or the law of diminishing marginal product.
cards.quote: This tendency of the MP to first increase and then fall is called the law of variable proportions or the law of diminishing marginal product.

source.section: 3.4 The Law of Diminishing Marginal Product and the Law of Variable Proportions

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What are factor proportions?
cards.back: Factor proportions represent the ratio in which the two inputs are combined to produce output.
cards.quote: Factor proportions represent the ratio in which the two inputs are combined to produce output.

source.section: 3.4 The Law of Diminishing Marginal Product and the Law of Variable Proportions

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: The MP curve therefore, looks like an ____ ‘U’-shaped curve as in figure 3.2.
cards.back: The MP curve therefore, looks like an inverse ‘U’-shaped curve as in figure 3.2.
cards.quote: The MP curve therefore, looks like an inverse ‘U’-shaped curve as in figure 3.2.

source.section: 3.5 Shapes of Total Product, Marginal Product and Average Product Curves

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Similarly, when AP falls, MP has to be ____ than AP.
cards.back: Similarly, when AP falls, MP has to be less than AP.
cards.quote: Similarly, when AP falls, MP has to be less than AP.

source.section: 3.5 Shapes of Total Product, Marginal Product and Average Product Curves

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: When does a production function display Constant Returns to Scale (CRS)?
cards.back: When a proportional increase in all inputs results in an increase in output by the same proportion, the production function is said to display Constant returns to scale (CRS).
cards.quote: When a proportional increase in all inputs results in an increase in output by the same proportion, the production function is said to display Constant returns to scale (CRS).

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: When does a production function display Increasing Returns to Scale (IRS)?
cards.back: When a proportional increase in all inputs results in an increase in output by a larger proportion, the production function is said to display Increasing Returns to Scale (IRS)
cards.quote: When a proportional increase in all inputs results in an increase in output by a larger proportion, the production function is said to display Increasing Returns to Scale (IRS)

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: When does Decreasing Returns to Scale (DRS) hold?
cards.back: Decreasing Returns to Scale (DRS) holds when a proportional increase in all inputs results in an increase in output by a smaller proportion.
cards.quote: Decreasing Returns to Scale (DRS) holds when a proportional increase in all inputs results in an increase in output by a smaller proportion.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Formula: constant returns to scale when both inputs x1, x2 are increased t (t > 1) times.
cards.back:
f (tx1 , tx2 ) = t.f (x1 , x2 )
the new output level f (tx1 , tx2 ) is exactly t times the previous output level f (x1 , x2 ).
cards.quote: can say that the production function exhibits constant returns to scale if we have, f (tx1 , tx2 ) = t.f (x1 , x2 ) ie the new output level f (tx1 , tx2 ) is exactly t times the previous output level f (x1 , x2 ).
cards.note: q = f (x1, x2) is output from x1 units of factor 1 and x2 units of factor 2; t (t > 1) is the factor by which both inputs are scaled up.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Define opportunity cost.
cards.back: Opportunity cost of some activity is the gain foregone from the second best activity.
cards.quote: Opportunity cost of some activity is the gain foregone from the second best activity.

source.section: 4.4.4 The Normal Profit and Break-even Point

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Formula: increasing and decreasing returns to scale when both inputs are increased t (t > 1) times.
cards.back:
the production function exhibits increasing returns to scale if, f (tx1 , tx2 ) > t.f (x1 , x2 ).
It exhibits decreasing returns to scale if, f (tx1 , tx2 ) < t.f (x1 , x2 ).
cards.quote: Similarly, the production function exhibits increasing returns to scale if, f (tx1 , tx2 ) > t.f (x1 , x2 ). It exhibits decreasing returns to scale if, f (tx1 , tx2 ) < t.f (x1 , x2 ).
cards.note: Here q = f (x1, x2) and both inputs x1, x2 are scaled up t (t > 1) times.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What does the cost function describe?
cards.back: Thus the cost function describes the least cost of producing each level of output given prices of factors of production and technology.
cards.quote: Thus the cost function describes the least cost of producing each level of output given prices of factors of production and technology.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Rs 1,000: house-safe pays 0, bank-1 pays 10 per cent, bank-2 5 per cent. Opportunity cost of investing it in the family business?
cards.back: The opportunity cost of investing the money in your family business is therefore the amount of forgone interest from the bank-1.
cards.quote: The opportunity cost of investing the money in your family business is therefore the amount of forgone interest from the bank-1.

source.section: 4.4.4 The Normal Profit and Break-even Point

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Define total fixed cost (TFC).
cards.back: The cost that a firm incurs to employ these fixed inputs is called the total fixed cost (TFC).
cards.quote: The cost that a firm incurs to employ these fixed inputs is called the total fixed cost (TFC).
cards.note: Fixed inputs are the factors that cannot be varied in the short run.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Define total variable cost (TVC).
cards.back: To produce any required level of output, the firm, in the short run, can adjust only variable inputs. Accordingly, the cost that a firm incurs to employ these variable inputs is called the total variable cost (TVC).
cards.quote: To produce any required level of output, the firm, in the short run, can adjust only variable inputs. Accordingly, the cost that a firm incurs to employ these variable inputs is called the total variable cost (TVC).

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Formula: total cost (TC) of a firm
cards.back: Adding the fixed and the variable costs, we get the total cost (TC) of a firm TC = TVC + TFC
cards.quote: Adding the fixed and the variable costs, we get the total cost (TC) of a firm TC = TVC + TFC
cards.note: TC = TVC + TFC.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Define short run average cost (SAC).
cards.back: The short run average cost (SAC) incurred by the firm is defined as the total cost per unit of output.
cards.quote: The short run average cost (SAC) incurred by the firm is defined as the total cost per unit of output.
cards.note: SAC = TC / q.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Define average variable cost (AVC).
cards.back: Similarly, the average variable cost (AVC) is defined as the total variable cost per unit of output.
cards.quote: Similarly, the average variable cost (AVC) is defined as the total variable cost per unit of output.
cards.note: AVC = TVC / q.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Formula: short run average cost (SAC) in terms of AVC and AFC
cards.back: SAC = AVC + AFC
cards.quote: SAC = AVC + AFC
cards.note: Short run average cost is the sum of average variable cost and average fixed cost.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Define short run marginal cost (SMC).
cards.back: The short run marginal cost (SMC) is defined as the change in total cost per unit of change in output
cards.quote: The short run marginal cost (SMC) is defined as the change in total cost per unit of change in output
cards.note: SMC = change in TC / change in q.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: When we change the level of output, whatever change occurs to total cost is entirely due to the change in total ____ cost.
cards.back: When we change the level of output, whatever change occurs to total cost is entirely due to the change in total variable cost.
cards.quote: When we change the level of output, whatever change occurs to total cost is entirely due to the change in total variable cost.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: For any level of output, the sum of marginal costs up to that level gives us the ____ at that level.
cards.back: For any level of output, the sum of marginal costs up to that level gives us the total variable cost at that level.
cards.quote: For any level of output, the sum of marginal costs up to that level gives us the total variable cost at that level.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: How is average fixed cost (AFC) found?
cards.back: AFC is the ratio of TFC to q.
cards.quote: AFC is the ratio of TFC to q.
cards.note: AFC = TFC / q, where q is output.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Total fixed cost, however, is ____ of the amount of output produced and remains constant for all levels of production.
cards.back: Total fixed cost, however, is independent of the amount of output produced and remains constant for all levels of production.
cards.quote: Total fixed cost, however, is independent of the amount of output produced and remains constant for all levels of production.

source.section: Shapes of the Short Run Cost Curves

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What does the total fixed cost (TFC) curve look like?
cards.back: It is, therefore, a horizontal straight line cutting the cost axis at the point c1.
cards.quote: It is, therefore, a horizontal straight line cutting the cost axis at the point c1.

source.section: Shapes of the Short Run Cost Curves

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: TFC is a constant. Therefore, as q increases, AFC ____.
cards.back: TFC is a constant. Therefore, as q increases, AFC decreases.
cards.quote: TFC is a constant. Therefore, as q increases, AFC decreases.

source.section: Shapes of the Short Run Cost Curves

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: AFC curve is, in fact, a ____.
cards.back: AFC curve is, in fact, a rectangular hyperbola.
cards.quote: AFC curve is, in fact, a rectangular hyperbola.

source.section: Shapes of the Short Run Cost Curves

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: What do we always get when we multiply any output q by its corresponding AFC?
cards.back: If we multiply any value q of output with its corresponding AFC, we always get a constant, namely TFC.
cards.quote: If we multiply any value q of output with its corresponding AFC, we always get a constant, namely TFC.

source.section: Shapes of the Short Run Cost Curves

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Formula: total fixed cost (TFC) from average fixed cost (AFC)
cards.back: TFC = AFC × quantity
cards.quote: TFC = AFC × quantity

source.section: Shapes of the Short Run Cost Curves

cards.note: On the AFC curve TFC is the area of the rectangle under the curve at that output.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Where do the SMC and AVC curves start from?
cards.back:
They start from the same point.
For the first unit of output, it is easy to check that SMC and AVC are the same. So both SMC and AVC curves start from the same point.
cards.quote: For the first unit of output, it is easy to check that SMC and AVC are the same. So both SMC and AVC curves start from the same point.

source.section: Shapes of the Short Run Cost Curves

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: The TVC at a particular level of output is given by the ____ up to that level.
cards.back: The TVC at a particular level of output is given by the area under the SMC curve up to that level.
cards.quote: The TVC at a particular level of output is given by the area under the SMC curve up to that level.

source.section: Shapes of the Short Run Cost Curves

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: As long as AVC is falling, SMC must be ____ than the AVC. As AVC rises, SMC must be ____ than the AVC.
cards.back: As long as AVC is falling, SMC must be less than the AVC. As AVC rises, SMC must be greater than the AVC.
cards.quote: As long as AVC is falling, SMC must be less than the AVC. As AVC rises, SMC must be greater than the AVC.

source.section: Shapes of the Short Run Cost Curves

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: For a price-taking firm, how is average revenue related to market price?
cards.back: For a price-taking firm, average revenue is equal to market price.
cards.quote: For a price-taking firm, average revenue is equal to market price.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Formula: total variable cost (TVC) from average variable cost (AVC)
cards.back: TVC = AVC × quantity
cards.quote: TVC = AVC × quantity

source.section: Shapes of the Short Run Cost Curves

cards.note: On the AVC curve TVC is the area of the rectangle under the curve at that output.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: How does SAC behave while the fall in AFC exceeds the rise in AVC, and after the rise in AVC becomes larger?
cards.back: Initially the fall in AFC is greater than the rise in AVC and SAC is still falling. But, after a certain level of production, rise in AVC becomes larger than the fall in AFC. From this point onwards, SAC is rising.
cards.quote: Initially the fall in AFC is greater than the rise in AVC and SAC is still falling. But, after a certain level of production, rise in AVC becomes larger than the fall in AFC. From this point onwards, SAC is rising.

source.section: Shapes of the Short Run Cost Curves

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: For a price-taking firm, how is marginal revenue related to market price?
cards.back: For a price-taking firm, marginal revenue is equal to market price.
cards.quote: For a price-taking firm, marginal revenue is equal to market price.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: The minimum point of SAC curve lies to the ____ of the minimum point of AVC curve.
cards.back: The minimum point of SAC curve lies to the right of the minimum point of AVC curve.
cards.quote: The minimum point of SAC curve lies to the right of the minimum point of AVC curve.

source.section: Shapes of the Short Run Cost Curves

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: As long as SAC is falling, SMC is ____ than the SAC. When SAC is rising, SMC is ____ than the SAC.
cards.back: As long as SAC is falling, SMC is less than the SAC. When SAC is rising, SMC is greater than the SAC.
cards.quote: As long as SAC is falling, SMC is less than the SAC. When SAC is rising, SMC is greater than the SAC.

source.section: Shapes of the Short Run Cost Curves

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Both the marginal product and the average product curves are ____ ‘U’-shaped.
cards.back: Both the marginal product and the average product curves are inverse ‘U’-shaped.
cards.quote: Both the marginal product and the average product curves are inverse ‘U’-shaped.

source.section: 3.5 Shapes of Total Product, Marginal Product and Average Product Curves

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: The marginal product curve cuts the average product curve from above at the ____ point of average product curve.
cards.back: The marginal product curve cuts the average product curve from above at the maximum point of average product curve.
cards.quote: The marginal product curve cuts the average product curve from above at the maximum point of average product curve.

source.section: 3.5 Shapes of Total Product, Marginal Product and Average Product Curves

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: Short run marginal cost, average variable cost and short run average cost curves are ____.
cards.back: Short run marginal cost, average variable cost and short run average cost curves are ‘U’-shaped.
cards.quote: Short run marginal cost, average variable cost and short run average cost curves are ‘U’-shaped.

source.section: Shapes of the Short Run Cost Curves

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: SMC curve cuts the AVC curve from below at the ____ point of AVC.
cards.back: SMC curve cuts the AVC curve from below at the minimum point of AVC.
cards.quote: SMC curve cuts the AVC curve from below at the minimum point of AVC.

source.section: Shapes of the Short Run Cost Curves

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: SMC curve cuts the SAC curve from below at the ____ point of SAC.
cards.back: SMC curve cuts the SAC curve from below at the minimum point of SAC.
cards.quote: SMC curve cuts the SAC curve from below at the minimum point of SAC.

source.section: Shapes of the Short Run Cost Curves

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: For different combinations of inputs, the production function shows the ____ quantity of output that can be produced.
cards.back: For different combinations of inputs, the production function shows the maximum quantity of output that can be produced.
cards.quote: For different combinations of inputs, the production function shows the maximum quantity of output that can be produced.

cards.subject: economics
cards.front: In the short run, some inputs cannot be varied. In the ____, all inputs can be varied.
cards.back: In the short run, some inputs cannot be varied. In the long run, all inputs can be varied.
cards.quote: In the short run, some inputs cannot be varied. In the long run, all inputs can be varied.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: ____ once said that the real progress of India did not mean simply the growth and expansion of industrial urban centres but mainly the ____.
cards.back: Mahatma Gandhi once said that the real progress of India did not mean simply the growth and expansion of industrial urban centres but mainly the development of the villages.
cards.quote: Mahatma Gandhi once said that the real progress of India did not mean simply the growth and expansion of industrial urban centres but mainly the development of the villages.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: What is rural development?
cards.back: Rural development is a comprehensive term. It essentially focuses on action for the development of areas that are lagging behind in the overall development of the village economy.
cards.quote: Rural development is a comprehensive term. It essentially focuses on action for the development of areas that are lagging behind in the overall development of the village economy.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: Name the areas that need fresh initiatives for rural development in India.
cards.back:
Development of human resources
Land reforms
Development of the productive resources of each locality
Infrastructure development
Special measures for alleviation of poverty
cards.quote: Development of human resources including – literacy, more specifically, female literacy, education and skill development – health, addressing both sanitation and public health – Land reforms – Development of the productive resources of each locality – Infrastructure development like electricity, irrigation, credit, marketing, transport facilities including construction of village roads and feeder roads to nearby highways, facilities for agriculture research and extension, and information dissemination – Special measures for alleviation of poverty and bringing about significant improvement in the living conditions of the weaker sections of the population emphasising access to productive employment opportunities

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: Development of human resources in rural India includes which two areas?
cards.back:
literacy, more specifically, female literacy, education and skill development
health, addressing both sanitation and public health
cards.quote: Development of human resources including – literacy, more specifically, female literacy, education and skill development – health, addressing both sanitation and public health

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: Name the infrastructure whose development rural India needs.
cards.back:
electricity
irrigation
credit
marketing
transport facilities including construction of village roads and feeder roads to nearby highways
facilities for agriculture research and extension
information dissemination
cards.quote: Infrastructure development like electricity, irrigation, credit, marketing, transport facilities including construction of village roads and feeder roads to nearby highways, facilities for agriculture research and extension, and information dissemination

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: What do scholars identify as the major reason for agriculture's growth slowdown after the 1991 reforms (NCERT 5.2)?
cards.back: Scholars identify decline in public investment since 1991 as the major reason for this.
cards.quote: Scholars identify decline in public investment since 1991 as the major reason for this.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: Besides falling public investment since 1991, which factors further impede rural development (scholars' view)?
cards.back:
inadequate infrastructure
lack of alternate employment opportunities in the industry or service sector
increasing casualisation of employment
cards.quote: inadequate infrastructure, lack of alternate employment opportunities in the industry or service sector, increasing casualisation of employment etc., further impede rural development.

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: Growth of rural economy depends primarily on ____, from time to time, to realise higher productivity in agriculture and non-agriculture sectors.
cards.back: Growth of rural economy depends primarily on infusion of capital, from time to time, to realise higher productivity in agriculture and non-agriculture sectors.
cards.quote: Growth of rural economy depends primarily on infusion of capital, from time to time, to realise higher productivity in agriculture and non-agriculture sectors.

source.section: 5.3 Credit and Marketing in Rural Areas

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: At the time of independence, ____ exploited small and marginal farmers and landless labourers by lending to them on high interest rates
cards.back: At the time of independence, moneylenders and traders exploited small and marginal farmers and landless labourers by lending to them on high interest rates
cards.quote: At the time of independence, moneylenders and traders exploited small and marginal farmers and landless labourers by lending to them on high interest rates

source.section: 5.3 Credit and Marketing in Rural Areas

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: What major change in rural credit occurred after 1969?
cards.back: A major change occurred after 1969 when India adopted social banking and multiagency approach to adequately meet the needs of rural credit.
cards.quote: A major change occurred after 1969 when India adopted social banking and multiagency approach to adequately meet the needs of rural credit.

source.section: 5.3 Credit and Marketing in Rural Areas

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: What is NABARD, and when was it set up?
cards.back: National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development (NABARD) was set up in 1982 as an apex body to coordinate the activities of all institutions involved in the rural financing system.
cards.quote: National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development (NABARD) was set up in 1982 as an apex body to coordinate the activities of all institutions involved in the rural financing system.

source.section: 5.3 Credit and Marketing in Rural Areas

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: Types: institutions in today's multi-agency structure of rural banking.
cards.back:
commercial banks
regional rural banks (RRBs)
cooperatives
land development banks
cards.quote: The institutional structure of rural banking today consists of a set of multi-agency institutions, namely, commercial banks, regional rural banks (RRBs), cooperatives and land development banks.

source.section: 5.3 Credit and Marketing in Rural Areas

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: Why have Self-Help Groups (SHGs) emerged in rural credit?
cards.back: Recently, Self-Help Groups (henceforth SHGs) have emerged to fill the gap in the formal credit system because the formal credit delivery mechanism has not only proven inadequate but has also not been fully integrated into the overall rural social and community development.
cards.quote: Recently, Self-Help Groups (henceforth SHGs) have emerged to fill the gap in the formal credit system because the formal credit delivery mechanism has not only proven inadequate but has also not been fully integrated into the overall rural social and community development.

source.section: 5.3 Credit and Marketing in Rural Areas

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: Since some kind of ____ is required, vast proportion of poor rural households were automatically out of the credit network.
cards.back: Since some kind of collateral is required, vast proportion of poor rural households were automatically out of the credit network.
cards.quote: Since some kind of collateral is required, vast proportion of poor rural households were automatically out of the credit network.

source.section: 5.3 Credit and Marketing in Rural Areas

cards.subject: economics
cards.unit: Current Challenges facing the Indian Economy
cards.front: How does a Self-Help Group (SHG) work?
cards.back: The SHGs promote thrift in small proportions by a minimum contribution from each member. From the pooled money, credit is given to the needy members to be repayable in small instalments at reasonable interest rates.
